papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: The Core, Conditional, and Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of compression pipelines and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis, or multi-teacher ensembles), KD routinely delivers large reductions in latency and memory while preserving most teacher performance. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy; KD is therefore best used as a first-line, integrated tool rather than a standalone cure.

papers_seen.author: Wells
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving protocols, and online/co-distillation schemes—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest accuracy loss when applied with task-aware design. Effective use of KD typically combines careful selection of what to transfer, attention to teacher–student capacity and data regimes, and integration with complementary compression mechanisms such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfection and bias transfer, data scarcity and domain shift, capacity and optimization mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and model size while often preserving most of the original performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline—choosing appropriate transfer targets, adapting objectives to student capacity and data regimes, and combining distillation with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher imperfections (including bias), data scarcity or privacy constraints, and difficulty preserving rare or structured behaviors require targeted mitigations, careful evaluation, and continued methodological and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Mason
papers_seen.title: Learning Student Networks via Feature Embedding
papers_seen.abstract: Deep convolutional neural networks have been widely used in numerous applications, but their demanding storage and computational resource requirements prevent their applications on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation aims to optimize a portable student network by taking the knowledge from a well-trained heavy teacher network. Traditional teacher-student based methods used to rely on additional fully-connected layers to bridge intermediate layers of teacher and student networks, which brings in a large number of auxiliary parameters. In contrast, this paper aims to propagate information from teacher to student without introducing new variables which need to be optimized. We regard the teacher-student paradigm from a new perspective of feature embedding. By introducing the locality preserving loss, the student network is encouraged to generate the low-dimensional features which could inherit intrinsic properties of their corresponding high-dimensional features from teacher network. The resulting portable network thus can naturally maintain the performance as that of the teacher network. Theoretical analysis is provided to justify the lower computation complexity of the proposed method. Experiments on benchmark datasets and well-trained networks suggest that the proposed algorithm is superior to state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods in terms of computational and storage complexity.

papers_seen.author: Chandler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller students by transferring predictive behavior, internal representations, or relational structure. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal domains, KD enables substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving much of teacher performance; it is most effective when combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation, and hardware-aware design). The literature also highlights several persistent challenges — teacher and capacity mismatch, optimization and data limitations, privacy and distribution shift — and converges on practical strategies such as careful choice of distillation signals, layer alignment, multi-teacher or online protocols, and synthetic-data or data-free approaches to operate under constrained access to original training data.

papers_seen.author: Collins
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact student models. A rich design space—what information to transfer (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive signals), how to schedule training (offline, online, progressive, or data-free), and how to combine KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search—makes KD applicable across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under compute, memory, and privacy constraints, but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (or synthesis), and explicit attention to robustness, bias, and distribution shift. Best results treat KD as an adaptable toolkit that must be tailored to task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Guerrero
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative, and federated settings, KD has been applied to reduce latency and memory, enable on-device or privacy-sensitive deployment, and in some cases improve robustness or calibration. The field offers a broad toolkit—logit-level supervision, intermediate-feature/attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, data-free or generator-assisted distillation, and ensembles or self-distillation—that practitioners combine with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical success is widespread but conditional: outcomes depend on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the availability and nature of distillation data, and task-aware choices about what and how to transfer. Persistent challenges include teacher–student mismatch, optimization gaps, distributional shift, preservation of low-frequency behaviors, and privacy/fairness trade-offs. Current research directions emphasize joint optimization of compression primitives, federated and cross‑modal distillation, improved data-free protocols, and automated teacher–student matching.

papers_seen.author: Dunn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically grounded approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. By transferring predictive behavior or internal representations, KD enables substantial reductions in latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance. Its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; when combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training, KD forms an essential, configurable component of modern compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Liu
papers_seen.title: Enabling Multimodal Generation on CLIP via Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The recent large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) of dual-stream architectures (e.g., CLIP) with a tremendous amount of image-text pair data, has shown its superiority on various multimodal alignment tasks. Despite its success, the resulting models are not capable of multimodal generative tasks due to the weak text encoder. To tackle this problem, we propose to augment the dual-stream VLP model with a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) via vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), enabling the capability for multimodal generation. VLKD is pretty data- and computation-efficient compared to the pre-training from scratch. Experimental results show that the resulting model has strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks, such as open-ended visual question answering and image captioning. For example, it achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy on the VQAv2 dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model with $7\times$ fewer parameters. Furthermore, the original textual language understanding and generation ability of the PLM is maintained after VLKD, which makes our model versatile for both multimodal and unimodal tasks.

papers_seen.author: Jennings
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Methods range from matching soft logits to aligning internal features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive signals, and they operate across full-data, few-shot, and data-free regimes. KD is most effective when designed as a task- and data-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline that also employs pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context-dependent and limited by teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution shift, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster, or specialized student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad and practical toolbox has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free/zero-shot protocols, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search—that is applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative settings. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when applied carefully, but success depends on student capacity, teacher design/quality, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices; important open problems remain in principled theory, fairness/privacy-aware protocols, heterogeneous and federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Owens
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression and Beyond
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a compression trick; it is a versatile, practically proven framework that enables resource-efficient deployment, privacy-preserving learning, cross-modal and cross-domain transfers, and even improvements in robustness. When combined with complementary techniques — feature mimicking, projector modules, teacher annealing, label-smoothing–style regularization, and data-free or federated protocols — distillation can address the main bottlenecks of modern deep and multilingual models: size, latency, heterogeneity of devices, limited or private data, and domain shift. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in any strategy for compressing or adapting deep models for real-world NLP and vision deployments.

papers_seen.author: Johnson

KD delivers strong empirical gains across modalities when teacher quality, student capacity, distilled signals, and data regimes are aligned; however, known failure modes (teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, propagation of teacher artifacts, and degradation on low‑frequency phenomena) require targeted remedies and validation for deployment.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy

In practice, distillation should be treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that integrates complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), explicit fairness and robustness interventions, and data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers predictive ability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, efficient student models. Across modalities and architectures, KD variants extend beyond matching teacher output probabilities to include internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, adversarial learning, selective sample supervision, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. These methods enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, reduce inference latency, support domain adaptation and federated settings, and in some cases improve student generalization beyond the teacher. Practical challenges include input/representation mismatches between teacher and student, propagation of teacher biases (e.g., low-frequency lexical errors), and the need for careful selection of what is distilled and how. Empirically, tailored distillation objectives and training procedures—such as internal-representation matching, progressive module replacement, ensemble distillation, and contrastive or relational objectives—have produced strong compression results across vision, language, graph-structured data, and generative scene models.

The literature demonstrates both the breadth of KD methods and concrete best practices to maximize effectiveness across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely adopted approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance across modalities, but its success is context-dependent: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data and augmentation choices, and optimization design. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies, and privacy- or domain-aware adaptations—rather than a universal, standalone cure-all. I argue KD should be the default core of model-compression workflows while being explicitly adapted to task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bender
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. A rich set of methods—ranging from logits/soft-target supervision to intermediate-feature matching, contrastive and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware variants—has been developed and is routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and architecture/parameter adaptations). Empirical and conceptual work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, signal choice, data availability or synthesis strategy, and careful integration with other compression tools. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a one-size-fits-all solution.

papers_seen.author: Chavez
papers_seen.title: Data-Free Knowledge Distillation for Deep Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in model compression have provided procedures for compressing large neural networks to a fraction of their original size while retaining most if not all of their accuracy. However, all of these approaches rely on access to the original training set, which might not always be possible if the network to be compressed was trained on a very large dataset, or on a dataset whose release poses privacy or safety concerns as may be the case for biometrics tasks. We present a method for data-free knowledge distillation, which is able to compress deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets to a fraction of their size leveraging only some extra metadata to be provided with a pretrained model release. We also explore different kinds of metadata that can be used with our method, and discuss tradeoffs involved in using each of them.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a strategy of training a student network with guide of the soft output from a teacher network. It has been a successful method of model compression and knowledge transfer. However, currently knowledge distillation lacks a convincing theoretical understanding. On the other hand, recent finding on neural tangent kernel enables us to approximate a wide neural network with a linear model of the network's random features. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the knowledge distillation of a wide neural network. First we provide a transfer risk bound for the linearized model of the network. Then we propose a metric of the task's training difficulty, called data inefficiency. Based on this metric, we show that for a perfect teacher, a high ratio of teacher's soft labels can be beneficial. Finally, for the case of imperfect teacher, we find that hard labels can correct teacher's wrong prediction, which explains the practice of mixing hard and soft labels.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has established itself as a primary mechanism for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate features and representations, and they are readily combined with quantization, pruning, ensembling, and domain-adaptation techniques. While KD frequently yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance degradation—and sometimes performance improvements—its success depends on careful method selection, teacher quality, data and sample selection, and complementary engineering such as layer alignment or teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Daniels
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques enable deployment of high-performing but large deep models by transferring knowledge from larger or more complex models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). Across vision, speech, recommendation, retrieval, and NLP tasks, KD has been adapted into many forms—single- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and federated variants, task-adaptive compression, and methods that target robustness, fairness, or cross-modal transfer. Empirical results show KD can yield large speed and size gains with modest performance loss and in some cases match or exceed teacher performance when combined with architectural or training strategies. Open challenges remain around teacher quality and heterogeneity, data availability, distribution shift, low-frequency phenomena, adversarial robustness, and deploying distillation in privacy-sensitive or resource-constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Understanding BERT Rankers Under Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Deep language models such as BERT pre-trained on large corpus have given a huge performance boost to the state-of-the-art information retrieval ranking systems. Knowledge embedded in such models allows them to pick up complex matching signals between passages and queries. However, the high computation cost during inference limits their deployment in real-world search scenarios. In this paper, we study if and how the knowledge for search within BERT can be transferred to a smaller ranker through distillation. Our experiments demonstrate that it is crucial to use a proper distillation procedure, which produces up to nine times speedup while preserving the state-of-the-art performance.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit—from soft-target (logit) transfer to feature- and relational-level objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free synthesis, and task-aware adaptations—has been developed and applied across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and objective design are aligned; persistent challenges include data scarcity, teacher–student architecture mismatch, transferred biases, and reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: BAM! Born-Again Multi-Task Networks for Natural Language Understanding
papers_seen.abstract: It can be challenging to train multi-task neural networks that outperform or even match their single-task counterparts. To help address this, we propose using knowledge distillation where single-task models teach a multi-task model. We enhance this training with teacher annealing, a novel method that gradually transitions the model from distillation to supervised learning, helping the multi-task model surpass its single-task teachers. We evaluate our approach by multi-task fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark. Our method consistently improves over standard single-task and multi-task training.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Hahn
papers_seen.title: PKD: General Distillation Framework for Object Detectors via Pearson Correlation Coefficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation(KD) is a widely-used technique to train compact models in object detection. However, there is still a lack of study on how to distill between heterogeneous detectors. In this paper, we empirically find that better FPN features from a heterogeneous teacher detector can help the student although their detection heads and label assignments are different. However, directly aligning the feature maps to distill detectors suffers from two problems. First, the difference in feature magnitude between the teacher and the student could enforce overly strict constraints on the student. Second, the FPN stages and channels with large feature magnitude from the teacher model could dominate the gradient of distillation loss, which will overwhelm the effects of other features in KD and introduce much noise. To address the above issues, we propose to imitate features with Pearson Correlation Coefficient to focus on the relational information from the teacher and relax constraints on the magnitude of the features. Our method consistently outperforms the existing detection KD methods and works for both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs. Furthermore, it converges faster. With a powerful MaskRCNN-Swin detector as the teacher, ResNet-50 based RetinaNet and FCOS achieve 41.5% and 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, which are 4.1\% and 4.8\% higher than the baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Berger
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensembled teachers to compact students. Across modalities and domains, KD methods—when combined with task-aware data strategies and complementary compression primitives—often recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployments under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Success requires careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Reyes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings, practitioners use KD to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of teacher performance. Modern distillation extends beyond matching output probabilities to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data- or privacy-aware variants. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that includes architecture-aware choices, pruning, quantization, curriculum or data strategies, and safeguards for fairness and robustness. Remaining challenges include teacher–student capacity mismatch, distributional and low-frequency phenomena, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and principled automation of distillation design.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Learning Student-Friendly Teacher Networks for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel knowledge distillation approach to facilitate the transfer of dark knowledge from a teacher to a student. Contrary to most of the existing methods that rely on effective training of student models given pretrained teachers, we aim to learn the teacher models that are friendly to students and, consequently, more appropriate for knowledge transfer. In other words, at the time of optimizing a teacher model, the proposed algorithm learns the student branches jointly to obtain student-friendly representations. Since the main goal of our approach lies in training teacher models and the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure is straightforward, most of the existing knowledge distillation methods can adopt this technique to improve the performance of diverse student models in terms of accuracy and convergence speed. The proposed algorithm demonstrates outstanding accuracy in several well-known knowledge distillation techniques with various combinations of teacher and student models even in the case that their architectures are heterogeneous and there is no prior knowledge about student models at the time of training teacher networks.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings. KD techniques transfer teacher behavior via soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational objectives, and can be extended to data-free, privacy-preserving, and adversarial regimes. Best results arise when distillation is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search); remaining challenges include data- or domain-limited scenarios, teacher–student mismatch, robustness and privacy trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, graph, and generative settings, KD techniques (logits, feature/attention matching, relational objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and ensemble/online schemes) often recover a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate data strategies, pretraining, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD has concrete limits — teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, rare‑token degradation, and failures under distribution shift or scarce/private data — which motivate task‑aware design, multi‑signal objectives, and integration with other compression primitives. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, domain examples, practical guidelines, and open challenges documented in the selected literature.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: An Indispensable but Context‑Dependent Toolbox
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When matched to task constraints, data regimes, and student capacity, KD reliably produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections and faces limits (data mismatch, capacity gaps, low-frequency behavior), so it must be applied as a principled, task-aware set of techniques combined with complementary compression practices.

papers_seen.author: Lucas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Primary, Context‑Aware Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically proven approach for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers. KD routinely achieves large reductions in inference cost and model size while recovering much of teacher performance, and it enables domain, modality, and privacy‑aware adaptations. However, KD is not a turnkey cure: its reliability depends on careful choices of what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy, and it should be applied as the core element of a broader, deployment‑aware compression portfolio that includes pruning, quantization, architecture search, and targeted data interventions.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression, Transfer, and Robustification in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is not merely a technique for shrinking models: it is a flexible paradigm that enables model compression, domain and modality transfer, continual adaptation, and improved interpretability and fairness. A range of strategies — from many-to-many layer alignment and feature mimicking to data-free synthesis, online peer teaching, and augmentation-aware distillation — make KD applicable across tasks (classification, generation, detection, ASR, GANs) and settings (distributed training, privacy-constrained, few-shot, multi-task). However, practical use requires careful design choices (what to transfer, how to match teacher and student, and how to handle teacher–student discrepancy and label-processing artifacts). When applied with methods matched to these considerations, KD consistently yields compact models that retain much of teacher performance while unlocking deployment and research scenarios otherwise infeasible for large, monolithic networks.

papers_seen.author: Rasmussen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Practical Necessity, Limits, and a Best-Practice Agenda
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical and widely applicable approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster students for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. Empirical work shows distillation can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling reduced memory, lower-latency inference, and new capabilities such as task-adaptive compression, multi-task transfer, and interpretable surrogates. At the same time, distillation is not a turnkey remedy: optimization challenges, dataset and distribution mismatches, teacher bias transfer, and design choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relational structure) strongly affect outcomes. The most reliable results come from combining KD with complementary techniques (teacher adaptation, selective or curriculum-driven sample selection, representation matching, low-precision numerics, and scaled training procedures) and from tailoring the procedure to task- and deployment-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware toolkit and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. However, its effectiveness depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, and data strategy; it must be applied conditionally with safeguards against error and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of methods for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD reliably reduces inference cost and memory while often preserving most of a teacher's performance. However, KD is not a standalone cure: its practical success requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle data limitations and privacy, and how to mitigate transferred biases and low-frequency failures. The strongest deployments treat KD as central but combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and safeguards (data strategies, curriculum, evaluation on robustness and fairness).

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Christian
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practical Findings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when combined with deployment-aware design choices and complementary compression tools. However, realizing robust, fair, and privacy-preserving compressed models requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and method selection.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and data‑free objectives—enable substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression primitives; open challenges remain in capacity mismatch, distributional robustness, preservation of rare behaviors, and privacy-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Oconnell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. When designed as part of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline — integrating pretraining, multi-signal transfer (logits, features, relational signals), data strategies, and compatible architecture choices — KD can preserve most teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its effectiveness is conditional: it depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the distilled signals and data, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases or rare-case failures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as the practical core of modern model-compression toolkits, outlines concrete mechanisms by which it helps, surveys domain- and task-specific variants that address common failure modes, and summarizes actionable design principles for robust, responsible deployment.

papers_seen.author: Sampson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient students. KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or deployment-ready compression: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, teacher–student alignment, and combination with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as the core of a task-aware, integrated compression pipeline — rather than a one-shot solution — achieves the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Carpenter
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and broadly applicable approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and generative tasks, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment. For deployment-ready compression, KD should be treated as a cornerstone technique that is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to close remaining optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal domains, a diverse set of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational structure) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, data‑free or self‑distillation) have been developed. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover much of a teacher’s performance while enabling lower latency, reduced memory use, and new deployment modes; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design of the transfer objective. Practical pipelines commonly pair KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task‑aware procedures (layer mapping, curriculum, teacher adaptation) to meet deployment constraints. Important open problems include robust transfer under distribution shift and data scarcity, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, principled automated design for heterogeneous student architectures, and privacy‑aware or data‑free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Dalton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible approach that reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD works via multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and training protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, adversarial, data‑free). Its practical value comes from being a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—rather than a single, automatic cure‑all. Realizing KD's benefits requires careful choices about teacher selection, student capacity and architecture, distilled signals, training data, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performance teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring information beyond hard labels. A broad toolkit has emerged — including logits/soft-label transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search — enabling deployment across vision, speech, language, generative, and multimodal settings. Empirical and theoretical work highlights gains in latency, memory, calibration, and sometimes robustness, while pointing to failure modes driven by teacher quality, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and distribution shift; best practice treats KD as a core element of a broader, context-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an essential, empirically validated approach for converting large teacher models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD methods—ranging from soft‑logit matching to intermediate‑feature and attention transfers, adversarial or contrastive objectives, and multi‑teacher schemes—regularly enable large reductions in inference cost and parameter footprint while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD’s effectiveness is strongly dependent on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data availability and quality, and optimization dynamics; therefore, reliable compression in practice requires combining KD with task‑aware design choices and complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data synthesis) and explicit mitigation strategies for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger (or specialized) teacher models to smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive structure), how mappings between teacher and student are implemented (layer alignment, projectors, many-to-many mappings), and how training is scheduled (fixed teacher, student-friendly teacher learning, meta-learning, or self-distillation). KD is frequently combined with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, progressive module replacement, and architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, mixup, data-free synthesis, domain adaptation) to meet deployment, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. While KD often yields strong empirical gains in accuracy, efficiency, and robustness, its success depends on teacher quality, the distilled signals chosen, data availability and complexity, and careful optimization; open problems remain in principled selection of distillation targets, mitigating transferred biases, and integrating KD optimally with other compression tools.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: An Advocated Conditional-First Approach
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, broadly applicable set of techniques that enable compact, efficient models suitable for real-world deployment in vision, language, speech, and multimodal systems. KD reliably reduces latency, memory, and compute requirements while often preserving much of a teacher model’s performance, but its success is conditional: on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. As a result, KD should be treated as a primary engineering primitive for compression that must be combined with task- and deployment-aware design, complementary compression techniques, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness. Future progress requires better theoretical understanding of transferable signals, automated teacher–student alignment, and methods that address privacy, distribution shift, and low-frequency behavior.

KD is most effective when integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation) and when its design is matched to teacher quality, student capacity, and data availability. Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single recipe, KD is an essential practical tool for model deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

Careful design, including multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, exposure to raw or synthesized data, and joint optimization with pruning or architecture search, makes KD an indispensable component of practical model-deployment toolkits.

papers_seen.title: The Efficacy and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into efficient students across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models, and reinforcement learning). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while offering substantial inference speedups and parameter reductions, and can be enhanced by targeted techniques (data augmentation, intermediate-layer matching, multi-teacher schedules, contrastive objectives, and meta-learning). However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends strongly on distillation procedure, data complexity, teacher–student alignment, and training dynamics. Practical deployment requires selecting distillation objectives and data strategies that address robustness, limited-data regimes, privacy/federation, and modality-specific needs.

papers_seen.author: Webb
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Sensitive Toolkit for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teachers to smaller students, but its success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to train, and how to integrate complementary compression methods. When designed as part of a task-aware pipeline—with attention to teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and privacy or fairness constraints—KD yields deployable models that retain much of teacher performance; treated naively it can propagate errors and fail under data- or capacity-mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Ruiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring behavior from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants — including soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free synthesis — are used alone or with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to reduce parameters, latency, and memory while attempting to retain teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals to task and student capacity, handling limited or private data, and mitigating transferred biases or rare-case failures. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity gaps, domain shift and data scarcity, privacy guarantees for data-free and federated settings, and automated teacher–student co-design for hardware-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Martinez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Configurable, and Context‑Dependent Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely adopted toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD is versatile—supporting logits, representation, and relational transfer—and integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, its success is context-dependent: teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and deployment constraints govern whether and how KD should be applied.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Versatile Toolkit with Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad set of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students. Across NLP and vision applications, KD enables deployment on resource-constrained hardware, supports privacy- and data-constrained settings, and can be adapted to preserve or transfer properties such as adversarial robustness, cross-modal behavior, and domain expertise. At the same time, KD interacts with factors such as teacher quality, data availability, label design, and training cost, and several specialized methods have been developed to address these practical trade-offs. This paper argues that KD is an indispensable, flexible approach for model compression and adaptation, and that best results arise from combining KD with complementary practices (e.g., pre-training, augmentation, curriculum selection, or generative replay) tailored to the deployment constraints and objectives.

papers_seen.author: Lindsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: A Central but Context‑Aware Compression Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring capabilities from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable students. KD workflows include matching teacher outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- and relational-structure transfer, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data-free variants; they are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. While KD often preserves most of a teacher’s performance and enables real-world deployment, its success is strongly context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architectural alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit handling of robustness, bias, and distribution-shift failure modes. Consequently, KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines but not a panacea—its value is maximized when integrated with task-aware engineering and complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Henry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of methods that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD can materially reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving much of teacher performance, and its variants (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational objectives, online/mutual schemes, and data-free synthesis) extend its applicability across tasks and deployment constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and the choice of which signals to transfer; practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware practices rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Bowen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed and applied with awareness of task constraints, teacher quality, student capacity, and available data, KD enables large reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: it must be integrated with complementary compression methods and explicit safeguards to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and propagation of teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have become central strategies for deploying large deep models under resource, latency, and privacy constraints. A diverse set of methods—ranging from soft-label distillation, intermediate feature and attention matching, layer mapping, adversarial and data-free techniques, to task-adaptive architecture search and meta-learning of teachers—have been proposed to transfer performance from bulky teachers to compact students. These approaches are applied across domains including vision, language, multi-modal systems, recommender systems, and domain-specific NLP, and they trade off fidelity to the teacher, generalization, and computational efficiency. Empirical results show that properly designed distillation pipelines can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while yielding substantial speedups and memory reductions, and in some settings can even improve fairness, robustness, or downstream generalization. Remaining challenges include aligning heterogeneous inputs and representations across teacher and student, coping with absent or private training data, and automatically selecting what and how to transfer for specific tasks and deployment constraints.
