papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to compress large neural models for deployment under resource constraints and to transfer task- and domain-specific priors across models. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal problems, distillation methods go beyond matching output probabilities: modern approaches match intermediate representations, attention patterns, contrastive structure, and task-specific signals. Practical success depends on aligning teacher and student inputs and architectures, choosing losses that capture relational or localized information, addressing dataset shifts (including low-frequency token behavior), and carefully choosing which teacher signals to transfer. Several family-specific solutions (detection, retrieval, non-autoregressive translation, graph learning, vision-language, and spoken QA) show distillation can both improve accuracy and reduce inference cost, but raise challenges around data availability, heterogeneity, and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and widely adopted approach for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods (logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data- or generator-based synthesis) and training regimes (offline, online, self-, and multi-teacher) are routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling practical deployment, but its effectiveness is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, available data or synthesis strategies, and mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher bias, optimization and capacity mismatch, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Spence
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques that should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of model-compression pipelines rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. Properly designed KD—choosing what signals to transfer, aligning teacher and student architectures, selecting or synthesizing suitable data, and integrating complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search—regularly yields compact models that preserve most teacher performance for deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints. However, KD has predictable failure modes (teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare outputs) that require explicit mitigation and evaluation in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Foundational, Versatile, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for transferring behavior from large teacher models to smaller students to meet deployment, privacy, and latency constraints. KD spans logits-based supervision, representation and feature matching, adversarial and generator-based data synthesis, multi-teacher or online schemes, and task- and domain-aware adaptations. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful training practices (projectors, curriculum, selective sampling), KD can recover much of teacher performance and enable new capabilities (cross-domain transfer, federated heterogeneity, and multi-modal compression). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: success depends on teacher–student compatibility, data availability (including data-free or few-shot regimes), distribution shift, and mitigation of propagated teacher errors or biases. Practitioners should treat KD as a flexible framework that must be adapted to task, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Context‑Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically proven approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD methods include logits matching, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, and variants that operate online, with multiple teachers, or without access to original training data. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component within a broader compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies; its benefits and limits depend on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful mitigation of bias and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Jimenez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. When treated as a configurable toolbox rather than a single algorithm, KD enables large reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance across modalities. Its effectiveness depends on task-aware choices—what signals to transfer, how to align architectures, how to generate or select transfer data, and which complementary compression techniques to combine. KD also has clear failure modes (data scarcity, teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher biases, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena) that require targeted remedies. With appropriate safeguards and joint optimization with pruning, quantization, or architecture search, KD should be a primary method in compression pipelines, applied conditionally and validated for the deployment context.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: FedZKT: Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer towards Resource-Constrained Federated Learning with Heterogeneous On-Device Models
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning enables multiple distributed devices to collaboratively learn a shared prediction model without centralizing their on-device data. Most of the current algorithms require comparable individual efforts for local training with the same structure and size of on-device models, which, however, impedes participation from resource-constrained devices. Given the widespread yet heterogeneous devices nowadays, in this paper, we propose an innovative federated learning framework with heterogeneous on-device models through Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer, named by FedZKT. Specifically, FedZKT allows devices to independently determine the on-device models upon their local resources. To achieve knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models, a zero-shot distillation approach is designed without any prerequisites for private on-device data, which is contrary to certain prior research based on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator. Moreover, this compute-intensive distillation task is assigned to the server to allow the participation of resource-constrained devices, where a generator is adversarially learned with the ensemble of collected on-device models. The distilled central knowledge is then sent back in the form of the corresponding on-device model parameters, which can be easily absorbed on the device side. Extensive experimental studies demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of FedZKT towards on-device knowledge agnostic, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning scenarios, such as heterogeneous on-device data and straggler effects.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models using targets ranging from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals. Across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data augmentation or synthetic-data generation) enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and domain constraints. Empirical results show distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can sometimes match or exceed teachers when distillation is carefully designed. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity mismatch, optimization and belief-matching limits, distribution shift and domain adaptation, preserving rare-token/low-frequency behavior, and avoiding transfer of teacher biases. This synthesis summarizes mechanisms, practical variants, representative empirical patterns, and recommended directions for research and deployment.

papers_seen.author: Heath
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis reviews empirical and methodological advances in knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques as applied across vision, language, generative models, retrieval, recommender systems, federated and lifelong learning. It summarizes mechanisms for transferring teacher knowledge to smaller students (soft labels, intermediate representations, curriculum and selective sample strategies), practical challenges (data availability, teacher cost, domain shift, privacy, and bias), and targeted solutions (data-free distillation, fast label generation, multi-teacher and domain-adaptive schemes, self-distillation, and distillation-aware pruning). The goal is to map what the provided literature reports about when distillation helps, when it can hurt, and which strategies are effective for different settings and tasks.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile approach to compressing large models for deployment and domain-specific use. Across modalities and tasks, KD can preserve much of the teacher's performance in compact students, but it must be combined with task-aware engineering—such as teacher adaptation, layer-wise selection, data augmentation, and hardware-aware pruning—to address heterogeneity, domain shift, and efficiency constraints. This article argues that KD is necessary but not sufficient: best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques chosen for the target modality, deployment constraints, and learning scenario.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a pragmatic pathway to compress large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Empirical work across vision, speech, language, multimodal and graph domains shows KD can retain much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory when combined with complementary compression tools. However, real-world success requires careful choice of teacher signals, data strategies, and optimization protocols to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and modality or deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices

However, distillation is not automatic: practitioner attention is needed to address teacher selection, data availability and distribution shift, capacity mismatch, low-frequency behavior, and risk of transferring biases or teacher artifacts.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis

Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that leverages complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP

papers_seen.author: Lopez

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques constitute a flexible toolkit for transferring behavior and internal structure from large, high‑capacity teacher models into smaller, faster, or deployment‑specific student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relations, and structured objectives) and across protocols (offline teacher→student, online/co‑distillation, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher, data‑free, and federated schemes). Empirical practice shows KD often retains a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling large reductions in compute, memory, and latency when combined with complementary compression methods and careful data and architecture choices. However, KD’s effectiveness is context dependent: it is sensitive to teacher quality and mismatch, student capacity, data availability and distribution, and the risk of propagating teacher artifacts (biases, low‑frequency errors). Remaining needs include principled theory linking distilled signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous or non‑i.i.d. data, and robust privacy/fairness guarantees for compressed models.

papers_seen.author: Sampson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient students. KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or deployment-ready compression: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, teacher–student alignment, and combination with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as the core of a task-aware, integrated compression pipeline — rather than a one-shot solution — achieves the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Arroyo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression techniques transfer information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Approaches vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention maps, channel statistics, or decision-boundary information), by whether original training data are available, and by whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work across vision, multimodal, speech, and natural language tasks shows that careful choices of transfer targets, loss formulations, teacher ensembles, and training schedules can yield compact models that approach — and in some cases match or exceed — teacher performance while enabling deployment under resource, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. Remaining challenges include optimization difficulties that prevent perfect belief matching, distribution-shift and heterogeneity issues in federated or data-free settings, and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Durham
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of methods for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—from soft-logit supervision to intermediate-feature and relational/contrastive objectives, online and multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols—enable reduced memory, latency, and communication costs while often preserving most teacher performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline that includes pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, and task- or data-aware procedures; its reliable application requires explicit attention to teacher–student compatibility, data availability, optimization schedules, and safeguards for bias, rare-case behavior, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become core methods for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers across computer vision, speech, graph-based learning, and NLP. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based teacher-student paradigm into feature- and representation-based distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, online and adversarial schemes, and task-specific adaptations (e.g., for BERT and non-autoregressive translation). Work also addresses robustness, privacy, few-shot compression, and practical efficiency (reduced compute and communication) for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Gross
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Path for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical tool that enables deployment of compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teachers to smaller students. KD supports many transfer targets and protocols and can materially reduce model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. The most reliable deployments treat KD as the central element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than the sole method.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Does Knowledge Distillation Really Work?
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a popular technique for training a small student network to emulate a larger teacher model, such as an ensemble of networks. We show that while knowledge distillation can improve student generalization, it does not typically work as it is commonly understood: there often remains a surprisingly large discrepancy between the predictive distributions of the teacher and the student, even in cases when the student has the capacity to perfectly match the teacher. We identify difficulties in optimization as a key reason for why the student is unable to match the teacher. We also show how the details of the dataset used for distillation play a role in how closely the student matches the teacher -- and that more closely matching the teacher paradoxically does not always lead to better student generalization.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and broadly effective family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, detection, translation, federated settings, and reinforcement learning show KD reduces parameters and latency, can improve generalization, and enables domain- and privacy-aware workflows. At the same time, KD has important failure modes—dependence on distillation data and teacher–student alignment, capability mismatches, and transfer of teacher errors or biases—that require targeted solutions. Best practice is to treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline, combined with representation-level matching, data strategies, architecture-aware transformations, and privacy- or domain-specific adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Paradigm for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical, and theoretically grounded approach to compressing and adapting deep models. Across modalities and tasks, KD enables compact students to inherit predictive performance, inductive biases, and application-specific properties (privacy, fairness, task-adaptivity) from larger or specialized teachers. Best practice combines logit-level, feature-level, and architecture-aware strategies, often augmented by multi-teacher, curriculum, or meta-learning schemes; privacy-preserving and data-free variants make KD suitable for sensitive or decentralized settings. We argue that KD should be a first-class tool in compression toolkits and outline concrete practices that are supported by empirical and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core Practical Tool for Model Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated paradigm that compresses large models into smaller, deployable students while also enabling robustness, domain and modality transfer, privacy-aware training, and architectural adaptation. When combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data-free synthesis, and task-aware training), carefully designed distillation pipelines provide favorable trade-offs between accuracy, latency, and resource consumption for practical deployments across vision, language, multimodal, and sequential tasks. Despite strong practical gains, reliable distillation depends on principled choices about what to transfer, teacher–student pairing, and data availability, and outstanding theoretical and empirical challenges remain in heterogenous, privacy-sensitive, and distribution-shifted settings.

papers_seen.author: Bishop
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for producing compact, faster models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, retrieval, and generative tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes—have been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of transferred errors and rare-output degradation. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical guidance, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Demand-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically versatile approach for compressing large models and transferring behavior to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities by matching logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Recent work extends KD to settings with no original data, privacy constraints, heterogeneous architectures, and specialized tasks (graphs, non‑autoregressive generation, lifelong learning). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher–student design, data strategies, and task-aware objectives, and important open problems remain (capacity mismatch, teacher bias transfer, preserving low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping, and rigorous theoretical understanding).

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed — including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or generative-sample approaches — and these techniques are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative models, and embedded settings shows that careful design of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data or synthetic samples to use is crucial: well-designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, distribution shift, and preserving rare or minority behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Bowen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Component for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed and applied with awareness of task constraints, teacher quality, student capacity, and available data, KD enables large reductions in inference cost while retaining much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: it must be integrated with complementary compression methods and explicit safeguards to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, distribution shift, and propagation of teacher errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Weeks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Central, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students. KD enables deployment under strict latency, memory, and privacy constraints and supports cross-modal and domain transfer. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data availability and privacy, and complementary compression and training practices. Reliable compression treats distillation as a core component of a broader, task-aware pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Recent Work
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Empirical results across vision, language, recommendation, multimodal, and generative domains show KD frequently preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Practical deployment favors combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), choosing appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, decision-boundary signals), and adopting data- and task-aware strategies. KD also has well-documented limitations — optimization obstacles that prevent perfect teacher matching, sensitivity to teacher quality and data regimes, and risks of propagating teacher biases or poor modeling of rare phenomena — which motivate targeted mitigations such as adversarial/sample-selection methods, multi-teacher and teacher-aware schemes, data-free or privacy-preserving formulations, and representation-level objectives. Overall, KD is best viewed as a flexible, task-aware toolkit whose effectiveness depends on matching methods and safeguards to the compression and deployment goals.

papers_seen.author: Christian
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practical Findings, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted set of techniques for producing compact, deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger teacher models into smaller students. Across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs when combined with deployment-aware design choices and complementary compression tools. However, realizing robust, fair, and privacy-preserving compressed models requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data regimes, and method selection.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Gill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and optimization problems, a consistent empirical story has emerged: carefully designed distillation objectives and workflows can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and composition of transfer data, and the use of complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or privacy, distribution shift, and preserving rare or long-tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated framework for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses multiple transfer signals and training protocols and is most effective when designed with task- and deployment-awareness. While KD frequently yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss, reliable deployment requires combining KD with complementary compression primitives and explicit measures to mitigate teacher imperfection, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias propagation.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (Selected 2017–2022 Literature)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Methods include soft-label distillation, feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, curriculum and selective-sample strategies, and task-adaptive architecture search. These approaches target deployment constraints (latency, memory, on-device compute), data-availability and privacy limitations, robustness, and domain-continuity, and have been adapted to detectors, generative models, retrieval systems, federated settings, and pre-trained language models. Empirical work demonstrates that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, internal features, relational/contrastive signals) and when/how to train (online, teacher-free, curriculum, few-shot) materially affects student performance and robustness. Open challenges include heterogeneity of data and architectures in distributed settings, theoretical understanding of what aspects of teacher knowledge are most valuable across tasks, and extending distillation to privacy- and domain-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Rogers
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring information from larger or richer models (teachers) into smaller, more efficient models (students). KD methods range from matching teacher output distributions to aligning internal representations and using synthesized or privatized data; they are effective across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks and are commonly integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance while improving inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and safeguards against propagating undesirable teacher properties. Current practice treats KD as a configurable component of wider compression pipelines rather than a single algorithm, and several methodological extensions and safeguards have been proposed to address its known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. KD methods operate at logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision boundaries and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data- or privacy-aware procedures. KD delivers strong practical benefits across modalities and tasks but requires careful teacher–student alignment, attention to data and privacy constraints, and complementary techniques to address capacity gaps, domain shift, and rare-token behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broad family of techniques for compressing large or expensive models into smaller, faster, or more deployable ones by transferring information from a teacher to a student. Methods differ in the form of transferred knowledge (soft logits, hidden features, contrastive distributions, synthetic data, or cross-modal alignments), in how and when distillation is applied (offline, online, layer-wise, task-adaptive, or data-free), and in the problems they target (classification, detection, generation, language tasks, graph learning, or novel-view synthesis). Empirical work demonstrates that appropriate choices about teacher signals, data manipulation, and architectural search can yield compact models that retain much of teacher performance across modalities; theoretical work begins to clarify when soft labels help and when hard labels or mixed supervision are needed. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps between teacher and student, dataset and fairness concerns, and scaling distillation reliably in large distributed settings.

papers_seen.author: Travis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of their performance. Across vision, speech, graphs, recommender systems, and NLP, KD has diversified from the original logits-based teacher-student protocol into feature- and representation-based objectives, data-free and generative approaches, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, online and collaborative strategies, and task-aware adaptations. Empirical work shows distilled students often reclaim much of teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, and data used for transfer are properly matched; however, optimization issues, data heterogeneity, and the risk of propagating teacher biases remain practical challenges. Complementary techniques—pruning, quantization, architecture search, pretraining, and careful layer alignment—regularly improve outcomes and are recommended for deployment in constrained environments.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Larson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is widely used to compress large neural models for deployment under resource constraints and to transfer task- and domain-specific priors across models. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal problems, distillation methods go beyond matching output probabilities: modern approaches match intermediate representations, attention patterns, contrastive structure, and task-specific signals. Practical success depends on aligning teacher and student inputs and architectures, choosing losses that capture relational or localized information, addressing dataset shifts (including low-frequency token behavior), and carefully choosing which teacher signals to transfer. Several family-specific solutions (detection, retrieval, non-autoregressive translation, graph learning, vision-language, and spoken QA) show distillation can both improve accuracy and reduce inference cost, but raise challenges around data availability, heterogeneity, and generalization.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations through multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational constraints) and can operate in offline, online, data‑free, and federated regimes. Its empirical strengths span vision, language, speech, multimodal, and distributed training settings. However, KD is not a standalone panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals and data strategy, and explicit steps to mitigate transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. The most reliable compression outcomes treat KD as the practical core of a task‑aware pipeline that integrates representation matching, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a pragmatic pathway to compress large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Empirical work across vision, speech, language, multimodal and graph domains shows KD can retain much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory when combined with complementary compression tools. However, real-world success requires careful choice of teacher signals, data strategies, and optimization protocols to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and modality or deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Caldwell
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical paradigm for producing compact, efficient models by transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. A diverse set of distillation objectives and workflows — including soft-logit matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and adversarial or curriculum-based training — has been developed and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, graphs) and tasks (classification, generation, detection, ranking, and more). When combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, KD routinely enables deployment in resource- and latency-constrained settings while often preserving most teacher performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher-student compatibility, data regimes, and mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer, optimization mismatch, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Green
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Not Panacea Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted technique for compressing large models into smaller ones and transferring capabilities across tasks and modalities. When thoughtfully designed—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), preparing or augmenting data, and matching teacher-student capacity—KD yields substantial gains in inference efficiency with modest performance loss and can enable deployment under tight latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, data availability, optimization dynamics, and architecture alignment; complementary tools (pretraining, projector modules, online schemes, and privacy-aware protocols) and careful engineering are often required to realize consistent, robust results. Open directions include principled data-free distillation, better theoretical characterizations of what is transferred, and joint co-design of architectures and distillation objectives for specific deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: The Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable technique for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more interpretable students across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains. KD can be combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and progressive replacement to yield compact models that preserve much of teacher performance, but its effectiveness depends on dataset complexity, teacher quality, and the choice of what and how to transfer. Addressing pitfalls such as harmful teacher supervision on particular samples, degraded signals for low-frequency outputs, data unavailability, privacy concerns, and fairness requires targeted strategies (selective distillation, adapted teachers, self-distillation, generative replay, or tailored objectives).

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach to compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. Across logits-based soft-targets, intermediate-feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free schemes, and architecture-aware strategies, KD routinely yields favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs in vision, language, retrieval, graphs, and generative tasks. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data and privacy constraints, and combination with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining gaps include robustness under distribution shift, preserving low-frequency/long-tail behavior, mitigating teacher artifacts and bias, and devising reliable procedures when original data are unavailable.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data schemes, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transfer signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under domain shift and heterogeneous devices, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Cardenas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central and Versatile but Insufficient Alone — Practical Position and Best Practices for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques that transfers information from larger or composite teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under resource or privacy constraints, and sometimes improve generalization. KD methods span logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and many teacher/student configurations. While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and alignment, student capacity, the data used for transfer, and integration with complementary compression methods; successful deployments therefore treat KD as a core component of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: Less is More: Task-aware Layer-wise Distillation for Language Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Layer-wise distillation is a powerful tool to compress large models (i.e. teacher models) into small ones (i.e., student models). The student distills knowledge from the teacher by mimicking the hidden representations of the teacher at every intermediate layer. However, layer-wise distillation is difficult. Since the student has a smaller model capacity than the teacher, it is often under-fitted. Furthermore, the hidden representations of the teacher contain redundant information that the student does not necessarily need for the target task's learning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel Task-aware layEr-wise Distillation (TED). TED designs task-aware filters to align the hidden representations of the student and the teacher at each layer. The filters select the knowledge that is useful for the target task from the hidden representations. As such, TED reduces the knowledge gap between the two models and helps the student to fit better on the target task. We evaluate TED in two scenarios: continual pre-training and fine-tuning. TED demonstrates significant and consistent improvements over existing distillation methods in both scenarios. Code is available at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: A Deep Hierarchical Approach to Lifelong Learning in Minecraft
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a lifelong learning system that has the ability to reuse and transfer knowledge from one task to another while efficiently retaining the previously learned knowledge-base. Knowledge is transferred by learning reusable skills to solve tasks in Minecraft, a popular video game which is an unsolved and high-dimensional lifelong learning problem. These reusable skills, which we refer to as Deep Skill Networks, are then incorporated into our novel Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Network (H-DRLN) architecture using two techniques: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, our novel variation of policy distillation (Rusu et. al. 2015) for learning skills. Skill distillation enables the HDRLN to efficiently retain knowledge and therefore scale in lifelong learning, by accumulating knowledge and encapsulating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network. The H-DRLN exhibits superior performance and lower learning sample complexity compared to the regular Deep Q Network (Mnih et. al. 2015) in sub-domains of Minecraft.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.
