papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller, efficient student models to reduce latency, memory, and deployment cost while often preserving much of the original performance. A broad toolkit has been developed—logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and channel-wise objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search—that is applied across vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD is effective in many settings but success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful objective and alignment choices; practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of a larger compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of methods for transferring knowledge from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, efficient student models so that students achieve improved accuracy, latency, or resource use while retaining much of teacher behavior. Methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, internal features, relational structure, or contrastive/global representations), how supervision is scheduled (offline, online, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and how distillation is combined with other compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows substantial gains across vision, language, graphs, recommendation, and generative models, but limitations remain around data availability, teacher-student mismatch, low-frequency information transfer, privacy constraints, and robustness under distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, practical framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient students for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A diverse toolkit of distillation objectives and protocols—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-/self-distillation, and data-free protocols—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and multimodal tasks. KD is most effective when integrated into task-aware pipelines that align teacher and student architectures, choose appropriate transfer signals, and combine distillation with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) while explicitly addressing limitations such as distribution shift, teacher-induced biases, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Graham
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable set of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-label matching to intermediate-feature, attention, and relational alignment—are combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data or systems strategies (multi-teacher supervision, synthetic-data generation, federated protocols) to produce favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs. The practical effectiveness of KD depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability, and mitigation of bias or robustness issues.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Task‑aware Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical framework for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across speech, vision, translation, and evaluation metrics, KD variants (soft labels, feature/attention matching, adversarial and data-free schemes, and self‑distillation) have enabled deployable models under latency, memory, privacy, and communication constraints. KD is not a panacea: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with distribution or capacity mismatch, and require task‑aware adaptations. When used as part of an integrated, task‑aware compression pipeline—combining layer‑wise alignment, pretraining, pruning/quantization, data augmentation, or synthetic data generation—KD reliably yields practical tradeoffs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Lin
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Necessary but Not Sufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and flexible framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings. KD preserves much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its effectiveness depends on choices about what is distilled, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is combined with complementary compression techniques. Practical success therefore requires integrating KD with task-aware engineering—data strategies, multi-objective compression (pruning/quantization/architecture search), teacher/student co-design, and privacy-aware protocols—to avoid known failure modes and meet real-world deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The KD toolkit has expanded beyond soft-targets to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, and data‑free or privacy-aware synthesis. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable domain adaptation, federated and privacy-sensitive workflows, and multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the distillation data, and mitigation of propagated errors, bias, and distribution-shift issues. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that leverages complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely used approach for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. A large and consistent body of work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities when the distilled signals, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen carefully. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness is context-dependent: it is bounded by data availability, teacher quality, capacity mismatch, and risks of transferring undesirable behaviors, so it is best applied as part of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), data strategies, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller, deployable student models. The literature shows that appropriately chosen distillation signals, teacher–student design, and data strategies allow compact models to recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and deployment cost. Practical pipelines commonly combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and adapt to constraints such as privacy, heterogeneous devices, and limited or unlabeled data. Despite widespread empirical success, important limitations persist—teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, degraded rare-output behavior, and theoretical gaps linking distillation signals to student generalization—motivating ongoing work in adaptive teacher selection, data-free distillation, and task-aware compression design.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Distilled Semantics for Comprehensive Scene Understanding from Videos
papers_seen.abstract: Whole understanding of the surroundings is paramount to autonomous systems. Recent works have shown that deep neural networks can learn geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) from a monocular video without any explicit supervision from ground truth annotations, particularly hard to source for these two tasks. In this paper, we take an additional step toward holistic scene understanding with monocular cameras by learning depth and motion alongside with semantics, with supervision for the latter provided by a pre-trained network distilling proxy ground truth images. We address the three tasks jointly by a) a novel training protocol based on knowledge distillation and self-supervision and b) a compact network architecture which enables efficient scene understanding on both power hungry GPUs and low-power embedded platforms. We thoroughly assess the performance of our framework and show that it yields state-of-the-art results for monocular depth estimation, optical flow and motion segmentation.

papers_seen.author: Garrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational, Practical, but Not Sufficiently Complete Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable approach for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. KD techniques extend beyond logit matching to feature- and layer-level alignment, attention and projection-based mappings, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and data-constrained regimes (few-shot, data-free). KD reliably improves deployment trade-offs (latency, memory, and sometimes robustness or privacy), but it has concrete limits—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity, and task-specific design needs—that make KD most effective when integrated with complementary compression and training practices.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Powell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that enable model compression, domain- and task-level transfer, privacy-preserving distillation, and improvements in interpretability and fairness. Empirical and methodological work shows KD can compress large models into efficient students, transfer inductive biases, support multi-task and lifelong learning, and enable data-free or zero-shot distillation when training data are unavailable. At the same time, KD faces concrete limitations due to data heterogeneity, teacher-student capacity mismatch, and the need to select or synthesize appropriate supervision; hybrid solutions that combine feature-level matching, adversarial sample synthesis, curriculum strategies, and architectural compression achieve the best practical results. Based on evidence across domains (vision, language, graphs, retrieval, reinforcement learning), we argue that KD should be used as part of an integrated compression pipeline that is task-aware, data-aware, and often combined with pruning, layer skipping, or module replacement to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Knight
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD methods span output-level soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online/self-distillation protocols. In practice, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case failures.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Robertson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or self-distillation—are combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to meet deployment constraints. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often preserves most teacher performance while enabling lower-latency, lower-memory, and privacy-aware deployment, but its success depends critically on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis strategies, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded performance on rare phenomena; these dependencies motivate configurable, task-aware KD pipelines rather than one-size-fits-all recipes.

papers_seen.author: Payne
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster, or specialized student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. A broad and practical toolbox has emerged—logit/soft-label transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free/zero-shot protocols, and architecture-aware combinations with pruning, quantization, and search—that is applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative settings. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance when applied carefully, but success depends on student capacity, teacher design/quality, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices; important open problems remain in principled theory, fairness/privacy-aware protocols, heterogeneous and federated settings, and robust distillation for generative and structured-output tasks.

papers_seen.author: Maldonado
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge by Mimicking Features
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a popular method to train efficient networks ("student") with the help of high-capacity networks ("teacher"). Traditional methods use the teacher's soft logits as extra supervision to train the student network. In this paper, we argue that it is more advantageous to make the student mimic the teacher's features in the penultimate layer. Not only the student can directly learn more effective information from the teacher feature, feature mimicking can also be applied for teachers trained without a softmax layer. Experiments show that it can achieve higher accuracy than traditional KD. To further facilitate feature mimicking, we decompose a feature vector into the magnitude and the direction. We argue that the teacher should give more freedom to the student feature's magnitude, and let the student pay more attention on mimicking the feature direction. To meet this requirement, we propose a loss term based on locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). With the help of this new loss, our method indeed mimics feature directions more accurately, relaxes constraints on feature magnitudes, and achieves state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We provide theoretical analyses of how LSH facilitates feature direction mimicking, and further extend feature mimicking to multi-label recognition and object detection.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing smaller, faster models from large teachers across vision, language, graph, and generative settings. KD supports deployment on constrained hardware, domain adaptation, improved interpretability, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware techniques. However, KD is not a panacea: its success depends on teacher quality, data and augmentation choices, objective design, and handling of distributional or architectural mismatch. Careful engineering and complementary compression techniques are necessary to realize KD's benefits in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Configurable First‑Line Strategy for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile, and empirically supported family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. It reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, the data regime, and deployment constraints. Therefore KD should be adopted as a first‑line, configurable component of integrated compression pipelines, combined with complementary methods and targeted safeguards to address known failure modes and domain-specific challenges.

papers_seen.author: Kane
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and mature family of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers, making it a central tool for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD has been extended far beyond simple logits matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. While KD routinely yields major efficiency gains and often recovers most teacher performance, reliable deployment requires task- and data-aware design choices and complementary compression methods; KD alone is not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Pham
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and broadly effective family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Empirical results across vision, language, ranking, detection, translation, federated settings, and reinforcement learning show KD reduces parameters and latency, can improve generalization, and enables domain- and privacy-aware workflows. At the same time, KD has important failure modes—dependence on distillation data and teacher–student alignment, capability mismatches, and transfer of teacher errors or biases—that require targeted solutions. Best practice is to treat KD as a central component of an integrated compression pipeline, combined with representation-level matching, data strategies, architecture-aware transformations, and privacy- or domain-specific adaptations.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: The Case for Pragmatic, Task-Aware Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated set of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers. Across vision, language, multimodal, and distributed settings, distillation can preserve or even improve accuracy while enabling deployments with constrained compute, memory, latency, and privacy requirements. However, its success depends on matching distillation objectives and procedures to task constraints (e.g., robustness, heterogeneity, data availability). When applied thoughtfully—using feature-based objectives, ensemble or adversarial strategies, data augmentation or data-free approaches, and task-adaptive compression—KD reliably delivers practical trade-offs between efficiency and effectiveness.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hoover
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best‑Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically essential tool for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across modalities. When integrated with complementary compression techniques and adapted to the data and deployment constraints, KD routinely yields students that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and inference cost. However, KD is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transferred signals, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data. Responsible application requires explicit mitigation of failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, degraded modeling of rare phenomena, distribution shift, and privacy risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline and provides practical recommendations for when and how to apply KD effectively in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Ramos
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely applied practical framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals), training protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, meta-learned teachers, curriculum-based schedules), and data regimes (full-data, few-shot, data-free, privacy-preserving federated protocols) has been developed and adapted across modalities. Empirical evidence shows KD frequently recovers a large portion of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, choice of distilled signals, and availability or synthesis of training data. Important open problems include handling teacher–student mismatches, preserving rare-token/long-tail behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher errors or biases, and formalizing best-practice co-designs that combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Gonzalez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal domains, a diverse set of distillation targets (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention or relational structure) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi‑teacher, data‑free or self‑distillation) have been developed. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover much of a teacher’s performance while enabling lower latency, reduced memory use, and new deployment modes; success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful design of the transfer objective. Practical pipelines commonly pair KD with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task‑aware procedures (layer mapping, curriculum, teacher adaptation) to meet deployment constraints. Important open problems include robust transfer under distribution shift and data scarcity, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, principled automated design for heterogeneous student architectures, and privacy‑aware or data‑free distillation strategies.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Practice, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central technique for transferring predictive capacity from large, high-capacity models (teachers) to smaller, efficient models (students). A wide range of KD objectives and protocols have been developed — from matching teacher logits to mimicking internal features, adversarially chosen samples, and data-free or zero-shot synthesis — and these are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of the teacher's performance and, when carefully engineered, support robustness, domain adaptation, privacy-preserving releases, and practical latency- or memory-constrained deployment. At the same time, KD’s effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and optimization choices, leaving open practical challenges around heterogeneous architectures, distribution shift, and preserving fine-grained behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

KD methods are diverse—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free protocols—and are most effective when integrated with complementary compression tools and deployment-aware data and optimization strategies. Empirical work shows KD routinely delivers substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss, but important limitations remain around teacher imperfection, teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, privacy, and reliable preservation of rare or structured behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Robbins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has established itself as a primary mechanism for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, speech, graph, and NLP tasks. KD methods range from matching teacher logits to aligning intermediate features and representations, and they are readily combined with quantization, pruning, ensembling, and domain-adaptation techniques. While KD frequently yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance degradation—and sometimes performance improvements—its success depends on careful method selection, teacher quality, data and sample selection, and complementary engineering such as layer alignment or teacher-student co-design.

papers_seen.author: Cohen
papers_seen.title: ALP-KD: Attention-Based Layer Projection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is considered as a training and compression strategy in which two neural networks, namely a teacher and a student, are coupled together during training. The teacher network is supposed to be a trustworthy predictor and the student tries to mimic its predictions. Usually, a student with a lighter architecture is selected so we can achieve compression and yet deliver high-quality results. In such a setting, distillation only happens for final predictions whereas the student could also benefit from teacher's supervision for internal components.   Motivated by this, we studied the problem of distillation for intermediate layers. Since there might not be a one-to-one alignment between student and teacher layers, existing techniques skip some teacher layers and only distill from a subset of them. This shortcoming directly impacts quality, so we instead propose a combinatorial technique which relies on attention. Our model fuses teacher-side information and takes each layer's significance into consideration, then performs distillation between combined teacher layers and those of the student. Using our technique, we distilled a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into 6-, 4-, and 2-layer counterparts and evaluated them on GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). Experimental results show that our combinatorial approach is able to outperform other existing techniques.

However, KD is context‑dependent: its effectiveness hinges on teacher–student alignment, data regime, and targeted safeguards against bias and distributional mismatch, so it should be applied as a configurable component within broader compression and deployment pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: AutoGAN-Distiller: Searching to Compress Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: The compression of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) has lately drawn attention, due to the increasing demand for deploying GANs into mobile devices for numerous applications such as image translation, enhancement and editing. However, compared to the substantial efforts to compressing other deep models, the research on compressing GANs (usually the generators) remains at its infancy stage. Existing GAN compression algorithms are limited to handling specific GAN architectures and losses. Inspired by the recent success of AutoML in deep compression, we introduce AutoML to GAN compression and develop an AutoGAN-Distiller (AGD) framework. Starting with a specifically designed efficient search space, AGD performs an end-to-end discovery for new efficient generators, given the target computational resource constraints. The search is guided by the original GAN model via knowledge distillation, therefore fulfilling the compression. AGD is fully automatic, standalone (i.e., needing no trained discriminators), and generically applicable to various GAN models. We evaluate AGD in two representative GAN tasks: image translation and super resolution. Without bells and whistles, AGD yields remarkably lightweight yet more competitive compressed models, that largely outperform existing alternatives. Our codes and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their accuracy. Empirical results across vision, language, retrieval, detection, generative models, and distributed settings show KD can close much of the performance gap between large and compact models, but best outcomes require tailoring what and how knowledge is transferred and combining distillation with complementary compression techniques and domain-aware procedures.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Mitigating Gender Bias in Distilled Language Models via Counterfactual Role Reversal
papers_seen.abstract: Language models excel at generating coherent text, and model compression techniques such as knowledge distillation have enabled their use in resource-constrained settings. However, these models can be biased in multiple ways, including the unfounded association of male and female genders with gender-neutral professions. Therefore, knowledge distillation without any fairness constraints may preserve or exaggerate the teacher model's biases onto the distilled model. To this end, we present a novel approach to mitigate gender disparity in text generation by learning a fair model during knowledge distillation. We propose two modifications to the base knowledge distillation based on counterfactual role reversal$\unicode{x2014}$modifying teacher probabilities and augmenting the training set. We evaluate gender polarity across professions in open-ended text generated from the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT$\unicode{x2012}$2 models and demonstrate a substantial reduction in gender disparity with only a minor compromise in utility. Finally, we observe that language models that reduce gender polarity in language generation do not improve embedding fairness or downstream classification fairness.

papers_seen.author: Garner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of methods for producing compact models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. Empirically, KD enables substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression and robustness measures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, faster, or more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, generative modeling, and multimodal tasks, KD methods trade off accuracy, latency, and resource use by transferring different forms of information (soft outputs, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, or synthesized training examples). Empirical work shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve generalization and deployment feasibility, but KD has practical limits tied to teacher–student capacity mismatch, data availability, bias transfer, and degradation on low-frequency phenomena. Effective deployment mixes careful choice of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, multi-teacher or confidence-weighting schemes, and integration with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Kane
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and mature family of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers, making it a central tool for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD has been extended far beyond simple logits matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. While KD routinely yields major efficiency gains and often recovers most teacher performance, reliable deployment requires task- and data-aware design choices and complementary compression methods; KD alone is not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, but Imperfect Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably transfers behavior from large teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in latency, memory and compute while preserving much of task performance. KD techniques span logits/soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level alignment, relational and contrastive signals, online and multi-teacher protocols, and data-free or domain-adaptive variants. Empirical evidence shows KD is a practical first-line strategy for deployment across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, but it is not a standalone cure: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, objective design, and careful integration with complementary compression tools. For robust, real-world deployment, KD should be treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with targeted engineering to mitigate failure modes such as capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad and practical toolkit—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and multi-teacher or self-distillation schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD frequently produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful design choices for distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Cervantes
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and specialized domains shows KD can recover much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and communication costs. Successful distillation depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, data availability and preparation, and integration with complementary compression methods. Treated as a toolbox—combining soft-targets with representation matching, progressive schedules, curriculum selection, and pruning/quantization—KD is a first‑order approach for real‑world compression when practitioners explicitly address its known limitations.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher–student soft-label transfer into a flexible set of methods that enable compact, fast, and often more robust models across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings. When designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and deployment demands, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, layer skipping, meta-learned teachers, or generative replay) reliably yields practical gains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to preserve robustness and fairness. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in compression pipelines: powerful and broadly applicable when paired with principled, task-centered decisions, but demand-aware and tuned to deployment objectives.
