papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, task‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners match soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data to train compact students. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and data strategies, and explicit teacher–student alignment; however, important limitations remain in distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, heterogeneous architectures, privacy and federated settings, and principled teacher selection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open challenges distilled from the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Evans
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses or adapts large or multi-modal models into smaller, faster, or specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, speech, generative models, and domain- or privacy-constrained settings, a diverse toolbox has been developed—soft-label supervision, intermediate feature and attention matching, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, self- and online-distillation, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and architecture-aware adaptations (e.g., pruning, layer skipping, NAS). Empirical results show that appropriately designed KD pipelines can produce compact models that approach teacher performance and enable deployment in resource-constrained environments, while practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and selection, and optimization design. Remaining challenges include principled theory linking teacher signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under heterogeneous architectures or non-iid data, privacy-and-fairness-aware protocols, and extending KD to complex generative and structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and within diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free/zero‑shot approaches). Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and can sometimes improve student generalization when objectives, data, and teacher–student design are well matched; however, success is context dependent and sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution shift, and risks of transferring teacher errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines carefully chosen distillation signals, layer-mapping and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) while adopting targeted safeguards for low‑frequency behaviors, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Schmidt
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically effective approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces inference cost, memory, and communication while often preserving most of a teacher's performance—but it is context dependent, requiring careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. Treated as the configurable core of a compression pipeline and combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware data strategies), KD enables deployable models for latency- and resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive settings; however, practitioners must explicitly address failure modes such as capacity mismatch, domain shift, low-frequency errors, and propagated biases.

papers_seen.author: Harrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically driven family of techniques to transfer knowledge from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Modern KD encompasses simple soft-target matching as well as richer objectives that imitate intermediate representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and contrastive signals; it is commonly combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Distillation succeeds across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks when aligned to task objectives, teacher–student capacity, and available data, but it has well-documented failure modes (capacity mismatch, teacher bias propagation, domain shift, and scarce/private data) that motivate task-aware design, data strategies, and privacy-preserving or data-free approaches.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models while retaining much of the original performance. A diverse family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial schemes, multi-teacher and self-supervised variants—has been developed and adapted across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs, and generative models). Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on choices of distillation targets, teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-specific adaptations. Open challenges include handling mismatches in capacity or data, preserving rare-token or long-tail behavior, and formalizing best practices for combining KD with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Short
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Conditional, and Integrative Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential method for producing compact models from larger teachers across modalities in deep learning and NLP. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD can transfer predictive behavior, intermediate representations, and inductive biases that yield substantial gains in latency, memory, and often accuracy. However, KD has concrete failure modes—teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias transfer, and distribution shift—that limit its effectiveness when used alone. The strongest, most reliable outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that combines careful teacher engineering, targeted distillation signals, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation.

papers_seen.author: Velasquez
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large (teacher) models to smaller (student) models. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, or self-distillation), and by constraints on data, privacy, and deployment hardware. Across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning, KD produces compact models that often retain much of teacher performance while enabling lower latency, lower memory, and operation under communication- or privacy-constrained settings. However, gains depend on teacher quality, data used for distillation, and architectural alignment; practical pipelines therefore combine KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design choices to close optimization and generalization gaps.

papers_seen.author: Davidson
papers_seen.title: Robust Re-Identification by Multiple Views Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: To achieve robustness in Re-Identification, standard methods leverage tracking information in a Video-To-Video fashion. However, these solutions face a large drop in performance for single image queries (e.g., Image-To-Video setting). Recent works address this severe degradation by transferring temporal information from a Video-based network to an Image-based one. In this work, we devise a training strategy that allows the transfer of a superior knowledge, arising from a set of views depicting the target object. Our proposal - Views Knowledge Distillation (VKD) - pins this visual variety as a supervision signal within a teacher-student framework, where the teacher educates a student who observes fewer views. As a result, the student outperforms not only its teacher but also the current state-of-the-art in Image-To-Video by a wide margin (6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId and 5% on VeRi-776). A thorough analysis - on Person, Vehicle and Animal Re-ID - investigates the properties of VKD from a qualitatively and quantitatively perspective. Code is available at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

papers_seen.author: Molina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques that transfer predictive behavior and internal representations from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models to achieve substantial reductions in model size and latency while preserving much of task performance. KD methods have diversified from classical logits-matching to include feature and attention matching, relational and many-to-many layer mappings, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and task- or data-aware adaptations. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, retrieval, and multimodal tasks, KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Although KD often yields strong empirical gains, its success depends on the choice and quality of teacher(s), the distilled signals, available data and augmentation strategy, and careful alignment between teacher and student; open challenges remain in robustness, distribution shift, low-data or data-free settings, and avoiding propagation of teacher errors.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted framework for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, speech, generation, retrieval, and detection tasks, a rich toolbox of distillation signals and protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to intermediate representation, attention/relational objectives, curriculum and online schemes, and data-free or adversarial sample synthesis. KD is most effective when combined with task-aware design, complementary compression methods, and careful handling of data and teacher–student compatibility. While distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, and privacy constraints, limitations remain related to capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias transfer, robustness under distribution shift, and low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Duran
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression — Powerful but Not Sufficient
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable, practically proven approach for transferring capabilities from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce latency, memory use, and energy while preserving much of task performance. KD excels when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, it is not a universal remedy. Reliable deployment requires treating KD as a configurable component of integrated compression pipelines with explicit provisions for teacher quality, data scarcity, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns.

papers_seen.author: Pennington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used and flexible approach for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models in deep learning and NLP. Over the past decade a wide family of KD variants has been developed — logits/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture or neural architecture search). Empirical evidence shows that KD often recovers a large share of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, which data to use or synthesize, and how to mitigate failure modes such as transferred bias, teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Osborne
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge from Deep Networks with Applications to Healthcare Domain
papers_seen.abstract: Exponential growth in Electronic Healthcare Records (EHR) has resulted in new opportunities and urgent needs for discovery of meaningful data-driven representations and patterns of diseases in Computational Phenotyping research. Deep Learning models have shown superior performance for robust prediction in computational phenotyping tasks, but suffer from the issue of model interpretability which is crucial for clinicians involved in decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a novel knowledge-distillation approach called Interpretable Mimic Learning, to learn interpretable phenotype features for making robust prediction while mimicking the performance of deep learning models. Our framework uses Gradient Boosting Trees to learn interpretable features from deep learning models such as Stacked Denoising Autoencoder and Long Short-Term Memory. Exhaustive experiments on a real-world clinical time-series dataset show that our method obtains similar or better performance than the deep learning models, and it provides interpretable phenotypes for clinical decision making.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Singh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Applications, Practical Trade-offs, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. KD methods vary in what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention patterns, relations, or generated samples), in the availability of original training data (data-rich, data-free, federated), and in whether distillation is performed offline, online, or jointly with teacher training. Across vision, language, ranking/retrieval, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, carefully designed distillation objectives combined with complementary compression mechanisms (pruning, quantization, architecture search) routinely yield compact models that approach teacher performance under practical constraints. However, the effectiveness of KD depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data selection and augmentation, and mitigation of risks such as propagated bias, privacy leakage, and poor modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines, using multi-teacher and confidence-weighting strategies, layer- and feature-matching, student-aware teacher design, and privacy-preserving or data-free synthesis when needed.

papers_seen.author: Zuniga
papers_seen.title: Large scale distributed neural network training through online distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Techniques such as ensembling and distillation promise model quality improvements when paired with almost any base model. However, due to increased test-time cost (for ensembles) and increased complexity of the training pipeline (for distillation), these techniques are challenging to use in industrial settings. In this paper we explore a variant of distillation which is relatively straightforward to use as it does not require a complicated multi-stage setup or many new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that online distillation enables us to use extra parallelism to fit very large datasets about twice as fast. Crucially, we can still speed up training even after we have already reached the point at which additional parallelism provides no benefit for synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. Two neural networks trained on disjoint subsets of the data can share knowledge by encouraging each model to agree with the predictions the other model would have made. These predictions can come from a stale version of the other model so they can be safely computed using weights that only rarely get transmitted. Our second claim is that online distillation is a cost-effective way to make the exact predictions of a model dramatically more reproducible. We support our claims using experiments on the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, ImageNet, and the largest to-date dataset used for neural language modeling, containing $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens and based on the Common Crawl repository of web data.

papers_seen.author: Brennan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Practical, and Careful Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach for compressing large neural models into compact, efficient students while preserving much of their performance. Across logits-based soft-label transfer, intermediate feature and attention matching, curriculum and sample-selection methods, adversarial and data-free variants, and module-replacement and pruning hybrids, KD enables deployment in latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained settings, supports domain and modality transfer, and is complementary to quantization and architecture search. However, reliable application requires attention to teacher quality, layer mapping, sample selection, and interactions with regularization and pretraining; when designed for the target task and environment, KD routinely yields compact models that approach teacher performance and unlock real-world deployment scenarios.

papers_seen.author: Medina
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. The literature develops a diverse toolbox—logit/soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or zero-shot protocols, and teacher-aware or student-aware training—often combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities (vision, language, speech, graphs, multimodal) when teacher–student compatibility, data strategy, and optimization design are carefully managed; it also faces limitations arising from dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher artifacts, especially on long-tail or low-frequency phenomena. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of compression and deployment workflows, tuned for task constraints and complemented by safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students that preserves much of teacher functionality while reducing latency, memory, and compute. KD methods span soft-logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and can be combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD delivers substantial practical benefits across modalities and tasks when applied as part of a task-aware compression pipeline, but it is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for producing compact models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The approach spans simple soft-label transfer to richer objectives that match intermediate representations, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and supports many protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free variants). KD is most effective when integrated into a broader compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum learning, and data strategies—and when choices about transfer targets, layer alignment, and data are tailored to task and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it has concrete failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, degradation on rare phenomena, privacy and fairness risks) that require targeted mitigations and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Sandoval
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Conditional Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable framework that enables compact, efficient models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. KD methods span logits, intermediate-feature and relational matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and cross-modal variants, and complementary integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. While KD often recovers much of a teacher’s performance and provides regularization benefits, its practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability and selection, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Effective deployment treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a one-shot cure, and addresses robustness, privacy, and distribution-shift concerns through protocol design and complementary techniques.

papers_seen.author: Parker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression strategies transfer information from larger or differently structured models to smaller, more efficient ones. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—matching teacher logits, intermediate representations, attention, or relational structure—enable large reductions in latency, memory, and communication while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical deployment benefits from combining KD with complementary methods (pre-training, pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from careful choices about what and how to transfer, which data to use, and how to design teacher-student pairings. Key challenges remain around teacher error propagation, low-frequency/rare behavior preservation, data and domain mismatch, privacy constraints, and heterogeneous deployment targets.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.author: Wong
papers_seen.title: Embracing the Dark Knowledge: Domain Generalization Using Regularized Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Though convolutional neural networks are widely used in different tasks, lack of generalization capability in the absence of sufficient and representative data is one of the challenges that hinder their practical application. In this paper, we propose a simple, effective, and plug-and-play training strategy named Knowledge Distillation for Domain Generalization (KDDG) which is built upon a knowledge distillation framework with the gradient filter as a novel regularization term. We find that both the ``richer dark knowledge" from the teacher network, as well as the gradient filter we proposed, can reduce the difficulty of learning the mapping which further improves the generalization ability of the model. We also conduct experiments extensively to show that our framework can significantly improve the generalization capability of deep neural networks in different tasks including image classification, segmentation, reinforcement learning by comparing our method with existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques. Last but not the least, we propose to adopt two metrics to analyze our proposed method in order to better understand how our proposed method benefits the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

papers_seen.author: Bowman
papers_seen.title: TRILLsson: Distilled Universal Paralinguistic Speech Representations
papers_seen.abstract: Recent advances in self-supervision have dramatically improved the quality of speech representations. However, deployment of state-of-the-art embedding models on devices has been restricted due to their limited public availability and large resource footprint. Our work addresses these issues by publicly releasing a collection of paralinguistic speech models that are small and near state-of-the-art performance. Our approach is based on knowledge distillation, and our models are distilled on public data only. We explore different architectures and thoroughly evaluate our models on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Our largest distilled model is less than 15% the size of the original model (314MB vs 2.2GB), achieves over 96% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks, and is trained on 6.5% the data. The smallest model is 1% in size (22MB) and achieves over 90% the accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Our models outperform the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 model on 6 of 7 tasks, and our smallest model outperforms the open source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks despite being 7% the size.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Garner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context‑Dependent Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of methods for producing compact models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teachers to smaller students. Empirically, KD enables substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while often preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD is not automatic: its success depends on deliberate choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and integration with complementary compression and robustness measures. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Ball
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Conditional Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while often preserving—and sometimes improving—task performance. KD methods operate at logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or decision boundaries and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data- or privacy-aware procedures. KD delivers strong practical benefits across modalities and tasks but requires careful teacher–student alignment, attention to data and privacy constraints, and complementary techniques to address capacity gaps, domain shift, and rare-token behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applied family of techniques for producing smaller, faster models from larger teachers by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD methods (logits, features, attention, relational, contrastive, multi‑teacher, online/self and data‑free variants) are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation to meet deployment constraints, but their success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful protocol design.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large neural models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad and practical toolbox has been developed—output-level (soft-target) matching, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, adversarial and data-free methods, online and multi-teacher protocols, and curriculum- or architecture-aware pipelines. Empirical evidence shows distilled students often recover most teacher performance and can improve generalization when objectives, layer mappings, and data choices are well matched to student capacity and task constraints. Success requires careful design around what to transfer, how to align layers and inputs, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate bias, rare-token degradation, and teacher errors; combining KD with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search) and using task-aware curricula or projectors typically yields better accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Taylor
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely adopted approach for producing compact models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models. The approach spans simple soft-label transfer to richer objectives that match intermediate representations, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and supports many protocols (offline, online/co-distillation, multi-teacher, self-distillation and data-free variants). KD is most effective when integrated into a broader compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum learning, and data strategies—and when choices about transfer targets, layer alignment, and data are tailored to task and deployment constraints. Empirical work shows KD often preserves most of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, but it has concrete failure modes (teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, degradation on rare phenomena, privacy and fairness risks) that require targeted mitigations and evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Ross
papers_seen.title: Ensemble Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation describes a method for training a student network to perform better by learning from a stronger teacher network. Translating a sentence with an Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is time expensive and having a smaller model speeds up this process. We demonstrate how to transfer the translation quality of an ensemble and an oracle BLEU teacher network into a single NMT system. Further, we present translation improvements from a teacher network that has the same architecture and dimensions of the student network. As the training of the student model is still expensive, we introduce a data filtering method based on the knowledge of the teacher model that not only speeds up the training, but also leads to better translation quality. Our techniques need no code change and can be easily reproduced with any NMT architecture to speed up the decoding process.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD variants include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structures, ensembling multiple teachers, adversarial and data-free distillation, and student- or task-aware curricula. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted for settings with limited or private data, federated training, and non‑standard outputs (e.g., generative or structured prediction). Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Ongoing research focuses on principled objectives, robust and private distillation, and task‑aware architectures for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary but Insufficient Core for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework that transfers information from large teacher models into smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving much of the teacher's performance. KD methods include logit/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or adversarial example synthesis. Empirical evidence across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks shows KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment on resource-constrained platforms; however, KD alone does not resolve challenges such as teacher–student capacity mismatch, data heterogeneity and scarcity, preservation of rare-token or long-tail behavior, and the transfer of teacher biases. Effective compression pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable core component that must be combined with task-aware engineering, complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search, hardware-aware design), and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical set of techniques for transferring behaviors and representations from larger or otherwise stronger models (teachers) to smaller or more constrained models (students). KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, speech, graph learning, reinforcement and lifelong learning—yielding work on algorithmic variants (self-distillation, multi-teacher, curriculum, adversarial, relational and loss-function innovations), data- and privacy-aware designs, and hardware-aware/low-precision deployments. Empirical work demonstrates KD can substantially reduce model size and latency while preserving much of the teacher performance, but theoretical and optimization limits remain: students often cannot perfectly match teachers and training/data choices matter greatly. Practical advances address these limits through better supervision signals, input-side design (data augmentation), alternate discrepancy measures, and privacy/communication constraints. The field continues to move toward more efficient, fair, private and domain-robust distilled models suitable for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Francis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques constitute a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. The field has expanded beyond simple logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and online protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when student capacity, data availability, and teacher–student alignment are appropriately managed, but important challenges remain including handling low-frequency phenomena, teacher bias propagation, distributional mismatch, and reliable transfer under data scarcity or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hicks
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, practical toolbox for compressing large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. The field encompasses a diverse set of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational maps, contrastive signals), multiple training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, multi-teacher and ensemble schemes), and data strategies that include data-driven, synthetic, and data-free approaches. KD is routinely integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and applied across modalities (NLP, vision, speech, generative models, recommender and graph systems). Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the distillation signal and its alignment, and the availability and curation of data; remaining challenges include preserving low-frequency behaviors, avoiding transfer of teacher biases, and maintaining robustness under distribution shift and limited-data regimes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an overall compression pipeline with task-aware signal selection, careful teacher–student co-design, and targeted mitigations for privacy, fairness, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings. KD techniques transfer teacher behavior via soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational objectives, and can be extended to data-free, privacy-preserving, and adversarial regimes. Best results arise when distillation is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search); remaining challenges include data- or domain-limited scenarios, teacher–student mismatch, robustness and privacy trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Parsons
papers_seen.title: Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent work has shown that more effective dense retrieval models can be obtained by distilling ranking knowledge from an existing base re-ranking model. In this paper, we propose a generic curriculum learning based optimization framework called CL-DRD that controls the difficulty level of training data produced by the re-ranking (teacher) model. CL-DRD iteratively optimizes the dense retrieval (student) model by increasing the difficulty of the knowledge distillation data made available to it. In more detail, we initially provide the student model coarse-grained preference pairs between documents in the teacher's ranking and progressively move towards finer-grained pairwise document ordering requirements. In our experiments, we apply a simple implementation of the CL-DRD framework to enhance two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models. Experiments on three public passage retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

papers_seen.author: Moreno
papers_seen.title: Learning Perception-Aware Agile Flight in Cluttered Environments
papers_seen.abstract: Recently, neural control policies have outperformed existing model-based planning-and-control methods for autonomously navigating quadrotors through cluttered environments in minimum time. However, they are not perception aware, a crucial requirement in vision-based navigation due to the camera's limited field of view and the underactuated nature of a quadrotor. We propose a learning-based system that achieves perception-aware, agile flight in cluttered environments. Our method combines imitation learning with reinforcement learning (RL) by leveraging a privileged learning-by-cheating framework. Using RL, we first train a perception-aware teacher policy with full-state information to fly in minimum time through cluttered environments. Then, we use imitation learning to distill its knowledge into a vision-based student policy that only perceives the environment via a camera. Our approach tightly couples perception and control, showing a significant advantage in computation speed (10 times faster) and success rate. We demonstrate the closed-loop control performance using hardware-in-the-loop simulation.

papers_seen.author: Cook
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a pragmatic pathway to compress large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and intermediate representations. Empirical work across vision, speech, language, multimodal and graph domains shows KD can retain much of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory when combined with complementary compression tools. However, real-world success requires careful choice of teacher signals, data strategies, and optimization protocols to address capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and modality or deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gray
papers_seen.title: BERT-of-Theseus: Compressing BERT by Progressive Module Replacing
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we propose a novel model compression approach to effectively compress BERT by progressive module replacing. Our approach first divides the original BERT into several modules and builds their compact substitutes. Then, we randomly replace the original modules with their substitutes to train the compact modules to mimic the behavior of the original modules. We progressively increase the probability of replacement through the training. In this way, our approach brings a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models. Compared to the previous knowledge distillation approaches for BERT compression, our approach does not introduce any additional loss function. Our approach outperforms existing knowledge distillation approaches on GLUE benchmark, showing a new perspective of model compression.

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Extract the Knowledge of Graph Neural Networks and Go Beyond it: An Effective Knowledge Distillation Framework
papers_seen.abstract: Semi-supervised learning on graphs is an important problem in the machine learning area. In recent years, state-of-the-art classification methods based on graph neural networks (GNNs) have shown their superiority over traditional ones such as label propagation. However, the sophisticated architectures of these neural models will lead to a complex prediction mechanism, which could not make full use of valuable prior knowledge lying in the data, e.g., structurally correlated nodes tend to have the same class. In this paper, we propose a framework based on knowledge distillation to address the above issues. Our framework extracts the knowledge of an arbitrary learned GNN model (teacher model), and injects it into a well-designed student model. The student model is built with two simple prediction mechanisms, i.e., label propagation and feature transformation, which naturally preserves structure-based and feature-based prior knowledge, respectively. In specific, we design the student model as a trainable combination of parameterized label propagation and feature transformation modules. As a result, the learned student can benefit from both prior knowledge and the knowledge in GNN teachers for more effective predictions. Moreover, the learned student model has a more interpretable prediction process than GNNs. We conduct experiments on five public benchmark datasets and employ seven GNN models including GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII and GLP as the teacher models. Experimental results show that the learned student model can consistently outperform its corresponding teacher model by 1.4% - 4.7% on average. Code and data are available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

papers_seen.author: Fox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Sensitive Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques that transfers behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller students, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost and model size while often preserving most of the original performance. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline—choosing appropriate transfer targets, adapting objectives to student capacity and data regimes, and combining distillation with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher imperfections (including bias), data scarcity or privacy constraints, and difficulty preserving rare or structured behaviors require targeted mitigations, careful evaluation, and continued methodological and theoretical work.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses many techniques — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure — and is effective across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks when designed around task constraints and student capacity. However, KD is not a stand‑alone solution: its practical success depends on data availability, teacher quality, student architecture, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, robustness deficits, and low-frequency behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies (including augmentation and data-free synthesis), and robustness or privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Henderson
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a practical, flexible approach to compressing large neural models into resource-efficient students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks — from language and retrieval to vision, generation, and graph learning — distillation techniques enable trade-offs between accuracy, compute, and memory that make deployment feasible on constrained hardware. However, the effectiveness of distillation depends strongly on the distillation objective, the information transferred (probabilities, internal representations, or structured signals), availability of original data, and care to avoid transferring undesirable teacher properties. When combined with complementary compression techniques (quantization, architecture search, low-precision training, or curriculum strategies), distillation can yield compact models that approach or sometimes even exceed teacher performance while meeting practical latency and size constraints.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Flexible Path to Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically effective family of techniques for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and often more socially or operationally suitable models. Across vision, speech, and NLP tasks KD has been shown to preserve much of teacher performance while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and in privacy-sensitive or distributed settings. KD is most effective when combined with complementary practices such as pre-training, data augmentation, careful layer-matching, ensemble guidance, and hardware-aware pruning.

papers_seen.author: Bailey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely used family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. The literature develops multi-level transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure), multi‑teacher and online variants, data-aware and data‑free protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely recovers much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and mapping between teacher and student are carefully managed; however, success is context-dependent and limited by optimization gaps, data scarcity, capacity mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher artifacts or biases. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable component of broader compression workflows tailored to deployment constraints such as latency, memory, privacy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Rosales
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teachers into compact students. KD variants—ranging from logits and feature matching to relational, contrastive, and data-free protocols—have been demonstrated across vision, speech, and NLP to deliver favorable accuracy–efficiency trade-offs. At the same time, KD’s success depends on teacher quality, signal choice, data regime, and careful training design, and it is most reliable when integrated with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a central, configurable element of any compression pipeline, but not as a standalone solution: use KD deliberately, combine it with other methods, and adopt practices that mitigate its failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Vaughn
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Demand-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an empirically powerful and practically versatile approach for compressing large models and transferring behavior to smaller students. KD succeeds across modalities by matching logits, intermediate features, attention, or relational structure and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Recent work extends KD to settings with no original data, privacy constraints, heterogeneous architectures, and specialized tasks (graphs, non‑autoregressive generation, lifelong learning). However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher–student design, data strategies, and task-aware objectives, and important open problems remain (capacity mismatch, teacher bias transfer, preserving low-frequency behaviors, principled layer mapping, and rigorous theoretical understanding).

papers_seen.author: Cannon
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression methods form a broad, practical toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, efficient student models. Over the past decade KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to representation-level matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data- or privacy-aware protocols—have been adapted to many tasks and modalities (vision, language, speech, multimodal, generative models, and federated settings). Empirical work shows KD frequently preserves most teacher performance while enabling large reductions in latency, memory, and parameter count; success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability, and optimization. Remaining challenges include principled theory for when and what to transfer, reliable distillation across heterogeneous architectures and non‑i.i.d. data, mitigation of bias and teacher errors, and robust data-free or privacy-preserving protocols.

papers_seen.author: Murphy
papers_seen.title: What is known about Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression strategies form a broad, practically driven toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or specialized teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, graph learning, self-supervision, and reinforcement learning—research has developed many algorithmic variants (logit and feature matching, attention/relational objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes), system-level protocols (federated, black-box, data-free), and architecture-aware methods (task-adaptive compression, neural architecture search, pruning and quantization combinations). Empirically, KD often substantially reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving a large fraction of teacher performance, but its success depends on teacher–student alignment, available data and augmentations, and task-specific design; remaining challenges include teacher bias transfer, degradation on low-frequency phenomena, domain shift, and heterogeneous-device constraints. Practical deployments balance distilled signals, data strategies, and architecture choices to achieve required trade-offs between accuracy, efficiency, privacy, and robustness.
