papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, the data used for distillation, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines — combining logits and feature objectives, projector modules, multi‑teacher or teacher‑adaptive designs, and data‑aware schedules — yields the most reliable results in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Feature-map-level Online Adversarial Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Feature maps contain rich information about image intensity and spatial correlation. However, previous online knowledge distillation methods only utilize the class probabilities. Thus in this paper, we propose an online knowledge distillation method that transfers not only the knowledge of the class probabilities but also that of the feature map using the adversarial training framework. We train multiple networks simultaneously by employing discriminators to distinguish the feature map distributions of different networks. Each network has its corresponding discriminator which discriminates the feature map from its own as fake while classifying that of the other network as real. By training a network to fool the corresponding discriminator, it can learn the other network's feature map distribution. We show that our method performs better than the conventional direct alignment method such as L1 and is more suitable for online distillation. Also, we propose a novel cyclic learning scheme for training more than two networks together. We have applied our method to various network architectures on the classification task and discovered a significant improvement of performance especially in the case of training a pair of a small network and a large one.

papers_seen.author: Cooke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, detection, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and attention-level imitation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher protocols—enable substantial efficiency gains while often preserving much of teacher performance. Success depends on choices about what to transfer, data strategy, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression (e.g., pruning, quantization, or architecture search). Practical deployments use task-aware adaptations, confidence- or curriculum-based weighting, and privacy- or federated-aware designs; remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, distribution shift, rare-output transfer, and principled theory for optimal transfer.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Barker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large, high-performing neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad and practical toolkit—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free protocols, and multi-teacher or self-distillation schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, speech, graphs, and generative tasks. KD frequently produces compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful design choices for distillation targets, teacher–student compatibility, data strategies, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Practical Model Compression: Central, Context-Sensitive, and Best Used in Hybrid Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. KD reliably transfers predictive behavior and internal structure across vision and NLP tasks and often recovers much of a teacher's performance, but it is not a universal cure: its reliability depends on what is distilled, how teachers and students are aligned, data availability, and complementary compression choices. Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline yields the most robust and deployable outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization instability limit off‑the‑shelf success. The strongest practical outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines that also employ pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task‑aware data procedures.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Is a Core Tool for Model Compression and Efficient NLP/Deep Learning Systems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile technique for producing compact, fast, and privacy-aware models across modalities. KD not only compresses large pretrained models for low-latency deployment, but also enables domain adaptation, federated and data-free scenarios, continual learning, and improved student generalization when combined with feature-level and architectural interventions. Together, methodological advances—ranging from feature mimicking and projector ensembles to student-friendly teachers and adversarial/data-free generation—make KD an essential component of modern model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Douglas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Sensitive Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile framework for transferring behavior and representations from large teacher models to smaller student models. When applied with appropriate objectives, layer mappings, data strategies, and safeguards, KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, graph, and generative tasks. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it interacts with teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, distribution shift, and fairness concerns. Treating KD as a configurable core of a compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, curriculum strategies, and privacy-aware protocols—yields the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Francis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques constitute a practical toolkit for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. The field has expanded beyond simple logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free generation, curriculum and online protocols, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when student capacity, data availability, and teacher–student alignment are appropriately managed, but important challenges remain including handling low-frequency phenomena, teacher bias propagation, distributional mismatch, and reliable transfer under data scarcity or privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related compression methods aim to transfer behavior and representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, efficient ones while retaining task performance. Across modalities and tasks, research has developed many complementary mechanisms — soft-label mimicry, intermediate representation matching, teacher-student curriculum designs, self-distillation, multi-teacher and online schemes, data- or generator-based transfer, and domain- or modality-specific adaptations — to balance accuracy, latency, and resource constraints. Empirical work shows that properly designed distillation can recover most teacher performance (and in some settings even surpass it) while enabling deployment on constrained hardware and improving reproducibility and privacy. Success depends on the distillation targets, the teacher-student pairing and training regime, the use of auxiliary data or synthetic examples, and task-specific modifications.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: Alvarado
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses large, high-performing neural networks into smaller, faster models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations from teacher to student. A broad family of distillation techniques has been developed—logit (soft-label) matching, feature and layer-wise mimicry, multi-teacher and confidence-weighted schemes, adversarial and contrastive objectives, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enabling deployment across vision, language, graphs, recommender systems, and federated settings. While distillation often preserves most teacher performance and can even improve student generalization, effectiveness depends on what is transferred, layer alignment, teacher quality, availability and match of data, and complementary compression methods. This synthesis summarizes the operational variants, key empirical findings, domain-specific applications, common failure modes, and practical recommendations distilled from the provided studies.

papers_seen.author: Bishop
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical framework for producing compact, faster models by transferring behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models. Across vision, language, retrieval, and generative tasks, KD variants—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature and attention imitation, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes—have been developed and combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of transferred errors and rare-output degradation. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical findings, practical guidance, and open challenges for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central and practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. A rich family of techniques — soft-target/logit distillation, feature and attention matching, projector and layer-mapping strategies, multi-teacher and teacher-free variants, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and privacy-aware formulations — enable large efficiency gains while trading off fidelity, robustness, and generalization in task- and data-dependent ways. Best practice is to treat KD as a toolbox: select what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which auxiliary methods (augmentation, selective sampling, privacy mechanisms) to combine for a given deployment constraint.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied collection of techniques for transferring information from large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, graphs, retrieval, and multimodal problems, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, curriculum strategies, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enable deployable models that trade modest accuracy loss for substantial gains in latency, memory, and energy use. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers and capacities, and how to prepare data), but success requires managing failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and sensitivity to distillation data. This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature reports about methods, mechanisms, applications, best practices, and open problems for KD-based model compression.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Mayo
papers_seen.title: Rethinking Soft Labels for Knowledge Distillation: A Bias-Variance Tradeoff Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is an effective approach to leverage a well-trained network or an ensemble of them, named as the teacher, to guide the training of a student network. The outputs from the teacher network are used as soft labels for supervising the training of a new network. Recent studies \citep{muller2019does,yuan2020revisiting} revealed an intriguing property of the soft labels that making labels soft serves as a good regularization to the student network. From the perspective of statistical learning, regularization aims to reduce the variance, however how bias and variance change is not clear for training with soft labels. In this paper, we investigate the bias-variance tradeoff brought by distillation with soft labels. Specifically, we observe that during training the bias-variance tradeoff varies sample-wisely. Further, under the same distillation temperature setting, we observe that the distillation performance is negatively associated with the number of some specific samples, which are named as regularization samples since these samples lead to bias increasing and variance decreasing. Nevertheless, we empirically find that completely filtering out regularization samples also deteriorates distillation performance. Our discoveries inspired us to propose the novel weighted soft labels to help the network adaptively handle the sample-wise bias-variance tradeoff. Experiments on standard evaluation benchmarks validate the effectiveness of our method. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation}.

papers_seen.author: Lynch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthetic Overview
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practical set of techniques for transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The approach has diversified beyond simple logits-matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, multiple training protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free), and task-aware adaptations such as layer mapping, projector modules, and synthetic-data strategies. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can deliver substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining most of a teacher’s performance; success in practice requires careful matching of distillation signals, attention to teacher–student alignment, and integration with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. It enables deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints across vision, language, and multimodal tasks while supporting robustness and transfer when combined with task-aware design. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its effectiveness depends on what is transferred, teacher and data quality, architectural alignment, and complementary compression techniques, and it can propagate teacher biases and fail on low-frequency or out-of-distribution phenomena unless mitigated.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Arnold
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Benefits, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, more efficient students to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, and multimodal tasks, KD has evolved from simple logits-matching into a configurable toolkit that includes feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance when applied with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and appropriate data strategies; however, important failure modes remain (teacher quality, student capacity, limited data, distribution shift, and propagation of biases), motivating integrated pipelines and targeted mitigation strategies for real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Engine for Practical Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical, widely adopted approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers in deep learning and NLP. KD methods vary by what is transferred (soft targets, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), how transfers are staged (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free), and which complementary compression techniques are combined (pruning, quantization, architecture search). In practice, KD reliably reduces latency and memory while often preserving much of teacher performance, but it has failure modes—teacher error propagation, difficulty with low-frequency phenomena, capacity and optimization mismatch, and privacy or data-limited regimes—that require task-aware design and integration with other compression strategies. Treated as a configurable component of compression pipelines and paired with targeted remedies, KD is a practical core mechanism for deployable model compression rather than a standalone solution.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Reid
papers_seen.title: Moonshine: Distilling with Cheap Convolutions
papers_seen.abstract: Many engineers wish to deploy modern neural networks in memory-limited settings; but the development of flexible methods for reducing memory use is in its infancy, and there is little knowledge of the resulting cost-benefit. We propose structural model distillation for memory reduction using a strategy that produces a student architecture that is a simple transformation of the teacher architecture: no redesign is needed, and the same hyperparameters can be used. Using attention transfer, we provide Pareto curves/tables for distillation of residual networks with four benchmark datasets, indicating the memory versus accuracy payoff. We show that substantial memory savings are possible with very little loss of accuracy, and confirm that distillation provides student network performance that is better than training that student architecture directly on data.

papers_seen.author: Shaffer
papers_seen.title: Selective Knowledge Distillation for Neural Machine Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models achieve state-of-the-art performance on many translation benchmarks. As an active research field in NMT, knowledge distillation is widely applied to enhance the model's performance by transferring teacher model's knowledge on each training sample. However, previous work rarely discusses the different impacts and connections among these samples, which serve as the medium for transferring teacher knowledge. In this paper, we design a novel protocol that can effectively analyze the different impacts of samples by comparing various samples' partitions. Based on above protocol, we conduct extensive experiments and find that the teacher's knowledge is not the more, the better. Knowledge over specific samples may even hurt the whole performance of knowledge distillation. Finally, to address these issues, we propose two simple yet effective strategies, i.e., batch-level and global-level selections, to pick suitable samples for distillation. We evaluate our approaches on two large-scale machine translation tasks, WMT'14 English->German and WMT'19 Chinese->English. Experimental results show that our approaches yield up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points improvements over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Model Compression and Transfer in Deep Learning
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger systems. Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

papers_seen.author: Wood
papers_seen.title: What Makes a "Good" Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation -- A Statistical Perspective
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a general neural network training approach that uses a teacher model to guide the student model. Existing works mainly study KD from the network output side (e.g., trying to design a better KD loss function), while few have attempted to understand it from the input side. Especially, its interplay with data augmentation (DA) has not been well understood. In this paper, we ask: Why do some DA schemes (e.g., CutMix) inherently perform much better than others in KD? What makes a "good" DA in KD? Our investigation from a statistical perspective suggests that a good DA scheme should reduce the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. A practical metric, the stddev of teacher's mean probability (T. stddev), is further presented and well justified empirically. Besides the theoretical understanding, we also introduce a new entropy-based data-mixing DA scheme, CutMixPick, to further enhance CutMix. Extensive empirical studies support our claims and demonstrate how we can harvest considerable performance gains simply by using a better DA scheme in knowledge distillation.

papers_seen.author: Sheppard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of teacher performance. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants—soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or adversarial synthesis—enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints and integrate with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD is highly effective when treated as a task-aware toolkit: careful choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data strategies, and combination with other compression primitives produces practical, deployable models. However, KD is not a panacea; its limitations (teacher errors, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias transfer, and distribution shift) require explicit mitigation, specialized protocols, and continued research into robust, privacy-preserving, and automated distillation methods.

papers_seen.author: Terry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Sensitive Path for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a proven and versatile technique for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed around appropriate transfer targets, teacher–student alignment, and data regimes, KD frequently enables substantial reductions in size and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, its effectiveness depends on task and deployment constraints, and KD must often be combined with complementary methods and task-aware design to avoid failure modes and to meet real-world requirements.

papers_seen.author: Kennedy
papers_seen.title: The Promise and Limits of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central method for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students while retaining much of the teacher's performance. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal domains, KD variants enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, promote interpretable surrogates, and support ensemble compression. However, KD also transfers teacher biases, faces optimization and data-distribution challenges, and requires careful choices of objectives, data augmentation, and teacher-student protocols to be effective in practice.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Alexander
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical approach for producing smaller, faster, and deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory use, and communication cost while often preserving much of teacher performance across modalities. However, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred undesirable behaviors. For robust, real-world deployment KD should be used as the core of an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), targeted data strategies, and safeguards for privacy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Patterson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile set of techniques that can compress large or ensemble models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. Across modalities and tasks KD variants—matching logits, internal features, attention maps, relational structure, and using data‑free or adversarial generation—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication when integrated with complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student pairing, and data strategies; unresolved issues remain around teacher error propagation, distribution shift, rare‑token preservation, and privacy constraints. Based on evidence across empirical and synthetic studies, KD should be treated as a first‑order, configurable component of compression pipelines, applied thoughtfully and combined with complementary techniques to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD techniques encompass output-level supervision (soft logits), representation- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, progressive module replacement, and online or multi-teacher protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling substantial reductions in parameter count and inference cost, but success is context-sensitive: it depends on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architecture alignment, the availability and distribution of data (including data-free or synthesized alternatives), and careful loss and layer-mapping choices. Practical pipelines therefore treat KD as a configurable toolbox to be combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and domain-, fairness-, or privacy-aware interventions. Remaining scientific and engineering challenges include principled selection of distillation targets, reliable distillation under limited or mismatched data, mitigation of transferred biases and rare-token degradation, theoretical understanding of when and why different KD objectives help, and automated, hardware-aware co-design for heterogeneous deployment.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, adaptable framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of the teachers' performance. Across modalities and tasks—classification, generation, retrieval, structured prediction, and language tasks—KD variants (logit transfer, feature- and attention-matching, adversarial and contrastive objectives, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols) provide concrete trade-offs between model size, compute, and accuracy. When combined with complementary strategies such as architecture search, pruning, low-precision numerics, or privacy mechanisms, distillation enables robust deployment on resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive platforms. However, distillation outcomes depend on teacher quality, data availability, teacher–student alignment, and design choices for objectives and training pipelines; tailored practices are therefore needed to realize KD's full potential and avoid failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Harvey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer knowledge from larger or multi-modal models to smaller or specialized models to reduce inference cost, enable deployment in constrained environments, and improve robustness or fairness. Across computer vision, natural language processing, speech, recommender systems, graph learning, generative modelling, and multimodal tasks, a broad set of mechanisms—soft-label supervision, feature- and attention-level matching, multi-teacher and ensemble methods, online/peer-distillation, and task- or domain-specific adaptations—have been developed. Empirical results demonstrate that distillation can yield compact models that approach teacher performance, accelerate training or inference, improve small-model self-supervised learning, and enable modality transfer, while theoretical and empirical analyses highlight factors that govern success: student capacity, teacher imperfection, data complexity, data augmentation, and bias-variance tradeoffs. Open challenges remain in principled theory, privacy-preserving and fairness-aware distillation, and extending distillation reliably to generative and highly structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Dudley
papers_seen.title: Attention-Guided Answer Distillation for Machine Reading Comprehension
papers_seen.abstract: Despite that current reading comprehension systems have achieved significant advancements, their promising performances are often obtained at the cost of making an ensemble of numerous models. Besides, existing approaches are also vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper tackles these problems by leveraging knowledge distillation, which aims to transfer knowledge from an ensemble model to a single model. We first demonstrate that vanilla knowledge distillation applied to answer span prediction is effective for reading comprehension systems. We then propose two novel approaches that not only penalize the prediction on confusing answers but also guide the training with alignment information distilled from the ensemble. Experiments show that our best student model has only a slight drop of 0.4% F1 on the SQuAD test set compared to the ensemble teacher, while running 12x faster during inference. It even outperforms the teacher on adversarial SQuAD datasets and NarrativeQA benchmark.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a central, practical framework for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-label supervision to representation and feature matching—and has been adapted for online, multi-teacher, self-supervised, data-free, cross-modal, and federated scenarios. Across vision, language, speech, and graph domains, careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher imperfections determines the success of compression. Best results arise when distillation is combined with complementary techniques (architecture adaptation, quantization, pruning, or curriculum strategies) and when practitioners attend to data-availability, distribution shift, and task-specific constraints.

papers_seen.author: Keith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Insufficient Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable mechanism for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when its objectives, data, and mappings are chosen with the target task and student capacity in mind; but KD alone does not guarantee production-ready compression. Reliable deployment requires integrating distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture design), careful data and teacher selection, layer and projector design, and explicit attention to robustness, fairness, and rare-behavior transfer.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Flexible, but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective and adaptable framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and NLP. KD supports many transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational structure) and training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), enabling substantial reductions in inference cost when integrated with complementary compression techniques. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, available data (or the ability to synthesize it), and deliberate mitigation of failure modes such as transferred bias, distribution shift, and degraded performance on rare outputs. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful when designed and combined with other methods, but requiring task‑aware engineering and explicit safeguards to be reliable in practice.

papers_seen.author: Byrd
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Indispensable but Task‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely applicable family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD variants have been successfully adapted across modalities and tasks, and when designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and student capacity, distillation yields substantial practical gains. However, KD has concrete limits—capacity mismatch, data scarcity, bias propagation, and failures on rare phenomena—that make it most effective when integrated into broader, task‑aware compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Harrington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, but Context-Aware Component of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and generative settings. KD reliably improves student performance when teacher quality, the form of transferred signals, and data/augmentation strategies are chosen to match the task and deployment constraints. However, KD is not sufficient by itself: best outcomes arise when distillation is integrated with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), careful data or augmentation strategies, and task- or architecture-aware adaptations. This article argues that KD should be treated as a core, configurable element of compression pipelines rather than a standalone cure-all, and it highlights empirical evidence, mechanisms, limitations, and practical recommendations drawn from recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and model compression have matured into a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models into smaller, faster, or more private models. Across computer vision, NLP, multimodal systems, federated settings, and generative models, researchers have combined soft-label (logit) distillation, intermediate feature/hint transfer, architecture transformation, quantization, pruning, and automated search to achieve significant reductions in memory, computation, or communication while largely preserving accuracy. Empirical work demonstrates that distillation can enable high-quality low-precision models, speed up inference and training, unify heterogeneous models without shared data, and make distributed learning more communication- and privacy-efficient. The field continues to refine when and what knowledge to transfer (e.g., logits vs. features vs. attention), how to handle multiple or unreliable teachers, how to design student-friendly teachers, and how to integrate distillation with other compression methods such as pruning and search.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The methods range from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational or contrastive structures, and they operate in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align layers, and how to handle limited or private data. While KD routinely yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, open challenges remain in teacher–student mismatch, distribution shift, robustness and fairness transfer, data-free/privacy-preserving distillation, and principled selection of distilled signals.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical and flexible pathway to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across NLP and other modalities, researchers have developed logit-level, representation-level, layer-wise, multi-teacher, data-free, privacy-aware, and task-aware distillation variants and combined KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and low-frequency phenomena materially affects student quality and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Pena
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Order, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: I argue that knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first-order technique for compressing and adapting deep models for practical deployment in vision and language systems. KD's flexibility—supporting logits, intermediate features, relational signals, online/multi-teacher regimes, and data-free variants—lets practitioners address latency, memory, on-device inference, privacy, and domain adaptation constraints. However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of transfer signals, data availability (or synthetic data methods), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Accordingly, KD should be used as a configurable toolkit combined with task-aware design, auxiliary compression methods, and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Harris
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become core methods for producing compact, efficient models from large teachers across computer vision, speech, graph-based learning, and NLP. Research has diversified beyond the original logits-based teacher-student paradigm into feature- and representation-based distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, online and adversarial schemes, and task-specific adaptations (e.g., for BERT and non-autoregressive translation). Work also addresses robustness, privacy, few-shot compression, and practical efficiency (reduced compute and communication) for deployment on constrained devices.

papers_seen.author: Herrera
papers_seen.title: Distilling Object Detectors with Fine-grained Feature Imitation
papers_seen.abstract: State-of-the-art CNN based recognition models are often computationally prohibitive to deploy on low-end devices. A promising high level approach tackling this limitation is knowledge distillation, which let small student model mimic cumbersome teacher model's output to get improved generalization. However, related methods mainly focus on simple task of classification while do not consider complex tasks like object detection. We show applying the vanilla knowledge distillation to detection model gets minor gain. To address the challenge of distilling knowledge in detection model, we propose a fine-grained feature imitation method exploiting the cross-location discrepancy of feature response. Our intuition is that detectors care more about local near object regions. Thus the discrepancy of feature response on the near object anchor locations reveals important information of how teacher model tends to generalize. We design a novel mechanism to estimate those locations and let student model imitate the teacher on them to get enhanced performance. We first validate the idea on a developed lightweight toy detector which carries simplest notion of current state-of-the-art anchor based detection models on challenging KITTI dataset, our method generates up to 15% boost of mAP for the student model compared to the non-imitated counterpart. We then extensively evaluate the method with Faster R-CNN model under various scenarios with common object detection benchmark of Pascal VOC and COCO, imitation alleviates up to 74% performance drop of student model compared to teacher. Codes released at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

papers_seen.author: Sampson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Insufficient Tool for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful, widely applicable approach that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models into smaller, efficient students. KD routinely yields substantial reductions in parameters, latency, and memory while retaining much of teacher performance across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, fair, or deployment-ready compression: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, data and augmentation strategies, teacher–student alignment, and combination with complementary compression techniques. Treating KD as the core of a task-aware, integrated compression pipeline — rather than a one-shot solution — achieves the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Adversarially Robust Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is effective for producing small, high-performance neural networks for classification, but these small networks are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. This paper studies how adversarial robustness transfers from teacher to student during knowledge distillation. We find that a large amount of robustness may be inherited by the student even when distilled on only clean images. Second, we introduce Adversarially Robust Distillation (ARD) for distilling robustness onto student networks. In addition to producing small models with high test accuracy like conventional distillation, ARD also passes the superior robustness of large networks onto the student. In our experiments, we find that ARD student models decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture in terms of robust accuracy, surpassing state-of-the-art methods on standard robustness benchmarks. Finally, we adapt recent fast adversarial training methods to ARD for accelerated robust distillation.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: An Indispensable but Context‑Dependent Toolbox
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students. When matched to task constraints, data regimes, and student capacity, KD reliably produces compact models that retain much of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. At the same time, KD transfers teacher imperfections and faces limits (data mismatch, capacity gaps, low-frequency behavior), so it must be applied as a principled, task-aware set of techniques combined with complementary compression practices.

papers_seen.author: Ramsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly effective and widely adopted framework for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD is best understood as a configurable core technique: it provides many transferable signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational maps, contrastive objectives, and synthesized data), and—when combined with complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search and coupled with task‑aware data strategies—can enable large reductions in size and latency while retaining much of the teacher's performance. However, KD is context dependent: teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data regime, and explicit measures for robustness, privacy, and fairness strongly shape outcomes. Practitioners should therefore treat KD as an essential but non‑turnkey component of integrated compression pipelines, selecting targets, mapping strategies, and safeguards to meet deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool Best Used in a Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students. It reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. KD should be treated as a core, necessary element of practical compression pipelines but not as a standalone solution: the best results come from integrating KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from applying context-aware design and mitigation for bias, robustness, and data constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walsh
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Current Methods, Findings, and Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer predictive and representational information from larger or composite models into smaller, faster, or resource-constrained models. A broad set of objectives — from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and relation-level imitation, contrastive and adversarial schemes, data-free synthesis, and teacher-student co-training — have been developed and adapted to modalities and tasks in NLP, vision, graphs, retrieval, and generative modeling. Empirical work shows that combining carefully chosen distillation objectives with task-aware student design, pretraining of compact architectures, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) achieves large inference speedups and parameter reductions while preserving most teacher performance. Open challenges include data-heterogeneity and federated limits, teacher error propagation, robustness and privacy preservation, and task-specific design for structured outputs; addressing these requires principled choice of what to transfer, how to select or synthesize data, and how to integrate KD into end-to-end compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Barrett
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Practical, and Context‑Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, versatile approach for producing compact models from larger teachers. Across tasks and modalities, KD variants transfer outputs or internal signals to reduce model size and latency while often preserving most task performance. Practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures and capacities, how to handle data (real, augmented, or synthetic), and how to combine distillation with complementary compression techniques. When treated as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, KD enables deployable models under latency, memory, and privacy constraints—but it is not a standalone panacea and requires task‑aware engineering to mitigate failure modes such as propagated teacher errors, distribution shift, and degraded long‑tail behavior.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for converting high-capacity teacher models into smaller, more deployable student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target matching to feature-, attention-, and relation-level alignment, as well as online, ensemble, and data-free variants—have enabled substantial reductions in model size and inference cost while often preserving most of the teacher's performance. Practical application requires careful choices about what to transfer, how to generate or select data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression tools.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. A diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure, and decision-boundary or synthetic-data signals), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, task- and layer-aware schedules), and architecture-aware adaptations (projectors, layer mapping, and combinations with pruning/quantization/NAS) has been developed. Empirically, properly designed distillation pipelines recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, and can be combined with complementary compression methods to meet device and domain requirements. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps, teacher–student capacity mismatch, distribution shift and data scarcity (including privacy- and data-free regimes), and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Contextual Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is an effective, broadly applicable set of methods for producing smaller, faster, and deployment-ready models by transferring information from large teacher models into compact students. KD techniques range from soft-label (logit) matching to intermediate-feature and relational objectives, and they have been adapted to settings with limited or no original training data, to multi-teacher or online schemes, and to combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. While KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve interpretability or privacy-aware deployment, its success depends on task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and distributional constraints. Consequently, KD is best treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline rather than as a plug-and-play cure-all.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring knowledge from larger, often ensemble or pre-trained, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD includes matching teacher outputs (soft logits), imitating intermediate representations, transferring attention or relational structures, and using multi-teacher, online, self-, or data-free protocols. In practice KD is combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware design to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy constraints. While KD frequently recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can improve student generalization, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and match, and careful choice of distillation signals; persistent challenges include optimization gaps, distribution shift, low-frequency/rare-case degradation, bias transfer, and federated or heterogeneous-device constraints. Ongoing work focuses on principled objectives, layer-mapping strategies, privacy- and data-aware distillation, and robust, task-aware pipelines for production deployment.

papers_seen.author: Warren
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Task-Aware, Multifaceted Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable toolkit rather than a single recipe—selecting what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to map teacher and student layers, and whether to synthesize or reweight data—KD reliably enables latency-, memory-, and privacy-aware deployment across vision, language, generative, and structured tasks. However, its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, and data availability; therefore best practice combines task-aware distillation objectives with complementary compression techniques and safeguards against transferred errors and biases.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practically indispensable technique for compressing and adapting large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD is highly versatile—supporting logits-, feature-, attention- and relation-level transfers, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and privacy- or data-constrained workflows—but it is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, data availability and distribution, and careful training protocol design. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines and combining it with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation, data augmentation, and curriculum strategies) leads to the most reliable deployment outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for producing smaller, faster, or deployment‑specialized models by transferring information from larger teacher models. KD succeeds most reliably when treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline: practitioners should select appropriate transfer targets (logits, features, attention, relational signals), adapt objectives to student capacity and data regime, and combine distillation with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data strategies). While KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance across modalities, it is not a universal cure—limitations such as teacher imperfection, capacity mismatch, data scarcity, and the risk of propagating biases require targeted mitigations and careful evaluation.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Preserving Privacy in Federated Learning with Ensemble Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm where local nodes collaboratively train a central model while the training data remains decentralized. Existing FL methods typically share model parameters or employ co-distillation to address the issue of unbalanced data distribution. However, they suffer from communication bottlenecks. More importantly, they risk privacy leakage. In this work, we develop a privacy preserving and communication efficient method in a FL framework with one-shot offline knowledge distillation using unlabeled, cross-domain public data. We propose a quantized and noisy ensemble of local predictions from completely trained local models for stronger privacy guarantees without sacrificing accuracy. Based on extensive experiments on image classification and text classification tasks, we show that our privacy-preserving method outperforms baseline FL algorithms with superior performance in both accuracy and communication efficiency.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.
