papers_seen.author: Bowers
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques are widely used to reduce the resource footprint of large neural networks while preserving performance. The literature surveys a range of approaches — from vanilla teacher-student soft-target transfers to layer-wise, attention- and channel-wise methods, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-preserving variants, and combinations with pruning and adversarial training — and demonstrates successful applications across NLP, speech, vision, graph, and multimodal problems. Empirical results show effective speedups and parameter reductions with modest accuracy loss; theoretical and empirical analyses also connect KD to label-smoothing and regularization effects that can improve generalization.

papers_seen.author: Berger
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable toolkit for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models. A wide range of distillation targets and protocols has been developed, and KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design. While distilled students often recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, important limitations and open problems remain—particularly around data scarcity, distribution shift, bias transfer, and principled selection of distillation signals.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Linkless Link Prediction via Relational Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown exceptional performance in the task of link prediction. Despite their effectiveness, the high latency brought by non-trivial neighborhood data dependency limits GNNs in practical deployments. Conversely, the known efficient MLPs are much less effective than GNNs due to the lack of relational knowledge. In this work, to combine the advantages of GNNs and MLPs, we start with exploring direct knowledge distillation (KD) methods for link prediction, i.e., predicted logit-based matching and node representation-based matching. Upon observing direct KD analogs do not perform well for link prediction, we propose a relational KD framework, Linkless Link Prediction (LLP), to distill knowledge for link prediction with MLPs. Unlike simple KD methods that match independent link logits or node representations, LLP distills relational knowledge that is centered around each (anchor) node to the student MLP. Specifically, we propose rank-based matching and distribution-based matching strategies that complement each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LLP boosts the link prediction performance of MLPs with significant margins, and even outperforms the teacher GNNs on 7 out of 8 benchmarks. LLP also achieves a 70.68x speedup in link prediction inference compared to GNNs on the large-scale OGB dataset.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Perry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, evidence-backed approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable models across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD methods — ranging from logits transfer to intermediate-feature matching, self-distillation, and selective-sample protocols — routinely enable substantial reductions in compute, memory, and latency while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not automatic: success depends on what information is transferred, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data choices, and integration with complementary compression techniques. When treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline, KD provides a practical route to deploy high-performing models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Russell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large models into smaller, faster students by transferring behavior through logits, intermediate representations, attention maps, relational signals, or synthesized data. Across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and multimodal tasks, KD has been combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to produce compact models that retain much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory and compute. Practical deployments have driven adaptations for data-free and privacy-aware regimes, federated and heterogeneous-device settings, domain adaptation, and task-aware layer mapping. Empirical evidence shows substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss in many settings, but challenges remain around teacher-student mismatch, data availability, distribution shift, robustness transfer, and the principled selection of what to transfer and when.

papers_seen.author: Soto
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Practices, Applications, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible framework for transferring predictive behavior and internal structure from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce inference cost, memory footprint, and communication while preserving much of task performance. Across modalities and tasks, distillation objectives range from matching output logits to imitating intermediate features, attention maps, relational structure, and contrastive signals, and are often combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability and alignment of data, and careful design of training objectives and pipelines. KD is widely applied in domains from NLP and information retrieval to healthcare, routing, and federated settings, but it has known failure modes (teacher bias transfer, low-frequency degradation, teacher–student mismatch, and distributional shift) that require task-aware remedies and integration with other compression primitives. Ongoing directions emphasize multi-signal objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, data-efficient and privacy-preserving protocols, and principled evaluation under deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Waller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Practical Core with Clear Limits — Guidance for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely useful set of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teacher's capability. KD spans logits transfer, intermediate feature mimicking, relational and attention-based objectives, self-distillation, ensemble-to-single transfer, and cross-modal variants. Applied thoughtfully — selecting what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which samples or layers to prioritize — KD can produce substantial gains in latency, memory, and sometimes robustness, but it is not a universal remedy: dataset mismatch, optimization difficulty, and propagation of teacher errors are real constraints. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a principled toolbox rather than a single recipe, summarizes practical patterns that succeed across tasks, highlights empirical failure modes, and gives evidence-backed recommendations for practitioners in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques that transfer information from larger, often multi-source or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings, KD has evolved beyond simple logit matching to include representation- and relation-level objectives, adversarial or data-free generation, online and self-distillation protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization and architecture search. These approaches routinely enable large reductions in inference cost and memory while preserving much of teacher performance, but reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data. Important open directions remain in principled theory, robust distillation under heterogenous and low-data regimes, and preserving long-tail or low-frequency behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, Practical Trade-offs, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to meet latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. The field encompasses a wide family of distillation targets and protocols (logit matching, feature- and attention-level transfer, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free and federated variants) and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, and other modalities shows that distilled students often recover much of the teacher’s performance, though outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-aware choices. Persistent challenges include handling limited or private data, transferring low-frequency/rare behaviors, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mappings for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a logits-matching trick into a broad, practical framework for shrinking and adapting large models while retaining much of their performance. Modern KD techniques include soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and attention alignment, multi- and ensemble-teacher schemes, online and distributed formulations, self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware variants. Across vision, language, recommendation, and domain-adaptation settings, KD is most effective when combined with complementary strategies (pretraining, pruning, quantization, curriculum or online training, and task-aware losses). Despite strong empirical successes, practitioners must attend to teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and domain mismatch; many current research directions focus on robust, privacy-preserving, and data-limited distillation for real-world deployment.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Rivera
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Integrated Framework for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical approach for producing compact models that retain much of the functionality of larger teachers. KD works across modalities, supports deployment under resource and privacy constraints, and also acts as a regularizer; however, it has concrete failure modes that require complementary methods and careful teacher–student design. I argue that KD should be treated as a central, configurable component of any compression pipeline, used in combination with representation-aware objectives, curriculum and data strategies, and targeted safeguards for bias, low-frequency behavior, and domain shift.

papers_seen.author: Diaz
papers_seen.title: Model Compression with Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation for Web Question Answering System
papers_seen.abstract: Deep pre-training and fine-tuning models (such as BERT and OpenAI GPT) have demonstrated excellent results in question answering areas. However, due to the sheer amount of model parameters, the inference speed of these models is very slow. How to apply these complex models to real business scenarios becomes a challenging but practical problem. Previous model compression methods usually suffer from information loss during the model compression procedure, leading to inferior models compared with the original one. To tackle this challenge, we propose a Two-stage Multi-teacher Knowledge Distillation (TMKD for short) method for web Question Answering system. We first develop a general Q\&A distillation task for student model pre-training, and further fine-tune this pre-trained student model with multi-teacher knowledge distillation on downstream tasks (like Web Q\&A task, MNLI, SNLI, RTE tasks from GLUE), which effectively reduces the overfitting bias in individual teacher models, and transfers more general knowledge to the student model. The experiment results show that our method can significantly outperform the baseline methods and even achieve comparable results with the original teacher models, along with substantial speedup of model inference.

papers_seen.author: Mccann
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and practical framework for producing compact models from larger teachers. When designed with attention to what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which complementary compression techniques to apply, KD reliably yields substantial efficiency gains with modest performance loss across modalities and tasks. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and careful treatment of bias, low-frequency phenomena, and domain shift. Best practice treats KD as a central component of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Methods span from classic logit-based distillation to feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and projector-based strategies, module-replacement and pruning approaches, and specialized protocols for cross-modal, federated, data-free, and generative settings. Applications range across NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive models), speech and paralinguistic embeddings, vision (image translation, novel-view synthesis), 3D detection, recommender systems, and graph neural networks. Research highlights include analyses that explain why distillation works, techniques that mitigate transfer of teacher errors, curricula and selection mechanisms for better sample usage, and approaches that adapt distillation to privacy- or resource-constrained environments. Together, these works map an ecosystem of practical techniques and open challenges for deploying compact, high-performing models in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Carrillo
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile method for transferring predictive behavior from larger teacher models to smaller student models, enabling substantial reductions in inference cost while retaining much of the original performance. KD spans logits-based supervision, feature and relational matching, adversarial or synthetic data generation, and architectural or curriculum adaptations. Its practical success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, how teachers and students are aligned, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD can enable deployment in latency- and resource-constrained settings and sometimes yield students that match or exceed teacher performance, but it also carries risks—propagating teacher errors and biases, struggling under data scarcity or mismatch, and requiring task-specific engineering. I argue KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines, applied conditionally with targeted remedies and validated against task and deployment constraints.

Treating KD as a configurable, task-aware component within an integrated compression pipeline yields the most robust and deployable outcomes.

Its practical value arises when KD is designed around task objectives, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and deployment constraints, and when it is combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search.

papers_seen.author: Bryant

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Context-Dependent Tools for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and model compression provide a practical, widely applicable route to produce smaller, faster, and often more robust models from larger teachers across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks. When combined with representation-matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher schemes, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. However, its success depends on teacher quality, the data used for distillation, careful choice of what is transferred, and attention to fairness and domain-shift risks. This paper argues that KD should be treated as an essential yet context-sensitive component of model deployment pipelines, and summarizes best-practice recommendations and promising directions to make distillation reliably effective in applied settings.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Insufficient Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD has expanded beyond simple logits matching into representation-, relation-, and data-aware methods and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the distillation data, and mitigation of privacy, robustness, and bias risks. For real-world deployment, KD should be used as the central component of an integrated compression pipeline tailored to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Brown
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained or privacy-sensitive settings. Work in this area has progressed beyond the original formulation of training a small student to match a teacher's output probabilities: modern approaches distill internal representations, perform many-to-many layer alignment, operate without access to original training data, combine multiple teachers or ensembles, and adapt to particular architectures and tasks (including graph networks, detectors, generative models, and language models). Practical concerns such as data heterogeneity, privacy guarantees, and robustness to distribution shift have motivated methods that use synthetic data, private perturbations, generative replay, and federated or online distillation protocols. The field continues to trade off fidelity to teacher behavior, compactness, task specificity, and deployability, with task-adaptive compression and representation-alignment methods emerging as especially effective for NLP and other structured prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Walker
papers_seen.title: BERT Learns to Teach: Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning
papers_seen.abstract: We present Knowledge Distillation with Meta Learning (MetaDistil), a simple yet effective alternative to traditional knowledge distillation (KD) methods where the teacher model is fixed during training. We show the teacher network can learn to better transfer knowledge to the student network (i.e., learning to teach) with the feedback from the performance of the distilled student network in a meta learning framework. Moreover, we introduce a pilot update mechanism to improve the alignment between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms that focus on an improved inner-learner. Experiments on various benchmarks show that MetaDistil can yield significant improvements compared with traditional KD algorithms and is less sensitive to the choice of different student capacity and hyperparameters, facilitating the use of KD on different tasks and models.

papers_seen.author: Ballard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for compressing large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Practical deployment treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of broader compression pipelines and adopts safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Villa
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses larger or composite models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives and workflows—soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive losses, data- or privacy-aware variants, and ensemble or self-distillation—has been adapted across modalities and tasks. When combined with task-aware design, selective data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, distillation produces practical, deployable models but requires careful mitigation of known limits such as capacity mismatch, teacher error transfer, data scarcity, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational Tool for Model Compression and Robust Deployment in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher→student logits-matching recipe into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing models and enabling deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and heterogeneous hardware. Modern KD variants transfer not only soft labels but also internal and feature representations, employ multi-teacher and curriculum strategies, and integrate with federated and data-constrained workflows. When matched to the task (e.g., feature-level distillation for representation-heavy NLP, projector adapters for mismatched architectures, or privacy-aware ensembles for federated settings), KD enables small models to approximate or sometimes match larger teachers while offering routes to improved robustness and inclusivity. However, realizing these gains requires attention to teacher quality, capacity gaps, the form of distilled information, and sample-wise effects of soft targets. I argue that KD should be treated as a first-order, configurable component of model-compression pipelines and present evidence-based practical recommendations for when and how to apply its variants.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Bell
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Essential, Versatile, and Bounded for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central, practical strategy for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students across modalities. KD provides flexible transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, relational signals), supports data-limited and privacy-sensitive regimes via synthetic- or generator-based approaches, and interoperates with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet latency and memory constraints. Nevertheless, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher–student alignment, data and capacity matching, and explicit mitigation of bias and distribution-shift risks, so it should be used as a configurable component within broader compression and deployment pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Phillips
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Practical, and Nuanced Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger or ensemble teachers. It supports a wide range of objectives—logit-level transfer, feature- and representation-level matching, relational and adversarial objectives, and many-to-many layer mappings—and is applicable across modalities (vision, language, graphs, generative models) and settings (offline, online, data-free, federated, multi-teacher). When combined with careful teacher-student co-design, targeted data strategies, and complementary compression techniques, KD enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while also serving secondary goals such as interpretability or robustness. KD is powerful but not automatic: success depends on matching objectives to tasks, mitigating teacher-induced errors or biases, and addressing optimization and data-distribution challenges.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Central, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. When combined with complementary compression primitives, careful choice of distillation targets and protocols, and task- or data-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis strategy, and attention to robustness, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a flexible toolkit that must be adapted to deployment constraints and complemented with privacy-, fairness-, and robustness-aware methods.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and recommender systems, KD methods have been developed to match outputs (soft targets), internal representations (features and attention), relational or contrastive signals, and task-specific rank or ordering information. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability (including data-free strategies), and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Trade-offs include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and optimization challenges; many works propose curricula, student-friendly teacher training, or multi-teacher and online protocols to mitigate these issues. The field has matured into a central engineering primitive for deployment, while continuing to pursue principled transfer objectives, privacy-aware distillation, and robust domain- and architecture-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Ballard
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile framework for compressing large, high-capacity teacher models into smaller, deployable student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. KD encompasses a range of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings shows KD frequently recovers much of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but its reliability depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals, and data strategies. Practical deployment treats KD as a configurable, task-aware component of broader compression pipelines and adopts safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency or long-tail behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Ashley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Patterns, and Practical Limits
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used set of techniques for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD variants include matching teacher logits, imitating intermediate representations, aligning attention or relational structures, ensembling multiple teachers, adversarial and data-free distillation, and student- or task-aware curricula. KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and adapted for settings with limited or private data, federated training, and non‑standard outputs (e.g., generative or structured prediction). Empirically, thoughtfully designed distillation pipelines often recover a large fraction of teacher performance and in many cases enable practical deployment trade-offs, but they are not universally effective: success depends on student capacity, data and distribution match, choice of teacher signals, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare‑phenomena degradation. Ongoing research focuses on principled objectives, robust and private distillation, and task‑aware architectures for structured outputs.

papers_seen.author: Mccall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Context‑Sensitive, and Best Used in Integrated Compression Pipelines
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller student models to reduce latency, memory, and compute while preserving much of task performance. Empirical work across vision, language, and multimodal tasks demonstrates that KD can produce deployable models with favorable efficiency–accuracy tradeoffs, but KD alone is not a universal cure: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher–student alignment, data availability (including data‑free synthesis), and mitigation of propagated errors or biases. For practical, robust compression, KD should be a central, configurable component of a task‑aware pipeline that incorporates complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and sample‑selection strategies, and targeted remedies for distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, and privacy constraints.

papers_seen.author: Bray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task‑Aware Tool for Model Compression (with Limits and Practical Remedies)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) provides a practical, versatile framework for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students. When applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate data strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, or architecture search), KD routinely yields compact models suitable for latency- and memory-constrained deployment. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality and compatibility with the student, the choice of distilled signals, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of teacher artifacts. Careful protocol design—pre-training compact architectures, selecting what to distill, using effective augmentation or data synthesis, and combining KD with complementary methods—produces the most reliable results in practice.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Findings, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically driven framework for transferring predictive and representational information from large or composite teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. The literature shows a broad set of distillation objectives (soft logits, intermediate feature matching, attention and relational transfer, contrastive and adversarial schemes), multiple training protocols (multi-teacher, self-distillation, data-free and synthetic-data approaches), and tight integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance in many settings, enable cross-modal and domain adaptation, and produce dramatic runtime and memory gains when applied with task-aware choices of signals, data, and student architectures. Important failure modes remain—teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, data availability and heterogeneity, and fairness/privacy concerns—so best practice treats KD as a configurable toolbox that must be tailored to the task, data regime, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as Central but Insufficient: A Task‑Aware, Pipeline‑Centric Position for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable set of techniques that reliably reduces inference cost by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models. Empirical evidence across vision, language, multimodal, and speech tasks shows that carefully designed KD pipelines often recover most of teacher performance — and in some circumstances can even improve student generalization — but consistent success requires task‑aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to combine distillation with complementary compression methods. I argue KD should be treated as the default, central component of model‑compression workflows while being explicitly integrated into broader, deployment‑aware pipelines that address teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, fairness/privacy risks, and hardware constraints.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled, Task-Aware Toolbox for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a configurable, principled toolbox rather than a single recipe. When combined with representation-level objectives, layer-mapping, data- or teacher-aware curricula, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD reliably enables practical deployment of compact models while also serving as a lever for robustness, privacy, and fairness. However, KD is not automatic: optimization gaps, teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and low-frequency or minority behaviors limit out-of-the-box success and require targeted remedies. Practitioners should therefore select distillation signals, mapping strategies, and safeguards to align compression objectives with deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hernandez
papers_seen.title: R2L: Distilling Neural Radiance Field to Neural Light Field for Efficient Novel View Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Recent research explosion on Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) shows the encouraging potential to represent complex scenes with neural networks. One major drawback of NeRF is its prohibitive inference time: Rendering a single pixel requires querying the NeRF network hundreds of times. To resolve it, existing efforts mainly attempt to reduce the number of required sampled points. However, the problem of iterative sampling still exists. On the other hand, Neural Light Field (NeLF) presents a more straightforward representation over NeRF in novel view synthesis -- the rendering of a pixel amounts to one single forward pass without ray-marching. In this work, we present a deep residual MLP network (88 layers) to effectively learn the light field. We show the key to successfully learning such a deep NeLF network is to have sufficient data, for which we transfer the knowledge from a pre-trained NeRF model via data distillation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world scenes show the merits of our method over other counterpart algorithms. On the synthetic scenes, we achieve 26-35x FLOPs reduction (per camera ray) and 28-31x runtime speedup, meanwhile delivering significantly better (1.4-2.8 dB average PSNR improvement) rendering quality than NeRF without any customized parallelism requirement.

papers_seen.author: Silva
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become central tools for deploying high-capacity deep learning models in resource-constrained settings. Methods range from transferring soft labels to matching intermediate representations, leveraging ensembles or multiple teachers, synthesizing surrogate data for data-free distillation, and integrating distillation into federated and privacy-sensitive regimes. Empirical gains have been demonstrated across computer vision, generative modeling, graph learning, and natural language processing, while theoretical work and empirical studies highlight nuanced trade-offs related to regularization, sample selection, teacher quality, and heterogeneous/distributed data. Open challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher-student design, and compression of generative and transformer models for real-world low-latency deployment.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Is a Core Tool for Model Compression and Efficient NLP/Deep Learning Systems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile technique for producing compact, fast, and privacy-aware models across modalities. KD not only compresses large pretrained models for low-latency deployment, but also enables domain adaptation, federated and data-free scenarios, continual learning, and improved student generalization when combined with feature-level and architectural interventions. Together, methodological advances—ranging from feature mimicking and projector ensembles to student-friendly teachers and adversarial/data-free generation—make KD an essential component of modern model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied, practical framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. KD encompasses diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals), protocols (offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, data‑free), and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work shows KD can recover much of teacher performance across modalities and tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data strategies, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and distributional failures.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Open Problems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad toolkit of distillation targets and training protocols has been developed — including soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, multi-teacher schemes, and data-free or generative-sample approaches — and these techniques are routinely combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative models, and embedded settings shows that careful design of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data or synthetic samples to use is crucial: well-designed distillation pipelines can recover much of teacher performance while producing substantial efficiency gains, but challenges remain in data-scarce or privacy-sensitive regimes, heterogeneous teacher–student architectures, distribution shift, and preserving rare or minority behaviors.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Necessary Core and a Configurable Toolkit for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. KD succeeds across modalities and tasks when it is treated as a configurable toolkit—choosing what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to generate or select data, and which complementary compression techniques to combine. However, KD is conditional: its reliability depends on teacher quality, data design and availability, teacher–student alignment, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases. For robust, production-ready compression one should therefore treat KD as the core of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline that includes pre-training, multi-teacher or meta-teaching protocols, and deployment-aware primitives such as pruning or quantization.

papers_seen.author: Spence
papers_seen.title: Treating Knowledge Distillation as an Essential, Task‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques that should be treated as an essential, task-aware component of model-compression pipelines rather than a one-size-fits-all solution. However, KD has predictable failure modes (teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatch, distribution shift, and degradation on rare outputs) that require explicit mitigation and evaluation in real-world settings.

papers_seen.author: Sanders
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: Central, Conditional, and Best-Practice‑Driven for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a central and practical approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers across vision, language, speech, and multimodal settings. KD provides a flexible family of mechanisms (soft-targets, feature and attention matching, multi-teacher and self-distillation, data-free or federated protocols) that, when combined with complementary compression primitives and task-aware design, yield strong empirical trade-offs between efficiency and performance. However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of transferred biases. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component within an integrated compression pipeline rather than a standalone recipe.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware family of methods for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD uses a variety of transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory and latency constraints, and—when carefully applied—preserve much of teacher performance. Practical application treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, combining distillation with architecture design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: The Case for Knowledge Distillation as a Core Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, versatile approach to compressing large models into smaller, faster, and often more robust models across computer vision, NLP, multilingual metrics, and multimodal tasks. A range of complementary techniques — layer-wise mapping, data-free and zero-shot synthesis, self-distillation, adversarial and robust distillation, online/ensemble methods, and task-adaptive architecture search — together make distillation applicable under constraints such as limited data, privacy restrictions, heterogeneous devices, and production-scale training. I argue that adopting a portfolio of distillation strategies, chosen to match data availability and deployment constraints, yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, robustness, and interpretability for modern deep learning systems.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Findings and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques provide a practical path to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, latency, privacy, and domain constraints. Across modalities, KD variants—soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate representation and attention alignment, adversarial or data-free schemes, and online/self-distillation—routinely yield compact students that recover much of a teacher's performance when combined with careful data, optimization, and architecture choices. Practical success requires embedding KD in an integrated compression pipeline and attending to teacher/student design, data regimes, and known failure modes.

papers_seen.author: Whitney
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Component of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically grounded family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses a spectrum of transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational/contrastive signals, and synthetic-data protocols) and workflows (offline, online, multi-teacher, data-free, and federated). Empirical results across vision, language, speech, detection, and generative tasks show KD frequently preserves much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Because of these dependencies, KD is best applied as a configurable, integrated element of compression pipelines—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, and safeguards for robustness and fairness—rather than as a one-size-fits-all recipe.

papers_seen.author: Henson

papers_seen.author: Perry

papers_seen.author: Taylor

papers_seen.author: Hill

papers_seen.author: Mcdonald
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and pragmatic approach for producing compact models that retain much of the behavior of larger teachers. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and cross-device constraints when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, which examples to use, and how to align teacher and student. However, its success is conditional: careful selection of teacher signals, attention to data regimes and fairness, and integration with complementary compression methods are required for reliable real-world use.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data schemes, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transfer signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under domain shift and heterogeneous devices, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Reed
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Principled, Task-Aware Toolbox for Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as a configurable, principled toolbox rather than a single recipe. When combined with representation-level objectives, layer-mapping, data- or teacher-aware curricula, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search), KD reliably enables practical deployment of compact models while also serving as a lever for robustness, privacy, and fairness. However, KD is not automatic: optimization gaps, teacher–student mismatch, limited or private data, and low-frequency or minority behaviors limit out-of-the-box success and require targeted remedies. Practitioners should therefore select distillation signals, mapping strategies, and safeguards to align compression objectives with deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Pennington
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly used and flexible approach for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models in deep learning and NLP. Over the past decade a wide family of KD variants has been developed — logits/soft-target matching, intermediate feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble and multi-teacher schemes, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and layer-mapping strategies — and KD is commonly combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture or neural architecture search). Empirical evidence shows that KD often recovers a large share of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but its success depends on careful, task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, which data to use or synthesize, and how to mitigate failure modes such as transferred bias, teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: Survey of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP (Selected 2017–2022 Literature)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. Methods include soft-label distillation, feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and ensemble-based transfer, data-free or privacy-aware distillation, curriculum and selective-sample strategies, and task-adaptive architecture search. These approaches target deployment constraints (latency, memory, on-device compute), data-availability and privacy limitations, robustness, and domain-continuity, and have been adapted to detectors, generative models, retrieval systems, federated settings, and pre-trained language models. Empirical work demonstrates that careful choice of what to transfer (logits, internal features, relational/contrastive signals) and when/how to train (online, teacher-free, curriculum, few-shot) materially affects student performance and robustness. Open challenges include heterogeneity of data and architectures in distributed settings, theoretical understanding of what aspects of teacher knowledge are most valuable across tasks, and extending distillation to privacy- and domain-constrained deployments.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.
