papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses and transfers predictive ability from large, expensive teacher models to smaller, efficient student models. Across modalities and architectures, KD variants extend beyond matching teacher output probabilities to include internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, adversarial learning, selective sample supervision, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. These methods enable deployment on resource-constrained devices, reduce inference latency, support domain adaptation and federated settings, and in some cases improve student generalization beyond the teacher. Practical challenges include input/representation mismatches between teacher and student, propagation of teacher biases (e.g., low-frequency lexical errors), and the need for careful selection of what is distilled and how. Empirically, tailored distillation objectives and training procedures—such as internal-representation matching, progressive module replacement, ensemble distillation, and contrastive or relational objectives—have produced strong compression results across vision, language, graph-structured data, and generative scene models.

papers_seen.author: Potter
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible set of methods for transferring knowledge from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, or privacy. Across vision and natural language tasks, distillation targets range from soft logits to intermediate representations and relational signals; KD is frequently combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with domain- or task-specific procedures to improve efficacy. KD delivers strong empirical gains in many settings but is bounded by teacher quality, availability and match of data, teacher–student capacity gaps, and the risk of transferring teacher biases; effective application therefore requires task-aware choices of signals, data strategies, and often hybrid compression pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Sparks
papers_seen.title: Position: Knowledge Distillation as the First‑Line, Task‑Aware Core of Practical Model Compression (with Explicit Limits and Prescriptions)
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) should be treated as the primary, first‑line strategy for compressing large deep and NLP models into deployable students because it is flexible, empirically effective across modalities, and interoperable with complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on task‑aware choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment, data regime, and explicit mitigations for transferred bias, capacity mismatch, and low‑frequency behaviors. Practitioners should adopt KD as a configurable core within integrated pipelines that include task adaptation, selective or curriculum distillation, and complementary methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) to meet concrete deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Versatile, and Context-Dependent Toolkit for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical set of techniques for transferring behavior and representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable students. KD techniques — spanning soft-label/logit transfer, intermediate-representation matching, adversarial or data-free synthesis, and teacher-aware or multi-teacher strategies — repeatedly enable large reductions in model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on task and data properties, teacher–student alignment, optimization, and deployment constraints, and it works best when combined with complementary compression techniques and task-aware design choices.

papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Anderson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques form a diverse set of methods for producing smaller, faster, or more deployable models by transferring knowledge from larger or specialized models. Approaches span from simple soft-label supervision to richer transfers of internal representations, intermediate-layer mappings, attention-guided projections, adversarial feature alignment, and task- or device-aware compression. KD is used across domains—image classification, detection (2D and 3D), recommendation/CTR, language model compression, federated and heterogeneous-device learning, and reinforcement learning—and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or curriculum strategies. Recent work examines theoretical aspects (e.g., bias–variance tradeoffs and statistical interactions with data augmentation), practical design choices (teacher-student layer alignment, many-to-many mappings, ensemble teachers), and extensions that address privacy, fairness, and low-data regimes. Despite strong empirical success, open problems remain in understanding when particular KD variants best transfer generalization, how to measure and mitigate transferred biases, and how to optimally combine KD with other compression primitives for different constraints.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: Is Label Smoothing Truly Incompatible with Knowledge Distillation: An Empirical Study
papers_seen.abstract: This work aims to empirically clarify a recently discovered perspective that label smoothing is incompatible with knowledge distillation. We begin by introducing the motivation behind on how this incompatibility is raised, i.e., label smoothing erases relative information between teacher logits. We provide a novel connection on how label smoothing affects distributions of semantically similar and dissimilar classes. Then we propose a metric to quantitatively measure the degree of erased information in sample's representation. After that, we study its one-sidedness and imperfection of the incompatibility view through massive analyses, visualizations and comprehensive experiments on Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation. Finally, we broadly discuss several circumstances wherein label smoothing will indeed lose its effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool: Integrating Distillation with Representation, Data, and Architecture Strategies for Robust Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, more deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient to meet real-world deployment constraints: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention), and access to or synthesis of suitable training data. Best results arise when KD is embedded in an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level matching, projector or layer-mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Careful attention to optimization, robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors is required to avoid propagating teacher errors and to produce reliable compact models for downstream applications.

papers_seen.author: Montgomery
papers_seen.title: Object DGCNN: 3D Object Detection using Dynamic Graphs
papers_seen.abstract: 3D object detection often involves complicated training and testing pipelines, which require substantial domain knowledge about individual datasets. Inspired by recent non-maximum suppression-free 2D object detection models, we propose a 3D object detection architecture on point clouds. Our method models 3D object detection as message passing on a dynamic graph, generalizing the DGCNN framework to predict a set of objects. In our construction, we remove the necessity of post-processing via object confidence aggregation or non-maximum suppression. To facilitate object detection from sparse point clouds, we also propose a set-to-set distillation approach customized to 3D detection. This approach aligns the outputs of the teacher model and the student model in a permutation-invariant fashion, significantly simplifying knowledge distillation for the 3D detection task. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on autonomous driving benchmarks. We also provide abundant analysis of the detection model and distillation framework.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Strategy for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically indispensable approach to compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. When designed as part of a task-aware compression pipeline that includes appropriate distillation targets, data strategies, and complementary techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture adaptation), KD can preserve most of a teacher’s performance while meeting real-world constraints on latency, memory, and privacy. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the signals and data used for transfer, and careful mitigation of transferred biases and robustness failures. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable, evidence-driven toolkit that must be tailored to specific tasks and constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central Tool for Compression and Robust Transfer in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential technique for compressing large models and transferring useful knowledge to smaller or specialized models. Across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks, distillation enables faster inference, reduced memory footprint, and sometimes improved generalization when combined with complementary strategies (e.g., architecture search, pruning, or data management). However, distillation outcomes depend on data, teacher-student alignment, and training design; success requires adapting KD objectives and pipelines to the task and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Walters
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved into a broad, practical toolkit for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. Modern KD methods span simple soft-target matching to representation-, attention-, and relation-level transfer, and they are routinely combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware training protocols. Empirical work shows KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when teacher quality, student capacity, data, and transfer signals are carefully aligned; open problems include theory, robustness under distribution shift, preserving rare-token behavior, privacy, and principled automation of teacher–student alignment.

papers_seen.author: Curry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses information from large teacher models into smaller student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. Research and practice have developed a diverse toolkit — matching soft logits, imitating intermediate features and attention, using contrastive/relational objectives, generating or selecting distillation data, multi-teacher and online schemes, and combining KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work across vision, language, recommendation, speech, and multimodal tasks shows distilled students frequently recover much of teacher performance, though effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and alignment of objectives and representations. Key open problems include reliable transfer of rare or structured behaviors, robust distillation under data heterogeneity and privacy constraints, principled teacher selection and co-design, and automated, task-aware distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Hodges
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Ubiquitous, but Demand-Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely applicable approach for compressing high-capacity models into efficient students across modalities and tasks. Empirical results across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative settings show KD can recover much of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy, and device-heterogeneity constraints. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on how knowledge is represented and transferred (logits, features, attention, contrastive objectives), the alignment between teacher and student inputs, the data used for distillation, and attention to robustness, fairness, and privacy. Carefully chosen distillation algorithms and extensions (self-supervised distillation, meta-learned teachers, multi-teacher weighting, online and distributed schemes, and privacy-preserving perturbations) can mitigate common failure modes and broaden KD’s applicability in production and research settings.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression methods transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to reduce memory, compute, and latency while retaining much of task performance. Methods span soft-target (logit) matching, representation- and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and ensemble guidance, online and adversarial schemes, and data-free/zero-shot approaches. Empirical and theoretical work shows KD often acts both as a mechanism for knowledge transfer and as an implicit regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and the particular distillation objective. Practical deployments combine KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Aguirre
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques transfer information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students) to reduce inference cost, enable deployment on constrained devices, and support privacy- or resource-constrained settings. Approaches span soft-label distillation, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, data-free and zero-shot methods, multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, self-distillation, task- and modality-specific objectives, and combinations with pruning. Empirical work across vision, speech, 3D detection, recommender systems, and multiple NLP tasks demonstrates that carefully designed distillation strategies can yield compact models that approach teacher performance while significantly reducing latency and memory. The literature also provides growing theoretical insight into when and how distillation helps, and identifies open challenges including imperfect teachers, domain shift, low-frequency token fidelity, modality mismatch, and heterogeneous-device federated settings.

papers_seen.author: Daniel
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have become primary approaches for deploying high-performing deep models in resource-constrained settings. The literature spans methods that transfer soft-labels, internal feature representations, and ensemble knowledge; extensions address teacher imperfections, data scarcity or privacy, task-specific adaptations for NLP and vision, and hardware-aware compression. Empirical work demonstrates that careful design choices—such as which signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student layers, whether to incorporate self-distillation or multi-teacher training, and how to combine pruning or low-precision numerics—substantially affect final accuracy and efficiency. The field also benefits from theoretical analyses that clarify when and why distillation helps. Remaining challenges include distilling robust semantics for low-frequency phenomena, distillation without access to original data, and co-design for hardware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Romero
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. The field encompasses a variety of distillation targets (soft logits, internal features, attention maps, relational and contrastive signals), protocols (offline teacher supervision, online/mutual teaching, self‑distillation, multi‑teacher ensembles), and auxiliary mechanisms (data‑free synthesis, projector layers, many‑to‑many layer mapping). Empirical work across vision, language, speech, recommendation, and graph domains shows distilled students can approach teacher performance when teacher quality, student capacity, data strategy, and architecture alignment are carefully addressed. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search, and when designers attend to failure modes including teacher error propagation, degraded rare‑token behavior, distributional mismatch, and fairness or privacy risks. Open directions include principled theory for when particular signals help, robust distillation under data scarcity or heterogeneous deployments, and reliable extensions to generative and structured‑prediction tasks.

papers_seen.author: Humphrey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multi-Modal Tool for Compression and Adaptation in Deep Learning: Strengths, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a broadly applicable approach for compressing and adapting deep models across modalities (text, vision, graphs, speech) and deployment scenarios (edge devices, federated clients, domain shifts). Empirical evidence shows KD can improve student generalization, enable small-footprint models, and facilitate domain- or modality-transfer when combined with representation-level objectives or adversarial/contrastive methods. However, its success depends on optimization, teacher-student design, data availability, and fairness considerations. I argue that KD should be treated as a flexible framework—one that combines logit-level supervision with representation-aware objectives, domain-aware selection of teacher signals, and explicit measures to mitigate undesirable side effects (e.g., lexical errors or bias)—to reliably produce compact, high-quality models for NLP and beyond.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Show, Attend and Distill:Knowledge Distillation via Attention-based Feature Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation extracts general knowledge from a pre-trained teacher network and provides guidance to a target student network. Most studies manually tie intermediate features of the teacher and student, and transfer knowledge through pre-defined links. However, manual selection often constructs ineffective links that limit the improvement from the distillation. There has been an attempt to address the problem, but it is still challenging to identify effective links under practical scenarios. In this paper, we introduce an effective and efficient feature distillation method utilizing all the feature levels of the teacher without manually selecting the links. Specifically, our method utilizes an attention-based meta-network that learns relative similarities between features, and applies identified similarities to control distillation intensities of all possible pairs. As a result, our method determines competent links more efficiently than the previous approach and provides better performance on model compression and transfer learning tasks. Further qualitative analyses and ablative studies describe how our method contributes to better distillation. The implementation code is available at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Fernandez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Deep Learning and NLP: Powerful, Conditional, and Best-Practice Driven
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile set of techniques for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers. KD can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, but its success is conditional on choices about what to transfer, the data used for distillation, teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. Treating KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines — combining logits and feature objectives, projector modules, multi‑teacher or teacher‑adaptive designs, and data‑aware schedules — yields the most reliable results in real deployments.

papers_seen.author: Joyce
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Theory, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related compression techniques have become central for deploying large deep models in latency- and resource-constrained settings. Across modalities and tasks, a consistent pattern is that distilled students can recover much of teacher performance when distillation addresses mismatches in architecture, data distribution, and input representations. Practical advances include multi-teacher and ensemble distillation, online and distributed distillation, data-free and zero-shot approaches, layer-wise and many-to-many layer mappings, task-aware selection of distilled information, and distillation formulations tailored to domain adaptation and federated settings. Theoretical and empirical analyses point to KD acting both as knowledge transfer and as a form of regularization; performance depends strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data augmentation, and instance-level selection of teacher signals. Remaining challenges include robust distillation under data heterogeneity, principled teacher selection, and aligning intermediate representations across heterogeneous detectors or modalities.

papers_seen.author: Henson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into compact student models. KD methods include output-level (soft logits) supervision, intermediate representation and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial or data-free sample generation, and online or multi‑teacher training. When combined with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and which data to use or synthesize, KD routinely yields large reductions in parameter count and latency while preserving most of teacher performance. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it is limited by teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and distribution shift, and risks such as propagated teacher biases and degraded rare-token or out‑of‑distribution behavior. Addressing these limits requires task-specific protocols, privacy‑ and robustness‑aware designs, and more principled, automated approaches to objective selection and layer alignment.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for transferring information from large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient students. KD variants—ranging from soft-logit matching to representation- and relation-based objectives, layer mapping, online/ensemble schemes, and data-synthesis methods—have been applied across vision, NLP, translation, retrieval, federated learning, and privacy-sensitive releases. When designed with task-awareness (selecting what to distill, aligning teacher and student, and engineering the distillation data and objectives) and combined with complementary compression tools, KD often yields favorable accuracy–efficiency tradeoffs. However, KD is not a universal remedy: optimization challenges, teacher–student mismatch, data heterogeneity, and potential transfer of teacher errors or biases require careful mitigation. Best practice is to treat KD as a first-class element of a compression toolbox—default to distillation but tailor its form to task and deployment constraints, and combine it with architectural, data, and privacy-aware procedures to achieve robust, deployable models.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques reduce model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger, more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, cheaper models (students). Empirical work demonstrates that carefully designed distillation protocols can retain much of teacher performance (and sometimes improve generalization) while enabling deployment constraints such as latency, memory, and privacy; theoretical analyses offer insight into when soft labels help and when hard labels are necessary. Remaining challenges include bridging capacity gaps, dealing with mismatched architectures and modalities, operating without original data, and guaranteeing privacy under compression.

papers_seen.author: Hardy

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable set of methods for transferring predictive behavior and representations from larger (teacher) models into smaller (student) models, enabling deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain mismatch. Empirical and theoretical work shows distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and stabilizes student training, but success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, availability and selection of data, and defenses against transferred biases and degraded modeling of rare phenomena. Practical deployments therefore treat distillation as a configurable component within compression pipelines, pairing distilled signals with task- and deployment-aware engineering.

This review synthesizes the main methods, empirical findings, and practical considerations reported across recent work, and highlights open challenges and promising directions.

papers_seen.author: Bernard
papers_seen.title: Reinforced Multi-Teacher Selection for Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In natural language processing (NLP) tasks, slow inference speed and huge footprints in GPU usage remain the bottleneck of applying pre-trained deep models in production. As a popular method for model compression, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from one or multiple large (teacher) models to a small (student) model. When multiple teacher models are available in distillation, the state-of-the-art methods assign a fixed weight to a teacher model in the whole distillation. Furthermore, most of the existing methods allocate an equal weight to every teacher model. In this paper, we observe that, due to the complexity of training examples and the differences in student model capability, learning differentially from teacher models can lead to better performance of student models distilled. We systematically develop a reinforced method to dynamically assign weights to teacher models for different training instances and optimize the performance of student model. Our extensive experimental results on several NLP tasks clearly verify the feasibility and effectiveness of our approach.

papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central but Context-Dependent Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of methods that transfers predictive behavior and internal structure from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD can materially reduce latency, memory, and energy costs while preserving much of teacher performance, and its variants (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational objectives, online/mutual schemes, and data-free synthesis) extend its applicability across tasks and deployment constraints. However, the benefits of distillation depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and the choice of which signals to transfer; practical deployments therefore treat KD as a configurable component integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware practices rather than as a standalone silver bullet.

papers_seen.author: Hill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Dependent Tool for Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces model size and inference cost by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD encompasses many techniques — from matching soft logits to aligning intermediate features, attention maps, and relational structure — and is effective across vision, language, speech, and graph tasks when designed around task constraints and student capacity. However, KD is not a stand‑alone solution: its practical success depends on data availability, teacher quality, student architecture, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases, robustness deficits, and low-frequency behavior. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core within an integrated compression pipeline that includes complementary methods such as pruning, quantization, architecture-aware design, data strategies (including augmentation and data-free synthesis), and robustness or privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Calderon
papers_seen.title: Learning Generalizable Models for Vehicle Routing Problems via Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Recent neural methods for vehicle routing problems always train and test the deep models on the same instance distribution (i.e., uniform). To tackle the consequent cross-distribution generalization concerns, we bring the knowledge distillation to this field and propose an Adaptive Multi-Distribution Knowledge Distillation (AMDKD) scheme for learning more generalizable deep models. Particularly, our AMDKD leverages various knowledge from multiple teachers trained on exemplar distributions to yield a light-weight yet generalist student model. Meanwhile, we equip AMDKD with an adaptive strategy that allows the student to concentrate on difficult distributions, so as to absorb hard-to-master knowledge more effectively. Extensive experimental results show that, compared with the baseline neural methods, our AMDKD is able to achieve competitive results on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances, which are either randomly synthesized or adopted from benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Notably, our AMDKD is generic, and consumes less computational resources for inference.

papers_seen.author: Branch
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Considerations
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable framework for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. KD techniques span soft-label/logit matching, intermediate-representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and online or mutual teaching protocols. In practice KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search), task- and data-aware strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and distributional shift. Remaining challenges include principled teacher–student design, reliable performance under data scarcity or heterogeneity, mitigation of bias transfer, and scalable data-free or privacy-preserving distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Allison
papers_seen.title: Why Knowledge Distillation Is a Core Tool for Model Compression and Efficient NLP/Deep Learning Systems
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a practical and versatile technique for producing compact, fast, and privacy-aware models across modalities. KD not only compresses large pretrained models for low-latency deployment, but also enables domain adaptation, federated and data-free scenarios, continual learning, and improved student generalization when combined with feature-level and architectural interventions. Together, methodological advances—ranging from feature mimicking and projector ensembles to student-friendly teachers and adversarial/data-free generation—make KD an essential component of modern model-compression toolkits.

papers_seen.author: Pierce
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression methods provide practical routes to deploy high-performing deep models under resource, privacy, and latency constraints. The literature has developed diverse approaches that transfer information via soft logits, intermediate features, attentional maps, channel-wise statistics, and online mutual learning; adaptations address task-specific compression, data-free or few-shot regimes, large-scale distributed training, and teacher-student co-optimization. Empirical and theoretical analyses highlight that distillation combines information transfer with regularization effects, and that selecting what, when, and how to transfer knowledge (e.g., logits vs. features, offline vs. online, task-aware filtering) is crucial to achieve favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across vision and language tasks.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students while attempting to preserve teacher performance. Work in KD spans matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, architecture search and task-adaptive compression, privacy-aware and federated settings, and domain- or task-specific adaptations. Empirical results show KD can yield dramatic reductions in size and compute with modest drops (or even gains) in downstream performance across speech, vision, and NLP tasks, but success depends on what is distilled (outputs versus internal features), optimization and dataset choices, and problem-specific design choices. The literature also identifies limitations and failure modes—optimization difficulties, data heterogeneity, and privacy constraints—that have motivated specialized protocols and theory. This synthesis summarizes the principal approaches, mechanistic explanations, representative empirical outcomes, and practical considerations for applying KD in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge distillation from multi-modal to mono-modal segmentation networks
papers_seen.abstract: The joint use of multiple imaging modalities for medical image segmentation has been widely studied in recent years. The fusion of information from different modalities has demonstrated to improve the segmentation accuracy, with respect to mono-modal segmentations, in several applications. However, acquiring multiple modalities is usually not possible in a clinical setting due to a limited number of physicians and scanners, and to limit costs and scan time. Most of the time, only one modality is acquired. In this paper, we propose KD-Net, a framework to transfer knowledge from a trained multi-modal network (teacher) to a mono-modal one (student). The proposed method is an adaptation of the generalized distillation framework where the student network is trained on a subset (1 modality) of the teacher's inputs (n modalities). We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in brain tumor segmentation with the BraTS 2018 dataset. Using different architectures, we show that the student network effectively learns from the teacher and always outperforms the baseline mono-modal network in terms of segmentation accuracy.

papers_seen.author: Lewis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models to enable deployment under compute, memory, latency, privacy, or domain constraints. A diverse toolbox of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention/relational structure, and decision-boundary or synthetic-data signals), training protocols (single/multi-teacher, online/self-distillation, task- and layer-aware schedules), and architecture-aware adaptations (projectors, layer mapping, and combinations with pruning/quantization/NAS) has been developed. Empirically, properly designed distillation pipelines recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks, and can be combined with complementary compression methods to meet device and domain requirements. Remaining challenges include optimization gaps, teacher–student capacity mismatch, distribution shift and data scarcity (including privacy- and data-free regimes), and trade-offs among accuracy, robustness, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Shields
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques transfer information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller, faster students to enable deployment under constraints of latency, memory, privacy, and compute. A diverse set of distillation targets and training paradigms—soft-label (logit) matching, intermediate feature and attention-map imitation, layer-wise mapping, adversarial and data-free generation of surrogate examples, online and multi-teacher schemes, self-distillation, and integration with architecture search or pruning—have been developed and adapted to vision, language, multimodal, and generative tasks. Empirical work shows KD often recovers most of the teacher's accuracy (and in some settings improves generalization or robustness) when combined with task-aware choices of signals to transfer, data augmentation, and teacher-student design; remaining gaps and failure modes are linked to teacher quality, data availability and distribution shift, heterogeneous architectures, and fairness or robustness concerns.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable family of techniques that transfers information from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models to reduce inference cost, memory, and latency while often retaining much of the teacher’s performance. The literature shows a diverse toolkit of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational structure, channel statistics, and contrastive signals), protocols (offline, online, self-, multi-teacher, and data-free variants), and task-aware adaptations (layer mapping, projector modules, synthetic-data generation, and curriculum/annealing). Empirical work across vision, language, graphs, multimodal tasks, and continual or federated settings demonstrates substantial efficiency gains but also highlights persistent challenges: teacher–student capacity and architecture mismatch, limited or unavailable training data, propagation of teacher biases or errors, distribution shift, and difficulties transferring rare or low-frequency behaviors. Practical success typically requires matching the distillation signal to task and student capacity and integrating KD with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search.

papers_seen.author: James
papers_seen.title: Robust Cross-Modal Representation Learning with Progressive Self-Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The learning objective of vision-language approach of CLIP does not effectively account for the noisy many-to-many correspondences found in web-harvested image captioning datasets, which contributes to its compute and data inefficiency. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training framework based on cross-modal contrastive learning that uses progressive self-distillation and soft image-text alignments to more efficiently learn robust representations from noisy data. Our model distills its own knowledge to dynamically generate soft-alignment targets for a subset of images and captions in every minibatch, which are then used to update its parameters. Extensive evaluation across 14 benchmark datasets shows that our method consistently outperforms its CLIP counterpart in multiple settings, including: (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval, without incurring added computational cost. Analysis using an ImageNet-based robustness test-bed reveals that our method offers better effective robustness to natural distribution shifts compared to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP itself. Lastly, pretraining with datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size shows that our improvements over CLIP tend to scale with number of training examples.

papers_seen.author: Gardner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, more expensive models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained students to enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. The literature has expanded from simple logit-matching to a diverse toolbox that includes intermediate-feature matching, attention and relational objectives, self- and multi-teacher schemes, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and hybrid pipelines that combine pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware search. Empirical work shows that with task-aware objectives and careful handling of teacher-student mismatches, distilled students can approach teacher performance across vision and language tasks, though important challenges remain around data scarcity, teacher imperfection, capacity mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Approaches, Applications, and Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: This synthesis summarizes methods, extensions, and applications of knowledge distillation and related model compression techniques in deep learning and NLP. It covers teacher-student paradigms (offline and online), multi-teacher and ensemble strategies, layer- and feature-based distillation, data-free and privacy-aware distillation, task-aware and architecture-aware adaptations, theoretical perspectives, and applications beyond classification (e.g., generation, detection, graph learning, and machine reading). The review highlights recurrent practical challenges—capacity mismatch, optimization difficulty, redundant teacher information, data and privacy constraints—and points to promising directions such as task-aware filtering, many-to-many layer mappings, and adversarial/data-free sample generation to enable distillation under limited resources or access.

papers_seen.author: Rowe
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD enables deployment under latency, memory, compute, and occasionally privacy constraints by matching teacher outputs, representations, or relational structure; it is routinely combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies (augmentation, synthetic data) to meet task- and deployment-specific requirements. While KD often preserves much of teacher performance, its success is context dependent and requires careful choices about distillation targets, teacher–student alignment, and data handling; open problems remain in principled target selection, robustness to distribution shift and rare outputs, and automated teacher–student matching.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, task‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners match soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data to train compact students. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and data strategies, and explicit teacher–student alignment; however, important limitations remain in distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, heterogeneous architectures, privacy and federated settings, and principled teacher selection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open challenges distilled from the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Pacheco
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation with Adversarial Samples Supporting Decision Boundary
papers_seen.abstract: Many recent works on knowledge distillation have provided ways to transfer the knowledge of a trained network for improving the learning process of a new one, but finding a good technique for knowledge distillation is still an open problem. In this paper, we provide a new perspective based on a decision boundary, which is one of the most important component of a classifier. The generalization performance of a classifier is closely related to the adequacy of its decision boundary, so a good classifier bears a good decision boundary. Therefore, transferring information closely related to the decision boundary can be a good attempt for knowledge distillation. To realize this goal, we utilize an adversarial attack to discover samples supporting a decision boundary. Based on this idea, to transfer more accurate information about the decision boundary, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier based on the adversarial samples supporting the decision boundary. Experiments show that the proposed method indeed improves knowledge distillation and achieves the state-of-the-arts performance.

papers_seen.author: Perez
papers_seen.title: DINE: Domain Adaptation from Single and Multiple Black-box Predictors
papers_seen.abstract: To ease the burden of labeling, unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to transfer knowledge in previous and related labeled datasets (sources) to a new unlabeled dataset (target). Despite impressive progress, prior methods always need to access the raw source data and develop data-dependent alignment approaches to recognize the target samples in a transductive learning manner, which may raise privacy concerns from source individuals. Several recent studies resort to an alternative solution by exploiting the well-trained white-box model from the source domain, yet, it may still leak the raw data through generative adversarial learning. This paper studies a practical and interesting setting for UDA, where only black-box source models (i.e., only network predictions are available) are provided during adaptation in the target domain. To solve this problem, we propose a new two-step knowledge adaptation framework called DIstill and fine-tuNE (DINE). Taking into consideration the target data structure, DINE first distills the knowledge from the source predictor to a customized target model, then fine-tunes the distilled model to further fit the target domain. Besides, neural networks are not required to be identical across domains in DINE, even allowing effective adaptation on a low-resource device. Empirical results on three UDA scenarios (i.e., single-source, multi-source, and partial-set) confirm that DINE achieves highly competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

papers_seen.author: Lee
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses larger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models by transferring predictive behavior or internal representations. A broad toolkit has emerged — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational/contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or synthetic-data schemes, and hybrid pipelines combining distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirically, KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, and objective design. Important open problems include principled theory linking transfer signals to student generalization, reliable distillation under domain shift and heterogeneous devices, and preserving rare or structured outputs in sequence tasks.

papers_seen.author: Morrison
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Central, Context-Dependent Tool Best Used in a Compression Portfolio
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster students. It reliably reduces inference cost and enables deployment across modalities when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or mismatched data. KD should be treated as a core, necessary element of practical compression pipelines but not as a standalone solution: the best results come from integrating KD with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from applying context-aware design and mitigation for bias, robustness, and data constraints.

papers_seen.author: Gibson
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses or transfers capabilities of large models into smaller ones via indirect supervision. Methods vary by what is transferred (logits, intermediate features, attention, relational structure), how teachers and students are paired (single, ensemble, multi-teacher, self-distillation), and practical constraints (limited data, privacy, cross-distribution generalization, modality mismatch). Empirical work across speech, vision, language, retrieval, graph, generative modeling, and medical imaging shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while gaining resource efficiency; theoretical analyses and diagnostic studies clarify mechanisms and guide designs such as projector layers, many-to-many layer mapping, and curriculum or data-augmentation strategies. Remaining challenges include distillation under data scarcity or privacy constraints, robust transfer of inductive biases, and principled layer-to-layer alignment for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Garcia
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) comprises a broad family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models to meet latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods operate at multiple levels (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational signals) and within diverse protocols (offline teacher→student, online/self-distillation, multi‑teacher, and data‑free/zero‑shot approaches). Empirical evidence shows KD often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance and can sometimes improve student generalization when objectives, data, and teacher–student design are well matched; however, success is context dependent and sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability and distribution shift, and risks of transferring teacher errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that combines carefully chosen distillation signals, layer-mapping and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, and architecture search) while adopting targeted safeguards for low‑frequency behaviors, privacy, and fairness.

papers_seen.author: Allen
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practically motivated family of techniques for transferring behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. KD methods operate at multiple levels of abstraction (output logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), can be adapted to scarce- or privacy-constrained data regimes, and are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design to meet deployment constraints. Empirically, KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance across vision and language tasks, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, the choice of transfer targets, and the availability or synthesis of appropriate distillation data. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline rather than a turnkey solution.

papers_seen.author: Cox
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, multimodal, and federated settings, a diverse set of distillation targets and training protocols have been developed to meet compute, memory, latency, privacy, and domain constraints. When designed in a task- and capacity-aware manner and combined with complementary compression methods, distillation often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance; however, important limitations remain, including teacher–student capacity mismatch, data scarcity or privacy constraints, distribution shift, and trade-offs involving robustness and fairness. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical prescriptions, and the main open problems identified in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Chambers
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Sensitive Component of Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and empirically validated approach for producing compact, deployable models from larger teachers. KD reliably reduces latency and parameter counts while preserving much of teacher performance when its objectives, data strategy, and teacher–student alignment are chosen with task and deployment constraints in mind. However, KD is not a universal solution: capacity mismatch, teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization instability limit off‑the‑shelf success. The strongest practical outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core within hybrid compression pipelines that also employ pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task‑aware data procedures.

papers_seen.author: Burke
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile technique for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving or sometimes improving task performance. When treated as a configurable, task-aware component and combined with complementary compression techniques (e.g., pruning, quantization, layer mapping, or data synthesis), KD yields favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across modalities and supports deployment under latency, privacy, and data-constraint requirements. However, realizing KD's benefits reliably requires attention to teacher quality, student capacity, what signals are transferred, how layers are aligned, and which training data or augmentations are used.

papers_seen.author: Kelley
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Practical, Context-Aware Advocacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across modalities and tasks. When treated as a flexible, task-aware toolbox—combining logits, feature and relational objectives, multi-teacher or ensemble signals, and data-aware input strategies—KD reliably enables deployments under latency, memory, privacy, and domain-shift constraints. However, KD is context-dependent: its success hinges on teacher quality, signal selection, data availability, and careful alignment of teacher and student. Best results come from integrating KD with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and from adopting targeted practices to mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer and failures on low-frequency phenomena.

papers_seen.author: King
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Insufficient Tool: Integrating Distillation with Representation, Data, and Architecture Strategies for Robust Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and broadly applicable approach for producing smaller, more deployable models from large teachers in deep learning and NLP. However, KD alone is rarely sufficient to meet real-world deployment constraints: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, the choice of distilled signals (logits, features, attention), and access to or synthesis of suitable training data. Best results arise when KD is embedded in an integrated compression pipeline that combines representation-level matching, projector or layer-mapping modules, data and curriculum strategies, and architecture-aware compression (pruning, quantization, or layer skipping). Careful attention to optimization, robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors is required to avoid propagating teacher errors and to produce reliable compact models for downstream applications.

papers_seen.author: Marshall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: A Central, Practical, and Responsible Strategy for Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, widely applicable set of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers. When combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture design) and tailored to task and data constraints, KD unlocks deployment on latency-, memory-, and privacy-constrained platforms while supporting modalities from language to vision and multimodal systems. However, KD is not automatic: careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to handle limited or private data, and how to mitigate transfer of undesirable behaviors (bias, rare-token degradation) are required for responsible, robust outcomes.

papers_seen.author: Flores
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks, researchers have extended KD beyond soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level alignment, contrastive and relational objectives, online and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. Practical success depends on teacher quality and student capacity, the choice of distilled signals, data availability or synthetic-data strategies, and combinations with complementary compression methods such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include principled understanding of when particular signals help, handling heterogeneous or non-iid data in federated settings, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and reliably scaling distillation in large distributed systems.

papers_seen.author: Wilson
papers_seen.title: What is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad, practical family of techniques for transferring information from large, often multi-modal or ensemble teachers into smaller, faster student models to enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Across vision and language tasks KD has been adapted into many forms — soft-target (logit) matching, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, online and offline protocols, and data-free or zero-shot schemes — and is frequently combined with complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can recover much of teacher performance in many settings when teacher quality, student capacity, and appropriate data or synthesis strategies are addressed; theoretical and empirical analyses highlight KD’s role both as knowledge transfer and as a regularizer. Despite broad success, KD faces limits from teacher–student mismatch, limited or heterogeneous data, and propagation of teacher artifacts; current best practice is to treat KD as one element of an integrated, task-aware compression pipeline.

papers_seen.author: Coleman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Central, but Contextual Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, production-ready approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster, or more deployable students. When combined with complementary compression primitives, careful choice of distillation targets and protocols, and task- or data-aware design, KD routinely produces compact models that retain a large fraction of teacher performance. However, KD is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis strategy, and attention to robustness, low-frequency phenomena, and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a flexible toolkit that must be adapted to deployment constraints and complemented with privacy-, fairness-, and robustness-aware methods.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: What Is Known About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used, practically validated set of techniques for transferring information from high-capacity teacher models into smaller students so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. The KD toolkit has expanded beyond soft-targets to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, and data‑free or privacy-aware synthesis. Empirical evidence shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable domain adaptation, federated and privacy-sensitive workflows, and multimodal-to-mono-modal transfer. However, KD’s success is context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the distillation data, and mitigation of propagated errors, bias, and distribution-shift issues. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline that leverages complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and task-aware engineering.

papers_seen.author: Adkins
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context-Dependent Framework for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and widely adopted approach for compressing large models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their predictive performance. KD operates at multiple levels—from soft-target (logit) supervision to representation- and layer-wise alignment—and integrates naturally with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and data-augmentation or curriculum strategies. Empirical evidence across vision, language, generative models, and retrieval shows distilled students often recover a large fraction of teacher accuracy and can add benefits such as improved generalization or interpretability when applied carefully. However, KD is not a universal solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data regime, optimization choices, and explicit handling of teacher biases and distribution shift. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component in a broader compression pipeline, chosen and tuned to the task, data availability, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Hall
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods—ranging from soft-target/logit matching to intermediate-feature, attention, relational, and data‑free objectives—enable substantial reductions in inference cost, memory, and latency while often preserving a large fraction of teacher performance. Practical success is conditional on task-aware choices about distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and integration with complementary compression primitives; open challenges remain in capacity mismatch, distributional robustness, preservation of rare behaviors, and privacy-aware deployment.
