papers_seen.author: Obrien
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a broad toolbox for transferring predictive capacity from large, expensive models to smaller, faster, or privacy-preserving models. Methods range from soft-logit supervision to internal representation matching, contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and self-distillation schemes, and integration with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical evidence across vision, NLP, graphs, and federated settings shows KD can recover much of a teacher's performance in resource-constrained deployments, while challenges remain in teacher selection, data availability, bias propagation, and task-specific design.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central tools for shrinking model size and latency while preserving performance across computer vision, natural language processing, recommendation, and federated settings. Research has expanded beyond the original logits-matching paradigm into feature mimicking, many-to-many layer mapping, teacher engineering, multi-teacher schemes, data- and privacy-constrained distillation, and task-adaptive compression. Empirical and theoretical work highlights important interactions between data complexity, teacher strength, inductive bias, and augmentation strategies, and identifies practical challenges including model-heterogeneity, data heterogeneity, and the need for robust data-free methods. The field increasingly emphasizes not only how to distill but also what to distill (logits, features, inter-class relations, view- or task-specific knowledge) and how to adapt distillation to application constraints (privacy, federated settings, domain shifts, resource budgets).

papers_seen.author: Rodriguez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Practical Trade-offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted strategy for producing smaller, faster, or more interpretable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact student models. A wide range of techniques has been developed that go beyond matching final outputs to include intermediate representation matching, attention/feature imitation, contrastive and relational objectives, and architecture-aware optimization; KD is commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and neural architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work across vision, language, speech, graphs, and reinforcement learning demonstrates that careful selection of teacher signals, student capacity, data regimes, and auxiliary compression methods strongly affects final trade-offs between efficiency and task performance.

papers_seen.author: Snyder
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a powerful and widely applicable approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring information beyond hard labels. KD is most effective when treated as a central element of a broader compression portfolio that includes architecture-aware design, pre-training, pruning/quantization, and privacy- or data-aware protocols. Practical deployment benefits from careful choices about what to transfer (logits, features, relations), how to align teacher and student, and when to apply auxiliary methods; remaining challenges include robustness under distributional shift, teacher imperfections, low-frequency token fidelity, and privacy-sensitive or heterogeneous-device settings.

papers_seen.author: Bryant
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, task-aware family of methods for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, deployable student models. KD uses a variety of transfer targets and training protocols to reduce inference cost, enable deployment under memory and latency constraints, and—when carefully applied—preserve much of teacher performance. Practical application treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline, combining distillation with architecture design, pruning, quantization, data strategies, and explicit safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression: Powerful, Versatile, but Context-Dependent
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a core technique for compressing large models and transferring their knowledge into smaller, faster models for deployment in resource-constrained settings and domain-specific applications. Advances in layer- and feature-level transfer, many-to-many layer mapping, data- and augmentation-aware practices, and federated or privacy-sensitive adaptations have expanded KD's applicability across vision, NLP, and graph domains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: it can propagate teacher errors, struggle under data heterogeneity, and depend critically on teacher quality, data choices, and optimization design. Best outcomes follow when practitioners combine KD with complementary techniques (careful layer matching, feature mimicking, data selection/augmentation, and pruning or quantization) and explicitly address heterogeneity and teacher reliability.

papers_seen.author: Davenport
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Mechanisms, Applications, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broad and practical family of techniques for transferring information from larger or otherwise stronger teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD encompasses matching teacher outputs (soft labels), aligning internal representations and features, transferring relational or contrastive structure, and using curriculum or search to adapt students and their architectures. Applied across vision, language, retrieval, generation, and federated settings, KD enables latency and memory reductions, on-device deployment, ensemble compression, and privacy-aware releases. Effectiveness depends on what is distilled, teacher–student compatibility, data and optimization choices, and problem-specific designs; as a result, KD functions best as a toolbox of choices (targets, mappings, curricula, privacy/robustness safeguards) rather than a single recipe. Remaining challenges include theoretical understanding of which teacher signals matter across tasks, robustness under data heterogeneity, privacy-preserving distillation, and automated, deployment-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Avila
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Task‑Aware Toolbox — Powerful but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. However, KD has clear limits — capacity and architecture mismatch, data scarcity and distribution shift, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or bias — so it is best used as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture co-design, and explicit fairness/privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, Challenges, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation comprises a broad set of techniques that transfer predictive behavior or internal representations from larger (teacher) models to smaller (student) models to enable deployment under constraints of compute, memory, latency, and privacy. Over the past decade researchers have extended simple logit-matching to feature-, relation-, and layer-wise objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, data-free and privacy-aware protocols, and integrations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work demonstrates that distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance across vision, language, recommendation, and other modalities, but success depends on student capacity, alignment of targets and layers, the nature and availability of distillation data, and mitigation of transferred biases or teacher errors. Ongoing priorities are principled objectives for what to transfer, robust and private distillation under heterogeneous and federated data, and automated teacher–student design for practical deployments.

papers_seen.author: Charles
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Demand-Aware Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, broadly applicable framework for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of the teachers' utility. KD methods span output matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, self- and ensemble-distillation, meta-learned and student-friendly teacher designs, and data- or task-aware adaptations. Empirical work across vision, speech, graph, and language tasks demonstrates KD’s ability to deliver large reductions in model size and compute with modest performance loss, and in many cases to improve robustness or generalization when combined with appropriate procedures. At the same time, KD’s reliability depends on choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle limited or private data; addressing these constraints through architectural design, curriculum and meta-learning, augmentation and synthetic-data strategies, and multi-teacher or online schemes is central to practical deployment.

papers_seen.author: Edwards
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression: Benefits, Limits, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from large teacher models to smaller student models to meet latency, memory, and deployment constraints. KD is most effective when treated as a configurable, task‑aware component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with data strategies, architecture design, and complementary techniques such as pruning and quantization—rather than as a one‑size‑fits‑all recipe. Its strengths include strong empirical gains across modalities and tasks and support for privacy- or data‑limited settings; its limits include teacher bias transfer, capacity mismatches, optimization and distribution‑shift failures, and degradation on rare or fine‑grained outputs. Practical deployment requires explicit attention to what signals are transferred, how teacher and student are aligned, and how distillation is integrated with other compression and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Jordan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Central Practical Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of large teachers. KD encompasses a range of targets and protocols—output-level supervision, intermediate representation matching, adversarial and data-free synthesis, multi-teacher and self-distillation—and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression techniques. While KD routinely delivers favorable efficiency–accuracy trade-offs in vision, language, recommender, and multimodal systems, realizing those gains in practice requires attention to teacher–student alignment, data availability and privacy, fairness and low-frequency behavior, and method selection for the deployment constraints at hand.

papers_seen.author: Robinson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Practical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely applied approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, faster, or deployment-specialized students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A large family of distillation objectives and training protocols has been developed—ranging from soft-label (logit) matching to feature- and layer-wise imitation, relational and contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free schemes, and online or multi-teacher setups—and these are frequently combined with complementary compression techniques such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows KD can recover much of a teacher’s performance while lowering latency and memory, but practical success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, availability or synthesis of data, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. Open problems include robust and private distillation under data scarcity and distribution shift, preserving rare-token or low-frequency behavior, avoiding propagation of teacher biases, and automating teacher–student mapping for heterogeneous architectures.

papers_seen.author: Huff
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, widely applicable approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, deployable students. When treated as a configurable toolkit—selecting appropriate distillation signals, aligning teacher and student capacity, and combining distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or task-adaptive architecture search)—practitioners routinely obtain compact models that retain much of teacher performance. Success requires explicit attention to teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, optimization schedules, and safeguards against transferred biases or degraded rare-token behavior.

papers_seen.author: Ibarra
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as the Practical Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible, and widely applicable approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable ones. It supports multiple information-transfer mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals) and can be adapted to constrained settings (limited data, privacy, heterogeneous devices). KD is most effective when used as part of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, or pretraining—and when practitioners mitigate known failure modes such as bias transfer, rare-token degradation, or teacher–student mismatch. With careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers, which data to use), KD enables substantial reductions in model size and latency while largely preserving task performance across modalities.

papers_seen.author: Suarez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Trade‑offs
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring information from larger, more expensive teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. KD supports multiple transfer signals (soft labels, features, attention/relations, contrastive objectives) and modes (offline, online, multi‑teacher, data‑free), and is widely used across modalities including NLP, vision, recommender systems, GANs, and reinforcement learning. Practical deployment of KD hinges on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability and augmentation, and mitigation of bias and distributional failures; combining KD with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and deployment‑aware safeguards typically yields the best trade‑offs.

papers_seen.author: Crosby
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques form a broad, practical toolkit for turning large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable models. Across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and federative settings, distillation can preserve much of a teacher's predictive quality while reducing inference latency, memory footprint, and communication costs. Different distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, contrastive signals) and training protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, multi-teacher, data-free/zero-shot) make KD adaptable to diverse deployment constraints. At the same time, distillation has well-documented failure modes—transfer of teacher biases, degradation on rare or low-frequency phenomena, sensitivity to data heterogeneity and teacher–student capacity mismatch—and practical success depends on task-aware design choices and often combining KD with pruning, quantization, or architecture search. The field thus treats KD as a multifaceted, application-driven set of methods whose best practice is to match signals, data, and student capacity to deployment needs while applying targeted mitigations for privacy, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Murray
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical set of techniques for compressing large teacher models into smaller, deployable student models in deep learning and NLP. KD can preserve much of teacher performance while reducing latency, memory, and compute, but its success depends on task-aware choices: what signals to transfer (logits, features, attention, relations), teacher–student alignment, available data (real, synthetic, or none), and complementary compression strategies (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Responsible and robust deployment further requires addressing distribution shift, low‑frequency or structured outputs, privacy and fairness concerns, and principled selection of distillation targets. I argue KD should be treated as a configurable toolkit — often essential for practical compression — rather than a turnkey solution; practitioners should select and combine distillation recipes according to capacity, data, and deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Wells
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, more deployable student models. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD techniques—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature- and relation-level objectives, multi- and self-distillation, data-free or privacy-preserving protocols, and online/co-distillation schemes—enable substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute with modest accuracy loss when applied with task-aware design. Effective use of KD typically combines careful selection of what to transfer, attention to teacher–student capacity and data regimes, and integration with complementary compression mechanisms such as pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher imperfection and bias transfer, data scarcity and domain shift, capacity and optimization mismatch, and reliably distilling structured or generative outputs.

papers_seen.author: Kim
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Multifaceted Strategy for Model Compression, Adaptation and Privacy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is more than a single recipe for shrinking large models: it is a flexible family of techniques that enables accurate, efficient and deployable models across modalities and tasks. KD can compress huge pretrained language and vision models into lightweight architectures with large speed and memory gains while retaining most of the teacher performance. It also supports variant protocols—online, self-distillation, multi-teacher, representation-level and contrastive forms—that trade off efficiency, robustness, and generalization. Beyond raw compression, KD can enable domain adaptation, privacy-preserving model release, and fairness-aware training when combined with appropriate design choices. However, KD is not a panacea: teacher quality, data heterogeneity, and mismatch between teacher and student inputs/architectures can limit gains and must be addressed by specific strategies such as multi-teacher ensembles, confidence weighting, input alignment, or theoretical safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Decker
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, widely used approach for transferring predictive behavior from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller, efficient students. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods extend beyond logits-matching to include intermediate-feature and attention-level transfer, data-free and privacy-aware variants, multi-teacher and online protocols, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture design. Empirical work shows KD can yield compact models that retain much teacher performance, but success depends on careful selection of what and how to transfer, data availability, and the match between teacher and student.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis from Selected Literature
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, practical family of methods for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models to smaller student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Across vision, language, graph, and generative settings, KD techniques (logits, feature/attention matching, relational objectives, adversarial and data‑free protocols, and ensemble/online schemes) often recover a large fraction of teacher performance when paired with appropriate data strategies, pretraining, and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). KD has concrete limits — teacher error propagation, capacity mismatch, rare‑token degradation, and failures under distribution shift or scarce/private data — which motivate task‑aware design, multi‑signal objectives, and integration with other compression primitives. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, domain examples, practical guidelines, and open challenges documented in the selected literature.

papers_seen.author: Armstrong
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible and practical family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models into smaller student models so that compact models can approach teacher performance while meeting latency, memory, privacy, and deployment constraints. KD has diversified from simple soft-label matching to include feature- and attention-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, online and self-distillation, and data- or privacy-aware protocols. Empirical evidence shows KD routinely yields large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss across modalities, but its success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher–student alignment and capacity, data availability (including data-free methods), and careful mitigation of transferred biases and other failure modes. Best practice treats KD as a configurable core of a broader compression pipeline that integrates complementary techniques such as pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies.

papers_seen.author: Rhodes
papers_seen.title: Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: It is challenging to perform lifelong language learning (LLL) on a stream of different tasks without any performance degradation comparing to the multi-task counterparts. To address this issue, we present Lifelong Language Knowledge Distillation (L2KD), a simple but efficient method that can be easily applied to existing LLL architectures in order to mitigate the degradation. Specifically, when the LLL model is trained on a new task, we assign a teacher model to first learn the new task, and pass the knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation. Therefore, the LLL model can better adapt to the new task while keeping the previously learned knowledge. Experiments show that the proposed L2KD consistently improves previous state-of-the-art models, and the degradation comparing to multi-task models in LLL tasks is well mitigated for both sequence generation and text classification tasks.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models while retaining much of the original performance. A diverse family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial schemes, multi-teacher and self-supervised variants—has been developed and adapted across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs, and generative models). Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on choices of distillation targets, teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-specific adaptations. Open challenges include handling mismatches in capacity or data, preserving rare-token or long-tail behavior, and formalizing best practices for combining KD with complementary compression techniques.

papers_seen.author: Doyle
papers_seen.title: DE-RRD: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: Recent recommender systems have started to employ knowledge distillation, which is a model compression technique distilling knowledge from a cumbersome model (teacher) to a compact model (student), to reduce inference latency while maintaining performance. The state-of-the-art methods have only focused on making the student model accurately imitate the predictions of the teacher model. They have a limitation in that the prediction results incompletely reveal the teacher's knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender system, called DE-RRD, which enables the student model to learn from the latent knowledge encoded in the teacher model as well as from the teacher's predictions. Concretely, DE-RRD consists of two methods: 1) Distillation Experts (DE) that directly transfers the latent knowledge from the teacher model. DE exploits "experts" and a novel expert selection strategy for effectively distilling the vast teacher's knowledge to the student with limited capacity. 2) Relaxed Ranking Distillation (RRD) that transfers the knowledge revealed from the teacher's prediction with consideration of the relaxed ranking orders among items. Our extensive experiments show that DE-RRD outperforms the state-of-the-art competitors and achieves comparable or even better performance to that of the teacher model with faster inference time.

papers_seen.author: Pitts
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Synthesis of Methods, Evidence, Limits, and Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical family of methods for compressing large models into smaller, more efficient students by transferring predictive behavior, intermediate representations, or structural relationships. KD techniques span soft-target matching, feature- and attention-level objectives, relational/contrastive signals, and protocols such as offline, online/self-distillation, multi-teacher, and data‑free variants. Across vision, language, graph, and multimodal tasks KD routinely reduces latency, memory, and compute while recovering much of teacher performance, but its success is context-dependent: outcomes hinge on signal choice, teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability or synthesis, and integration with complementary compression primitives. Practical deployment therefore treats KD as a configurable core of broader compression pipelines, guided by task-aware design, teacher–student co‑engineering, and targeted mitigations for bias, robustness, and distribution shift.

papers_seen.author: Torres
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely adopted and versatile family of methods for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across computer vision, natural language processing, and multimodal tasks. The literature converges on a toolbox of distillation objectives (logit/soft-target matching, intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, and data-free or generative approaches), multiple data regimes (full-data, few-shot/limited-data, and data-free/zero-shot), and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, low-precision numerics, and architecture search). Empirical work shows KD frequently recovers most teacher performance and can act as both information transfer and regularizer, but its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, choice of transfer signals, and data availability. Remaining practical challenges include teacher–student mismatch, transfer of teacher errors or biases, preserving low-frequency and structured outputs, privacy- and federated-learning constraints, and automating task-aware distillation pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Roman
papers_seen.title: Fair Feature Distillation for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: Fairness is becoming an increasingly crucial issue for computer vision, especially in the human-related decision systems. However, achieving algorithmic fairness, which makes a model produce indiscriminative outcomes against protected groups, is still an unresolved problem. In this paper, we devise a systematic approach which reduces algorithmic biases via feature distillation for visual recognition tasks, dubbed as MMD-based Fair Distillation (MFD). While the distillation technique has been widely used in general to improve the prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge, there has been no explicit work that also tries to improve fairness via distillation. Furthermore, We give a theoretical justification of our MFD on the effect of knowledge distillation and fairness. Throughout the extensive experiments, we show our MFD significantly mitigates the bias against specific minorities without any loss of the accuracy on both synthetic and real-world face datasets.

papers_seen.author: Mills
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Applications, and Practical Insights
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from large, expensive models (or ensembles) to smaller, efficient models. Methods include logit-based distillation, feature- or representation-based matching, self-distillation, multi-teacher strategies, data-free and privacy-preserving approaches, and combinations with pruning or architecture search. KD has been applied across modalities and domains—vision, language, graphs, reinforcement learning, generative models, and healthcare—demonstrating gains in inference efficiency, robustness, generalization, and interpretability when appropriately designed. Open challenges remain around data availability, teacher–student mismatch, selection of distilled signals and samples, and principled integration with other compression techniques; recent work proposes meta-learning teachers, adaptive teacher weighting, projector modules, and task-adaptive compression as practical remedies.

papers_seen.author: House
papers_seen.title: The Centrality of Knowledge Distillation for Practical Deep and NLP Models
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques are indispensable for moving state-of-the-art deep models from research to real-world deployment. By transferring predictive behavior, representations, or relational structure from larger or specialized teachers to smaller students, KD enables faster inference, smaller footprints, better generalization across domains, privacy-preserving sharing, and adaptation to heterogeneous hardware and data constraints. Realizing these benefits in practice requires combining algorithmic advances (multi-teacher regimes, curriculum and projector design, augmentation and adversarial synthesis), systems thinking (federated and client-inclusive protocols), and attention to pitfalls (mismatched objectives, erased class relations). Together, the literature shows KD is not a niche trick but a broad, flexible toolkit for addressing latency, capacity, distribution shift, privacy, and interpretability in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Collaborative Distillation for Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer
papers_seen.abstract: Universal style transfer methods typically leverage rich representations from deep Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models (e.g., VGG-19) pre-trained on large collections of images. Despite the effectiveness, its application is heavily constrained by the large model size to handle ultra-resolution images given limited memory. In this work, we present a new knowledge distillation method (named Collaborative Distillation) for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer to reduce the convolutional filters. The main idea is underpinned by a finding that the encoder-decoder pairs construct an exclusive collaborative relationship, which is regarded as a new kind of knowledge for style transfer models. Moreover, to overcome the feature size mismatch when applying collaborative distillation, a linear embedding loss is introduced to drive the student network to learn a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Extensive experiments show the effectiveness of our method when applied to different universal style transfer approaches (WCT and AdaIN), even if the model size is reduced by 15.5 times. Especially, on WCT with the compressed models, we achieve ultra-resolution (over 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU for the first time. Further experiments on optimization-based stylization scheme show the generality of our algorithm on different stylization paradigms. Our code and trained models are available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

papers_seen.author: Thompson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, multimodal and generative settings. KD techniques transfer teacher behavior via soft logits, intermediate representations, attention or relational objectives, and can be extended to data-free, privacy-preserving, and adversarial regimes. Best results arise when distillation is combined with task-aware design choices and complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search); remaining challenges include data- or domain-limited scenarios, teacher–student mismatch, robustness and privacy trade-offs.

papers_seen.author: Jones
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and allied model-compression techniques transfer information from large, high-capacity teacher models to smaller, more efficient student models. The literature shows a diverse set of objectives and protocols—soft-label matching, feature- and layer-level alignment, many-to-many layer mappings, multi-teacher ensembles, data-free or privacy-preserving distillation, and adversarial or generator-based sample augmentation—that together enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints while trading off accuracy, robustness, and fairness. Empirical results indicate distilled students often approach teacher performance with substantially lower cost, but important limitations persist (teacher bias transfer, low-frequency token degradation, data access constraints, and capacity mismatch), motivating hybrid pipelines that combine KD with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and careful teacher–student design.

papers_seen.author: Roberts
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, practically validated framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, speech, graph, and generative tasks. KD supports multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational and contrastive signals), can operate in multi-teacher and data-free settings, and integrates with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data strategy (including synthetic or public data when originals are unavailable), and task-aware objective design. KD has documented failure modes — e.g., propagation of teacher errors or biases, difficulty preserving low-frequency phenomena, and distributional mismatch — which motivate targeted remedies such as multi-signal objectives, teacher scheduling, meta-learned teachers, and joint optimization with other compression tools. Treated as a configurable component of a broader compression pipeline rather than a single recipe, KD is an essential practical tool for model deployment under resource, privacy, and latency constraints.

papers_seen.author: Jackson
papers_seen.title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Mutual Contrastive Learning for Visual Recognition
papers_seen.abstract: The teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) aims to train an ensemble of multiple student models collaboratively and distill knowledge from each other. Although existing online KD methods achieve desirable performance, they often focus on class probabilities as the core knowledge type, ignoring the valuable feature representational information. We present a Mutual Contrastive Learning (MCL) framework for online KD. The core idea of MCL is to perform mutual interaction and transfer of contrastive distributions among a cohort of networks in an online manner. Our MCL can aggregate cross-network embedding information and maximize the lower bound to the mutual information between two networks. This enables each network to learn extra contrastive knowledge from others, leading to better feature representations, thus improving the performance of visual recognition tasks. Beyond the final layer, we extend MCL to intermediate layers and perform an adaptive layer-matching mechanism trained by meta-optimization. Experiments on image classification and transfer learning to visual recognition tasks show that layer-wise MCL can lead to consistent performance gains against state-of-the-art online KD approaches. The superiority demonstrates that layer-wise MCL can guide the network to generate better feature representations. Our code is publicly avaliable at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

papers_seen.author: Santos
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied framework for compressing large models, improving generalization, and transferring capabilities across modalities and deployment constraints. Research spans teacher-student paradigms (including multi-teacher and self-distillation), data-free and zero-shot distillation, task-adaptive compression, and applications to specialized tasks (detection, retrieval, translation, multimodal learning, federated settings, and graph problems). Empirical work shows KD can yield large speed and size gains while retaining much of the teacher's performance, but also exposes important limitations tied to optimization, data used for distillation, and potential bias transfer. Recent methods address these limitations via curriculum scheduling, confidence- or reinforcement-based teacher weighting, task-adaptive architecture search, domain- and modality-aware losses, and efficient label-generation or student-focused training regimes.

papers_seen.author: Simpson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Promise, Limits, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger teacher models into smaller students. KD methods vary in their transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational signals), training paradigms (offline, online, multi‑teacher, meta‑learned teachers, data‑free synthesis), and integration with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Empirical work across retrieval, vision, speech, and NLP shows distilled students frequently recover a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing inference cost, but reliable deployment requires task‑aware design choices, careful teacher–student alignment, suitable data strategies (including synthesis or privacy‑aware protocols), and explicit safeguards against propagated teacher artifacts and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Ferrell
papers_seen.title: AlphaNet: Improved Training of Supernets with Alpha-Divergence
papers_seen.abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is an effective technique for automating efficient neural architecture design. Weight-sharing NAS builds a supernet that assembles all the architectures as its sub-networks and jointly trains the supernet with the sub-networks. The success of weight-sharing NAS heavily relies on distilling the knowledge of the supernet to the sub-networks. However, we find that the widely used distillation divergence, i.e., KL divergence, may lead to student sub-networks that over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, leading to inferior performance of the sub-networks. In this work, we propose to improve the supernet training with a more generalized alpha-divergence. By adaptively selecting the alpha-divergence, we simultaneously prevent the over-estimation or under-estimation of the uncertainty of the teacher model. We apply the proposed alpha-divergence based supernets training to both slimmable neural networks and weight-sharing NAS, and demonstrate significant improvements. Specifically, our discovered model family, AlphaNet, outperforms prior-art models on a wide range of FLOPs regimes, including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS. We achieve ImageNet top-1 accuracy of 80.0% with only 444M FLOPs. Our code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

papers_seen.author: Frost
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has become a practical and flexible pathway to compress large neural models into smaller, faster students while preserving much of their performance. Across NLP and other modalities, researchers have developed logit-level, representation-level, layer-wise, multi-teacher, data-free, privacy-aware, and task-aware distillation variants and combined KD with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet deployment constraints. Empirical work shows that careful choice of what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data and low-frequency phenomena materially affects student quality and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Cortez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models from larger teachers across vision, language, and multimodal settings. It can recover much of a teacher's performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, or privacy constraints, and it interacts naturally with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. However, distillation's success depends on the distillation objective, teacher–student alignment, data strategy, and task-specific considerations; when these are not addressed it can propagate teacher errors, struggle with rare outputs, or fail due to optimization issues. Best practice is to treat KD as a configurable component of compression pipelines—combining logits, intermediate feature matching, projector modules, multi-teacher or teacher-adaptive designs, and data-aware schedules—to maximize student utility in real-world deployments.

papers_seen.author: Davis
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a widely used framework for transferring predictive behavior from large, expensive teachers to smaller, efficient students. Across vision, language, recommendation, graph, and multimodal tasks, KD has been extended beyond logits-matching into feature and layer-level mimicry, online and self-distillation, adversarial and contrastive objectives, task-adaptive architecture search, and combinations with pruning and quantization. Empirical results show KD enables substantial latency and memory reductions while often preserving accuracy, improving calibration, and helping robustness; success depends strongly on choices about what to transfer, teacher quality, data and augmentation, and alignment strategies between heterogeneous models.

papers_seen.author: Cowan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques aim to transfer knowledge from large, expensive models to smaller, efficient models while preserving performance. Across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings, researchers have applied KD for inference speedup, deployment on resource-constrained devices, privacy-preserving model release, and enhanced robustness or interpretability. Methods vary from standard teacher–student soft-label supervision to data-free distillation, adversarially chosen boundary samples, many-to-many layer mappings, generative replay, and architecture-aware compression. Empirical results show KD can yield large efficiency gains with modest accuracy loss when combined with task-aware design, careful sample selection, and appropriate optimization; challenges remain around distributional mismatch, low-frequency token handling, heterogeneous architectures, and privacy/validation in data-free scenarios. Emerging directions include task-adaptive compressed models, joint optimization of pruning and KD, federated/distilled learning across heterogeneous devices, and cross-modal distillation for generative capabilities.

papers_seen.author: Ruiz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a family of techniques for transferring behavior from large or ensemble teacher models to smaller, deployable students. Across modalities and tasks, KD variants — including soft-target/logit transfer, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, multi-teacher and online schemes, and data-free synthesis — are used alone or with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to reduce parameters, latency, and memory while attempting to retain teacher performance. Practical success depends on matching distillation signals to task and student capacity, handling limited or private data, and mitigating transferred biases or rare-case failures. Important open problems include teacher–student capacity gaps, domain shift and data scarcity, privacy guarantees for data-free and federated settings, and automated teacher–student co-design for hardware-aware deployment.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Context‑Dependent, Foundational Toolbox for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile approach for producing compact, efficient models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to smaller student models. KD encompasses many mechanisms (soft logits, intermediate feature and attention alignment, relational and contrastive objectives, data‑free and multi‑teacher schemes) and is most effective when integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, curriculum, domain adaptation). Its power for deployment in resource‑ or privacy‑constrained settings is well documented; however, KD is not universally sufficient. Success depends on careful choices about what to transfer, teacher‑student compatibility, data availability, and mitigation of failure modes such as optimization mismatch, bias transfer, and degradation on rare phenomena. The pragmatic stance advocated here is to treat KD as a configurable component of a broader compression and deployment pipeline, tuned to task, data regime, and safety constraints.

papers_seen.author: Webster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Practical, Task-Aware Core of Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable and practically essential approach for compressing large deep models into smaller, faster, or specialized models. When designed around task constraints, student capacity, and available data, KD preserves much of a teacher's capabilities while enabling deployment under compute, memory, latency, and privacy limits. Its greatest value comes from treating distillation as a configurable toolkit—combining soft-targets, representation matching, adversarial or data-free sample synthesis, and multi-teacher or self-distillation—with complementary compression techniques to meet real-world constraints. Success requires careful handling of teacher–student alignment, data scarcity, distribution shift, and bias transfer, but a task-aware, hybrid pipeline makes KD one of the most practical routes to effective model compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.author: Yu
papers_seen.title: Best Practices and Limitations of Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a broadly applicable and powerful approach for compressing models across modalities, but its effectiveness depends on design choices spanning what is distilled (logits, features, internal representations), how inputs are prepared (augmentation, sample selection), how multiple teachers are reconciled, and whether robustness or task-specific structure is considered. Recent work shows that combining soft-target regularization with feature- and intermediate-representation matching, careful input-side interventions, and adaptive distillation objectives yields the best tradeoffs between compression, accuracy, and robustness across vision, language, multimodal, graph, and generative-model settings.

papers_seen.author: Manning
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Central, Practical, but Insufficient — A Position and Recommended Practice
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and widely adopted framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of teacher performance. Empirical evidence across vision and language shows that KD can reduce inference cost, latency, and memory requirements and enable deployment under privacy, communication, and resource constraints. However, KD alone does not guarantee robust, unbiased, or optimal compressed models: failures arise from teacher–student mismatch, limited or absent data, transfer of teacher errors and biases, poor handling of low-frequency phenomena, and vulnerability under distribution shift or adversarial attack. Practical compression therefore treats KD as a core component within an integrated pipeline—combining representation-aware objectives, curriculum and sample-selection strategies, adversarial or synthetic-data generation for data-scarce regimes, and complementary compression steps (pruning, quantization, architecture search) to realize reliable, resource-aware students.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Spears
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a First-Class, Task-Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and versatile framework for producing compact models that retain much of the performance and useful properties of larger teachers. KD has repeatedly proven effective across modalities and tasks, enabling efficient deployment on constrained hardware, supporting domain and modality transfer, and integrating with complementary compression techniques. However, its benefits are conditional: success depends on teacher quality, data design, augmentation, and careful objective selection, and KD can transfer teacher errors or undesirable biases unless explicitly mitigated. Treating KD as a configurable toolkit—combining logit-level supervision, representation matching, data-side interventions, and deployment-aware protocols—yields the best trade-offs between efficiency, accuracy, and robustness.

papers_seen.author: Duncan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Analyses, and Applications
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a central technique for compressing and adapting large neural models into smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models while retaining much of their performance. A diverse set of KD approaches operate at the level of final outputs (logits), intermediate features, layer relations, or via adversarial and data-generation mechanisms. KD has been adapted across modalities and tasks — from NLP transformer compression to GAN and speech-model compression, cross-modal transfer, federated settings, and domain-specific applications — and interacts strongly with concerns about robustness, fairness, and transfer of inductive biases. Empirical and theoretical work has clarified when and why various KD variants help, and highlights open challenges in data heterogeneity, teacher-student mismatch, and automatic discovery of compact architectures.

papers_seen.author: Nelson
papers_seen.title: Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applied collection of techniques for transferring information from large, high-performing teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across vision, language, graphs, retrieval, and multimodal problems, distillation methods—ranging from soft-target (logit) matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, curriculum strategies, ensemble-to-single-model transfer, and data- or privacy-aware variants—enable deployable models that trade modest accuracy loss for substantial gains in latency, memory, and energy use. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance when combined with careful design choices (what to transfer, how to align layers and capacities, and how to prepare data), but success requires managing failure modes such as capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, and sensitivity to distillation data. This synthesis summarizes what the provided literature reports about methods, mechanisms, applications, best practices, and open problems for KD-based model compression.

papers_seen.author: Richards
papers_seen.title: TextKD-GAN: Text Generation using KnowledgeDistillation and Generative Adversarial Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Text generation is of particular interest in many NLP applications such as machine translation, language modeling, and text summarization. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) achieved a remarkable success in high quality image generation in computer vision,and recently, GANs have gained lots of interest from the NLP community as well. However, achieving similar success in NLP would be more challenging due to the discrete nature of text. In this work, we introduce a method using knowledge distillation to effectively exploit GAN setup for text generation. We demonstrate how autoencoders (AEs) can be used for providing a continuous representation of sentences, which is a smooth representation that assign non-zero probabilities to more than one word. We distill this representation to train the generator to synthesize similar smooth representations. We perform a number of experiments to validate our idea using different datasets and show that our proposed approach yields better performance in terms of the BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) measure compared to traditional GAN-based text generation approaches without pre-training.

papers_seen.author: Rivas
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Empirical Patterns, and Open Challenges
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques form a rich, task-sensitive toolbox for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger or ensemble teacher models to compact students. Practitioners move beyond simple logit matching to transfer internal representations, attention patterns, relational structure, and decision-boundary information, and they combine distillation with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and data strategies (augmentation, synthetic or data-free generation). Empirical results across vision, language, generative models, and structured prediction show distilled students often recover much of teacher performance and can enable deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but distillation also has failure modes—teacher bias transfer, sensitivity to data availability, capacity mismatch, and degraded modeling of low-frequency phenomena—that require targeted mitigations and continued theoretical and empirical work.

papers_seen.author: Dean
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context-Aware Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a central and practical approach for compressing large neural models into smaller, faster, and sometimes more interpretable students across vision, language, multimodal, and domain-specific tasks. KD’s flexibility—transferring soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, or relational/contrastive signals—lets practitioners tailor compression to hardware, privacy, or accuracy constraints. Empirical evidence shows that when distillation is designed task- and capacity-aware and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, or progressive module replacement), students can recover much of teacher performance and gain robustness or interpretability in particular settings. At the same time, KD is not automatic: teacher quality, data availability or synthesis, teacher–student mismatch, and the risk of transferring teacher errors or biases require careful protocols (sample selection, layer mapping, objective weighting, and privacy- or robustness-aware extensions). I argue KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component of compression pipelines—powerful and broadly applicable, but demand-aware and paired with best practices to realize its potential reliably.

papers_seen.author: Adams
papers_seen.title: A Closer Look at Deep Learning Heuristics: Learning rate restarts, Warmup and Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: The convergence rate and final performance of common deep learning models have significantly benefited from heuristics such as learning rate schedules, knowledge distillation, skip connections, and normalization layers. In the absence of theoretical underpinnings, controlled experiments aimed at explaining these strategies can aid our understanding of deep learning landscapes and the training dynamics. Existing approaches for empirical analysis rely on tools of linear interpolation and visualizations with dimensionality reduction, each with their limitations. Instead, we revisit such analysis of heuristics through the lens of recently proposed methods for loss surface and representation analysis, viz., mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA), and hypothesize reasons for the success of the heuristics. In particular, we explore knowledge distillation and learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup using mode connectivity and CCA. Our empirical analysis suggests that: (a) the reasons often quoted for the success of cosine annealing are not evidenced in practice; (b) that the effect of learning rate warmup is to prevent the deeper layers from creating training instability; and (c) that the latent knowledge shared by the teacher is primarily disbursed to the deeper layers.

papers_seen.author: Harrell
papers_seen.title: No One Left Behind: Inclusive Federated Learning over Heterogeneous Devices
papers_seen.abstract: Federated learning (FL) is an important paradigm for training global models from decentralized data in a privacy-preserving way. Existing FL methods usually assume the global model can be trained on any participating client. However, in real applications, the devices of clients are usually heterogeneous, and have different computing power. Although big models like BERT have achieved huge success in AI, it is difficult to apply them to heterogeneous FL with weak clients. The straightforward solutions like removing the weak clients or using a small model to fit all clients will lead to some problems, such as under-representation of dropped clients and inferior accuracy due to data loss or limited model representation ability. In this work, we propose InclusiveFL, a client-inclusive federated learning method to handle this problem. The core idea of InclusiveFL is to assign models of different sizes to clients with different computing capabilities, bigger models for powerful clients and smaller ones for weak clients. We also propose an effective method to share the knowledge among multiple local models with different sizes. In this way, all the clients can participate in the model learning in FL, and the final model can be big and powerful enough. Besides, we propose a momentum knowledge distillation method to better transfer knowledge in big models on powerful clients to the small models on weak clients. Extensive experiments on many real-world benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning accurate models from clients with heterogeneous devices under the FL framework.

papers_seen.author: Johnson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses high-capacity teacher models into smaller student models by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A broad family of distillation objectives—ranging from soft-logit matching to feature-, attention- and layer-wise alignment, relational/contrastive signals, adversarial and data-free sample synthesis, and meta- or multi-teacher schemes—has been developed and applied across vision, language, retrieval, graph, and federated settings. In practice, KD is most effective when combined with task- and architecture-aware design choices and complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search). Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, limited or private data, and optimization stability; proposed remedies emphasize task-aware filtering of teacher signals, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-aware protocols.

papers_seen.author: Mcmillan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task-Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from a simple teacher–student soft-label transfer into a flexible set of methods that enable compact, fast, and often more robust models across vision, language, multimodal and generative settings. When designed with awareness of task constraints, data availability, and deployment demands, KD combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, layer skipping, meta-learned teachers, or generative replay) reliably yields practical gains. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its effectiveness depends on choices about what to transfer (logits, features, attention), how to align teacher and student architectures, how to handle limited or private data, and how to preserve robustness and fairness. This paper argues that KD should be treated as a first-class, configurable component in compression pipelines: powerful and broadly applicable when paired with principled, task-centered decisions, but demand-aware and tuned to deployment objectives.

papers_seen.author: Smith
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical and flexible framework for compressing large models into smaller, deployable ones while preserving much of their performance. Across vision, language, graph, and generative modeling, KD methods vary by what is transferred (teacher logits, internal representations, attention, relational structure), how layers are aligned or projected, and how data constraints (limited access, privacy, or distribution shift) are handled. Empirical work demonstrates that combining output-level and representation-level objectives, using layer-mapping or projector modules, and adapting training data or curricula yields the best trade-offs between compactness and accuracy. Despite wide success, effective distillation requires careful choices about teacher quality, distilled signals, sample selection, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and low-frequency behaviors.
