papers_seen.author: Foster
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation has emerged as a broad set of techniques to compress large or ensemble models into smaller, faster, or more deployable models while preserving performance. Research spans logits-based distillation, feature and representation matching, intermediate-layer alignment, adversarial and self-supervised schemes, curriculum and online protocols, and task-adaptive or privacy-preserving variants. Practical work demonstrates successful applications across NLP (including compressing BERT), vision, graph learning, retrieval, object detection, and large-scale distributed training, with ongoing research focused on teacher design, data augmentation, and robustness under limited or heterogeneous data.

papers_seen.author: Clark
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Methods, Findings, and Best Practices
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has evolved from simple teacher-to-student logit matching into a broad toolkit for compressing, adapting, and deploying deep models across vision, language, multimodal, and structured domains. Modern KD transfers soft targets, intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, or synthesized data; it operates in offline, online, multi-teacher, cross-modal, and data-constrained regimes and is frequently combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Empirical work shows distilled students can approach teacher performance while reducing compute, memory, and latency, but success depends on teacher quality, capacity matching, data/augmentation strategy, and careful design of objectives and layer mappings. This synthesis summarizes methods, empirical patterns, applications, and practical recommendations documented in the provided literature.

papers_seen.author: Fowler
papers_seen.title: SEED: Self-supervised Distillation For Visual Representation
papers_seen.abstract: This paper is concerned with self-supervised learning for small models. The problem is motivated by our empirical studies that while the widely used contrastive self-supervised learning method has shown great progress on large model training, it does not work well for small models. To address this problem, we propose a new learning paradigm, named SElf-SupErvised Distillation (SEED), where we leverage a larger network (as Teacher) to transfer its representational knowledge into a smaller architecture (as Student) in a self-supervised fashion. Instead of directly learning from unlabeled data, we train a student encoder to mimic the similarity score distribution inferred by a teacher over a set of instances. We show that SEED dramatically boosts the performance of small networks on downstream tasks. Compared with self-supervised baselines, SEED improves the top-1 accuracy from 42.2% to 67.6% on EfficientNet-B0 and from 36.3% to 68.2% on MobileNet-v3-Large on the ImageNet-1k dataset.

papers_seen.author: Lindsey
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: A Central but Context‑Aware Compression Strategy
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible family of techniques for transferring capabilities from larger teacher models into smaller, more deployable students. KD workflows include matching teacher outputs, aligning intermediate representations, attention- and relational-structure transfer, multi-teacher and online protocols, and data-free variants; they are commonly combined with pruning, quantization, and architecture search to meet latency, memory, and privacy constraints. While KD often preserves most of a teacher’s performance and enables real-world deployment, its success is strongly context-dependent: it relies on teacher quality and design, student capacity and architectural alignment, the availability or synthesis of suitable data, and explicit handling of robustness, bias, and distribution-shift failure modes. Consequently, KD should be treated as a central component of compression pipelines but not a panacea—its value is maximized when integrated with task-aware engineering and complementary compression methods.

papers_seen.author: Lopez
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as an Essential but Insufficient Toolbox for Practical Model Compression
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated approach for compressing high-capacity models into smaller, deployable students across vision, language, and multimodal tasks. KD has expanded beyond simple logits matching into representation-, relation-, and data-aware methods and is most effective when combined with architecture-aware design, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and alignment, the distillation data, and mitigation of privacy, robustness, and bias risks. For real-world deployment, KD should be used as the central component of an integrated compression pipeline tailored to task and resource constraints.

papers_seen.author: Burgess
papers_seen.title: Synthesis: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated set of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger teacher models (or ensembles) into smaller, more efficient student models so they can be deployed under latency, memory, compute, and privacy constraints. KD methods include output-level supervision, intermediate-feature and attention matching, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, online and multi-teacher protocols, and progressive or task-aware procedures. Empirical work across vision, language, retrieval, generative and multimodal tasks shows that when KD is integrated with complementary compression techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with task- and data-aware engineering, it often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance while substantially reducing resource cost. Practical success is conditional on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy. Important open challenges remain in principled selection of distillation targets, reliable transfer under data scarcity and distribution shift, avoiding propagation of teacher biases and rare-token degradation, and automated, hardware-aware co-design.

papers_seen.author: Morris
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central but Context‑Sensitive Strategy for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable method for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and communication while often retaining much of teacher performance; it admits many transfer targets (logits, features, attention maps, relational signals) and protocols (offline, online, data-free, multi‑teacher). However, KD is not universally sufficient: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability and alignment, and careful objective and pipeline design. Best practice treats KD as a core element of an integrated, task-aware compression strategy combined with complementary techniques (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware mapping) and targeted remedies for failure modes such as capacity mismatch, distribution shift, rare-token degradation, and bias transfer.

papers_seen.author: Hurst
papers_seen.title: Ranking Distillation: Learning Compact Ranking Models With High Performance for Recommender System
papers_seen.abstract: We propose a novel way to train ranking models, such as recommender systems, that are both effective and efficient. Knowledge distillation (KD) was shown to be successful in image recognition to achieve both effectiveness and efficiency. We propose a KD technique for learning to rank problems, called \emph{ranking distillation (RD)}. Specifically, we train a smaller student model to learn to rank documents/items from both the training data and the supervision of a larger teacher model. The student model achieves a similar ranking performance to that of the large teacher model, but its smaller model size makes the online inference more efficient. RD is flexible because it is orthogonal to the choices of ranking models for the teacher and student. We address the challenges of RD for ranking problems. The experiments on public data sets and state-of-the-art recommendation models showed that RD achieves its design purposes: the student model learnt with RD has a model size less than half of the teacher model while achieving a ranking performance similar to the teacher model and much better than the student model learnt without RD.

papers_seen.author: Avila
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: An Essential, Task‑Aware Toolbox — Powerful but Not a Panacea
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically essential approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across vision and language tasks. KD reliably reduces inference cost and often preserves a large fraction of teacher performance when applied with task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to handle data, privacy, and deployment constraints. However, KD has clear limits — capacity and architecture mismatch, data scarcity and distribution shift, and the risk of propagating teacher errors or bias — so it is best used as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture co-design, and explicit fairness/privacy safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Mcguire
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Context‑Dependent Component of Compression Portfolios
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) reliably reduces the deployment cost of large deep models while preserving much of their predictive and representational power. Rather than being a single recipe, KD is best treated as a flexible, task- and capacity-aware instrument that should be combined with complementary compression tools (e.g., pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with careful choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student, and how to mitigate teacher-induced failure modes for robust deployment.

papers_seen.author: Knight
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Task‑Aware Component of Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Directions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practical paradigm for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while preserving much of their performance. When treated as a configurable element of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with complementary methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search, data strategies, or privacy-preserving protocols), KD routinely yields strong empirical gains across vision, language, multimodal, and federated settings. However, KD is not a one‑size‑fits‑all remedy: its success depends on teacher quality, teacher–student alignment, the choice of distillation signals, data availability or synthesis, and explicit measures to mitigate propagated errors, distribution shift, and fairness or privacy concerns. I argue KD should be used as a task‑aware toolbox—selected and tuned to task, data, and deployment constraints—rather than as a single fixed recipe.

papers_seen.author: Bush
papers_seen.title: Multi-Label Image Classification via Knowledge Distillation from Weakly-Supervised Detection
papers_seen.abstract: Multi-label image classification is a fundamental but challenging task towards general visual understanding. Existing methods found the region-level cues (e.g., features from RoIs) can facilitate multi-label classification. Nevertheless, such methods usually require laborious object-level annotations (i.e., object labels and bounding boxes) for effective learning of the object-level visual features. In this paper, we propose a novel and efficient deep framework to boost multi-label classification by distilling knowledge from weakly-supervised detection task without bounding box annotations. Specifically, given the image-level annotations, (1) we first develop a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model, and then (2) construct an end-to-end multi-label image classification framework augmented by a knowledge distillation module that guides the classification model by the WSD model according to the class-level predictions for the whole image and the object-level visual features for object RoIs. The WSD model is the teacher model and the classification model is the student model. After this cross-task knowledge distillation, the performance of the classification model is significantly improved and the efficiency is maintained since the WSD model can be safely discarded in the test phase. Extensive experiments on two large-scale datasets (MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE) show that our framework achieves superior performances over the state-of-the-art methods on both performance and efficiency.

papers_seen.author: Bass
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation and related model-compression techniques transfer information from larger or specialized teacher models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained student models. Across modalities and tasks, researchers have developed many variants—logit transfer, feature- and attention-level matching, relational and contrastive objectives, ensemble- and teacher-aware algorithms, data-free and few-shot protocols, and meta-learned teachers—to address practical deployment constraints (latency, memory, privacy, device heterogeneity) while also pursuing robustness, fairness, and task adaptation. This synthesis summarizes dominant methods, representative applications, empirical patterns, and common failure modes that guide practical use and future research.

papers_seen.author: Pearson
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundational but Context‑Aware Toolkit for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible approach for producing compact, deployable models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD succeeds by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations through multiple signals (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational constraints) and can operate in offline, online, data‑free, and federated regimes. Its empirical strengths span vision, language, speech, multimodal, and distributed training settings. However, KD is not a standalone panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, the choice of distilled signals and data strategy, and explicit steps to mitigate transferred biases, low‑frequency failures, and distribution shift. The most reliable compression outcomes treat KD as the practical core of a task‑aware pipeline that integrates representation matching, data and curriculum strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, or architecture-aware design.

papers_seen.author: Matthews
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Provided Studies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted family of techniques for compressing large neural models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. A wide variety of distillation targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or relational maps), protocols (offline teacher→student, online/mutual, self-distillation, data-free), and integrations with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search) have been developed. Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and can enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints, while remaining sensitive to teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and distributional mismatch.

papers_seen.author: Barnes
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Methods in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques have become central to making large deep models practical for deployment. Research has explored diverse teacher-student architectures, alternatives to relying on original training data, adaptations to heterogeneous devices and federated settings, methods that transfer intermediate representations (features, relations, attention), adversarial and ensemble strategies, and task- or domain-specific compression. Empirical work across NLP, vision, reinforcement learning, recommendation, graph and 3D detection demonstrates that careful design of the distillation objective, choice of teacher(s), and selection of data (real, synthetic, or none) strongly affect student performance and efficiency. Remaining challenges include handling data heterogeneity, preserving low-frequency or minority information, and designing teacher models that are optimal for transfer. This review synthesizes findings across these directions and highlights practical approaches and open problems.

papers_seen.author: Morton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Task-Aware Tool for Model Compression: Strengths, Limits, and Practical Prescriptions
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a practical, flexible paradigm for transferring behavior and internal representations from large teacher models into smaller student models so they can be deployed under compute, memory, latency, or privacy constraints. When designed with task-aware objectives, careful teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture-aware search), distillation routinely yields substantial efficiency gains while retaining much of teacher performance. However, distillation is not a universal solution: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability, and the distillation signals chosen; it can propagate teacher artifacts and struggles with optimization gaps, capacity mismatch, and low-frequency behavior. Addressing these limits requires joint teacher–student design, confidence- or curriculum-aware sample selection, data-free or privacy-aware synthesis when data are unavailable, and incorporation into broader compression pipelines tailored to deployment constraints.

papers_seen.author: Drake
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Dependent Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has matured into a versatile, empirically proven approach for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students across modalities and tasks. KD enables substantial trade-offs among accuracy, latency, memory, and privacy when paired with careful choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, and how to handle data constraints. However, KD is not a universal cure: its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity, data availability or synthesis, and mitigation of propagated errors or bias. Best practice treats KD as a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline combined with pruning, quantization, architecture search, and task-aware training protocols.

papers_seen.author: Key
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) encompasses a family of techniques for transferring predictive behavior and internal representations from larger, often ensemble, teacher models into smaller, more efficient student models. Across modalities and tasks, KD methods operate at the logit level, at intermediate representation and attention levels, and via relational or contrastive objectives; they are routinely combined with complementary compression tools (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and with data strategies ranging from augmentation to data-free synthesis. Empirically, well-designed distillation pipelines can produce compact models that recover a large fraction of teacher performance, enabling deployment under latency, memory, privacy and device constraints. Success depends on choices about what and how to transfer, the quality and alignment of teacher and student, and the availability or synthesis of suitable data; important open problems remain around distribution shift, bias/fairness transfer, low-frequency behavior, and principled theoretical understanding.

papers_seen.author: Rios
papers_seen.title: Improving Neural Topic Models using Knowledge Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: Topic models are often used to identify human-interpretable topics to help make sense of large document collections. We use knowledge distillation to combine the best attributes of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. Our modular method can be straightforwardly applied with any neural topic model to improve topic quality, which we demonstrate using two models having disparate architectures, obtaining state-of-the-art topic coherence. We show that our adaptable framework not only improves performance in the aggregate over all estimated topics, as is commonly reported, but also in head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

papers_seen.author: Moore
papers_seen.title: What We Know About Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile, empirically validated family of techniques for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students while retaining much of teacher performance. KD encompasses logit/soft-target transfer, intermediate-feature and relational objectives, multi- and self-distillation, online and data-free variants, and combinations with pruning, quantization, and architecture search. Its practical strengths include enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, improving generalization and some robustness properties, and serving as a core component of compression pipelines when used with task-aware design choices. At the same time, KD exhibits clear failure modes—teacher–student mismatch, bias transfer, poor preservation of low-frequency behaviors, and sensitivity to data availability and domain shift—that motivate complementary methods and targeted research into robust, privacy-preserving, and automated distillation protocols.

papers_seen.author: Williams
papers_seen.title: Zero-shot Knowledge Transfer via Adversarial Belief Matching
papers_seen.abstract: Performing knowledge transfer from a large teacher network to a smaller student is a popular task in modern deep learning applications. However, due to growing dataset sizes and stricter privacy regulations, it is increasingly common not to have access to the data that was used to train the teacher. We propose a novel method which trains a student to match the predictions of its teacher without using any data or metadata. We achieve this by training an adversarial generator to search for images on which the student poorly matches the teacher, and then using them to train the student. Our resulting student closely approximates its teacher for simple datasets like SVHN, and on CIFAR10 we improve on the state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (with 100 images per class), despite using no data. Finally, we also propose a metric to quantify the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the vicinity of decision boundaries, and observe a significantly higher match between our zero-shot student and the teacher, than between a student distilled with real data and the teacher. Code available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

papers_seen.author: Chapman
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis of Recent Approaches and Findings
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) has emerged as a practical and versatile family of techniques for producing smaller, faster, or otherwise specialized models by transferring information from larger or alternative teacher models. KD variants include offline teacher-student distillation, online mutual distillation, ensemble-to-student distillation, cross-task distillation, and teacher-aware or student-aware training. Beyond the canonical logit-matching objective, modern work distills intermediate representations, relational and contrastive structures, and task-specific signals to improve accuracy, robustness, fairness, privacy, generation, and inference latency. Empirical results across computer vision, speech, machine translation, retrieval, graph learning, and routing problems show KD can both compress models without large accuracy loss and improve distilled students in multiple dimensions (robustness, fairness, generalization, and deployment cost). However, distillation is not a panacea: its effectiveness depends on teacher quality and compatibility, the choice of distilled knowledge (logits vs features vs relations), data complexity, and careful training strategies (sample selection, curriculum, annealing, or joint teacher-student learning). This synthesis summarizes methods, motivations, practical techniques, and empirical patterns observed across recent studies.

papers_seen.author: Warner
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted, task‑aware toolkit for compressing large models into smaller, deployable students by transferring predictive behavior and internal representations. Across modalities and tasks, practitioners match soft logits, intermediate features, attention maps, relational or contrastive structures, and even synthesized or privacy-aware pseudo-data to train compact students. KD is most effective when combined with complementary compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture search), curriculum and data strategies, and explicit teacher–student alignment; however, important limitations remain in distribution shift, low‑frequency phenomena, heterogeneous architectures, privacy and federated settings, and principled teacher selection. This synthesis summarizes prevailing methods, empirical patterns, practical guidance, and open challenges distilled from the supplied literature.

papers_seen.author: Morgan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Challenges, and Practical Strategies
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model-compression techniques seek to transfer knowledge from larger or more expensive models (teachers) to smaller, faster, or more interpretable students. Over the past decade these approaches have been adapted across modalities and tasks — from image classification and object detection to sequence models and large pretrained language models — and have been combined with complementary compression methods such as pruning and low-precision quantization. Empirical and theoretical work has highlighted both the practical gains of distillation (improved student generalization, reduced latency and memory, enabling deployment) and key limitations (optimization gaps, distribution mismatch, loss of certain types of information). A range of innovations — feature- and attention-based matching, layer-wise/task-aware distillation, self-distillation, data-free distillation with generative replay, teacher adaptation, and weighted/importance-aware soft labels — have been proposed to close these gaps and extend KD to settings such as domain adaptation, privacy-preserving federated learning, cross-modal transfer, and low-resource devices.

papers_seen.author: Wright
papers_seen.title: A Synthesis of Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression Techniques in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and related model compression techniques have matured into a diverse set of methods for transferring information from larger or more expensive models to smaller, faster, or otherwise constrained models. Methods span from classic logit-based distillation to feature- and representation-level matching, adversarial and projector-based strategies, module-replacement and pruning approaches, and specialized protocols for cross-modal, federated, data-free, and generative settings. Applications range across NLP (BERT compression, machine translation, non-autoregressive models), speech and paralinguistic embeddings, vision (image translation, novel-view synthesis), 3D detection, recommender systems, and graph neural networks. Research highlights include analyses that explain why distillation works, techniques that mitigate transfer of teacher errors, curricula and selection mechanisms for better sample usage, and approaches that adapt distillation to privacy- or resource-constrained environments. Together, these works map an ecosystem of practical techniques and open challenges for deploying compact, high-performing models in real-world systems.

papers_seen.author: Dalton
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Configurable Tool for Practical Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature, flexible approach that reliably reduces model size and inference cost while preserving much of teacher performance across vision, language, speech, and multimodal tasks. KD works via multiple transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention, relational signals) and training protocols (offline, online, multi‑teacher, adversarial, data‑free). Its practical value comes from being a configurable component of an integrated compression pipeline—combined with pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies—rather than a single, automatic cure‑all. Realizing KD's benefits requires careful choices about teacher selection, student capacity and architecture, distilled signals, training data, and safeguards for robustness, fairness, and privacy.

papers_seen.author: Elliott
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: Methods, Evidence, and Practical Guidance
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, flexible toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models into compact students. Across vision, language, multimodal, generative, and recommender systems, KD methods have been developed to match outputs (soft targets), internal representations (features and attention), relational or contrastive signals, and task-specific rank or ordering information. Practical success depends on choices about what to transfer, teacher and student design, data availability (including data-free strategies), and integration with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, and architecture search). Trade-offs include capacity mismatch, propagation of teacher errors or biases, degraded performance on low-frequency phenomena, and optimization challenges; many works propose curricula, student-friendly teacher training, or multi-teacher and online protocols to mitigate these issues. The field has matured into a central engineering primitive for deployment, while continuing to pursue principled transfer objectives, privacy-aware distillation, and robust domain- and architecture-aware pipelines.

papers_seen.author: Kane
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation in Deep Learning and NLP: Essential, Powerful, but Context‑Aware
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and mature family of techniques that enables compact models to inherit much of the performance and functionality of larger teachers, making it a central tool for deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. KD has been extended far beyond simple logits matching to include intermediate-feature and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, multi- and self-distillation, and data-free or privacy-aware protocols. While KD routinely yields major efficiency gains and often recovers most teacher performance, reliable deployment requires task- and data-aware design choices and complementary compression methods; KD alone is not a universal remedy.

papers_seen.author: Baker
papers_seen.title: Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers with Distillation
papers_seen.abstract: In this paper, we study the problem of unifying knowledge from a set of classifiers with different architectures and target classes into a single classifier, given only a generic set of unlabelled data. We call this problem Unifying Heterogeneous Classifiers (UHC). This problem is motivated by scenarios where data is collected from multiple sources, but the sources cannot share their data, e.g., due to privacy concerns, and only privately trained models can be shared. In addition, each source may not be able to gather data to train all classes due to data availability at each source, and may not be able to train the same classification model due to different computational resources. To tackle this problem, we propose a generalisation of knowledge distillation to merge HCs. We derive a probabilistic relation between the outputs of HCs and the probability over all classes. Based on this relation, we propose two classes of methods based on cross-entropy minimisation and matrix factorisation, which allow us to estimate soft labels over all classes from unlabelled samples and use them in lieu of ground truth labels to train a unified classifier. Our extensive experiments on ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets show that our approaches significantly outperform a naive extension of distillation and can achieve almost the same accuracy as classifiers that are trained in a centralised, supervised manner.

papers_seen.author: Montoya
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Core, Practical, but Context-Sensitive Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a mature and widely applicable approach for producing smaller, faster, and often more deployable models by transferring information from larger or specialized models. It supports a broad range of objectives beyond raw compression—improving robustness, enabling domain adaptation, supporting privacy-aware or federated workflows, and permitting deployment on constrained hardware. KD methods range from simple soft-label matching to richer transfers of intermediate representations, attention patterns, and relational or contrastive structure. While KD frequently yields strong empirical gains, its effectiveness depends on teacher quality, alignment between teacher and student, data availability and distribution, and the choice of signals and losses. When applied with attention to these constraints and combined sensibly with other compression primitives (pruning, quantization, architecture design), KD is a practical foundational technique for real-world model compression in vision, language, and multimodal systems.

papers_seen.author: Cherry
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) and complementary model-compression techniques form a practical toolbox for converting large, high-performing models into smaller, faster, and more deployable students. Methods vary by what is transferred (soft logits, intermediate features, attention or channel information, relational structures), whether real training data are available, and whether the goal is efficiency, robustness, privacy, or domain adaptation. Empirical work shows that carefully chosen distillation targets, layer-mapping strategies, teacher selection (including ensembles), and combinations with pruning or architecture-aware compression can recover much of teacher performance and enable deployment under resource, latency, or privacy constraints. Remaining challenges include handling low-frequency phenomena, distributional mismatch in data-free or federated settings, and optimization or alignment difficulties between teacher and student architectures.

papers_seen.author: Cruz
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation as a Central, Context‑Aware Core of Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile and practically effective family of techniques for transferring information from large teacher models into smaller student models. KD routinely yields large efficiency gains (reduced memory, compute, and latency) while preserving much of teacher performance when applied with task‑aware objectives, appropriate teacher–student alignment, and complementary compression methods. However, KD is not a universal remedy: its success depends on what signals are transferred, teacher quality, student capacity, data availability (including privacy or data‑free regimes), and explicit mitigation of failure modes such as bias transfer and degraded handling of rare phenomena. Treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and combined with targeted algorithmic and engineering practices, KD enables practical, deployable compression across modalities and settings.

papers_seen.author: Knight

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically validated toolkit for producing smaller, faster, and more deployable models by transferring information from larger teacher models to compact students. KD methods span output-level soft-target matching, intermediate representation and attention imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial and data-free synthesis, and online/self-distillation protocols. In practice, KD is most effective when treated as a configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline that also uses pruning, quantization, architecture design, and data strategies; its success depends on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred biases and rare-case failures.

KD supports many transfer targets and training protocols and can be combined with pruning, quantization, pretraining, and data synthesis to meet deployment constraints. However, reliable outcomes require careful teacher–student design, attention to data and privacy constraints, and targeted solutions for failure modes such as distribution shift, optimization mismatch, and preserved low-frequency behavior.

papers_seen.author: Jackson

KD delivers substantial practical benefits across modalities and tasks when applied as part of a task-aware compression pipeline, but it is not a universal solution: its success depends on choices of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability or synthesis, and explicit mitigation of transferred errors or biases.

papers_seen.author: Ryan
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a practical, widely used framework for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, efficient student models while retaining much of the original performance. A diverse family of distillation objectives and workflows—ranging from soft-label/logit matching to feature- and representation-level imitation, relational and contrastive objectives, adversarial schemes, multi-teacher and self-supervised variants—has been developed and adapted across modalities (vision, language, multimodal, graphs, and generative models). Empirical work shows KD often recovers a large fraction of teacher performance and enables deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints, but outcomes depend strongly on choices of distillation targets, teacher quality and friendliness, student capacity, data availability and augmentation, and task-specific adaptations. Open challenges include handling mismatches in capacity or data, preserving rare-token or long-tail behavior, and formalizing best practices for combining KD with complementary compression techniques.

However, KD is not a plug-and-play cure: its success depends on teacher quality, the choice of transfer signals, data availability (or synthetic data methods), and explicit measures to mitigate bias, low-frequency degradation, and distribution shift. Accordingly, KD should be used as a configurable toolkit combined with task-aware design, auxiliary compression methods, and deployment-aware safeguards.

papers_seen.author: Flynn

KD reliably reduces latency, memory, and compute requirements while often preserving much of a teacher model’s performance, but its success is conditional: on teacher quality, student capacity and architecture, data availability, and careful choice of what and how to transfer. As a result, KD should be treated as a primary engineering primitive for compression that must be combined with task- and deployment-aware design, complementary compression techniques, and safeguards for robustness, privacy, and fairness. Future progress requires better theoretical understanding of transferable signals, automated teacher–student alignment, and methods that address privacy, distribution shift, and low-frequency behavior.

Across modalities and tasks—including classification, generation, retrieval, speech, and sequence prediction—distillation has been adapted to transfer ensemble knowledge, reduce computation and storage, improve generalization and fairness, enable private or federated deployment, and inject specialized inductive biases. While effective, distillation requires careful design choices (teacher quality, which examples to transfer, whether to use intermediate-layer alignment, robustness and privacy mechanisms) to avoid failure modes. This work argues that KD should be treated not just as a compression trick but as a unifying framework for controlled transfer of behaviors, and outlines empirical and theoretical findings that guide best practices for its application.

The strongest, most reliable outcomes arise when KD is treated as a configurable core of a broader, task-aware compression pipeline that combines careful teacher engineering, targeted distillation signals, data strategies, and complementary compression primitives such as pruning, quantization, and architecture adaptation.

Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, propagation of teacher errors and biases, data scarcity or privacy constraints, and instability in optimization; practical remedies emphasize task-aware signal selection, learned teacher adaptation, layer mapping strategies, and data-synthesis or privacy-preserving protocols. This review synthesizes empirical patterns, common mechanisms, practical recommendations, and open problems for KD-driven compression in deep learning and NLP.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible, empirically effective approach for producing compact models that retain much of the performance of larger teachers. KD enables deployment on resource-constrained devices, supports privacy-aware and data-limited settings, and generalizes across modalities (vision, language, graphs, and generative models). However, KD is not a silver bullet: its success depends on the choice of distilled signals, teacher–student alignment, data availability, and complementary engineering (pruning, quantization, architecture search, and training pipelines). Reliable, high-quality compression therefore treats distillation as a core technique within a broader, task-aware compression strategy rather than as a standalone solution.

papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a versatile set of techniques for transferring predictive and representational information from larger teacher models to smaller student models to meet deployment constraints such as latency, memory, and privacy. KD has been adapted to diverse transfer targets (soft logits, intermediate features, attention and relational maps), multi-teacher schemes, data-free or few-shot regimes, and domain- or task-adaptive pipelines. When combined with complementary compression methods (pruning, quantization, architecture search) and careful teacher–student design, KD routinely yields large reductions in model size and runtime while preserving most of the teacher's performance. However, distillation is not automatic: practitioner attention is needed to address teacher selection, data availability and distribution shift, capacity mismatch, low-frequency behavior, and risk of transferring biases or teacher artifacts.

papers_seen.author: Oliver
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation: A Core, Configurable, but Conditional Tool for Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly useful paradigm for compressing large models and transferring their capabilities to smaller, deployable students. KD enables substantial reductions in latency, memory, and compute while often preserving much of teacher performance, and its toolkit spans logits, intermediate features, attention and relational objectives, data-free synthesis, and online or multi-teacher schemes. However, KD is not a turnkey solution: reliable deployment requires task-aware choices about what to transfer, how to align teacher and student, how to source or synthesize data, and how to combine distillation with pruning, quantization, and architecture-aware design. When treated as the configurable core of an integrated compression pipeline and validated against distribution shift, capacity limits, and ethical concerns, KD delivers the best tradeoffs between efficiency and fidelity.

papers_seen.author: Gill
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation and Model Compression in Deep Learning and NLP: A Synthesis
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a flexible family of techniques for compressing large or ensemble teacher models into smaller, faster students by transferring predictive behavior and internal structure. Across vision, language, speech, graph, and optimization problems, a consistent empirical story has emerged: carefully designed distillation objectives and workflows can recover a large fraction of teacher performance while enabling deployment under latency, memory, and privacy constraints. Practical success depends on choices about what signals to transfer, how to align teacher and student architectures, the availability and composition of transfer data, and the use of complementary compression tools such as pruning, quantization, or architecture search. Remaining challenges include teacher–student mismatch, data scarcity or privacy, distribution shift, and preserving rare or long-tail phenomena.

papers_seen.author: White
papers_seen.title: Distilling portable Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation
papers_seen.abstract: Despite Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been widely used in various image-to-image translation tasks, they can be hardly applied on mobile devices due to their heavy computation and storage cost. Traditional network compression methods focus on visually recognition tasks, but never deal with generation tasks. Inspired by knowledge distillation, a student generator of fewer parameters is trained by inheriting the low-level and high-level information from the original heavy teacher generator. To promote the capability of student generator, we include a student discriminator to measure the distances between real images, and images generated by student and teacher generators. An adversarial learning process is therefore established to optimize student generator and student discriminator. Qualitative and quantitative analysis by conducting experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method can learn portable generative models with strong performance.

papers_seen.author: Lawrence
papers_seen.title: Distilling Knowledge From a Deep Pose Regressor Network
papers_seen.abstract: This paper presents a novel method to distill knowledge from a deep pose regressor network for efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Standard distillation relies on "dark knowledge" for successful knowledge transfer. As this knowledge is not available in pose regression and the teacher prediction is not always accurate, we propose to emphasize the knowledge transfer only when we trust the teacher. We achieve this by using teacher loss as a confidence score which places variable relative importance on the teacher prediction. We inject this confidence score to the main training task via Attentive Imitation Loss (AIL) and when learning the intermediate representation of the teacher through Attentive Hint Training (AHT) approach. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work which successfully distill the knowledge from a deep pose regression network. Our evaluation on the KITTI and Malaga dataset shows that we can keep the student prediction close to the teacher with up to 92.95% parameter reduction and 2.12x faster in computation time.

papers_seen.author: Miller
papers_seen.title: Knowledge Distillation for Improved Accuracy in Spoken Question Answering
papers_seen.abstract: Spoken question answering (SQA) is a challenging task that requires the machine to fully understand the complex spoken documents. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) plays a significant role in the development of QA systems. However, the recent work shows that ASR systems generate highly noisy transcripts, which critically limit the capability of machine comprehension on the SQA task. To address the issue, we present a novel distillation framework. Specifically, we devise a training strategy to perform knowledge distillation (KD) from spoken documents and written counterparts. Our work makes a step towards distilling knowledge from the language model as a supervision signal to lead to better student accuracy by reducing the misalignment between automatic and manual transcriptions. Experiments demonstrate that our approach outperforms several state-of-the-art language models on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset.

papers_seen.author: Ellis
papers_seen.title: On Representation Knowledge Distillation for Graph Neural Networks
papers_seen.abstract: Knowledge distillation is a learning paradigm for boosting resource-efficient graph neural networks (GNNs) using more expressive yet cumbersome teacher models. Past work on distillation for GNNs proposed the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which matches local structural relationships defined over edges across the student and teacher's node embeddings. This paper studies whether preserving the global topology of how the teacher embeds graph data can be a more effective distillation objective for GNNs, as real-world graphs often contain latent interactions and noisy edges. We propose Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD), which uses contrastive learning to implicitly preserve global topology by aligning the student node embeddings to those of the teacher in a shared representation space. Additionally, we introduce an expanded set of benchmarks on large-scale real-world datasets where the performance gap between teacher and student GNNs is non-negligible. Experiments across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures show that G-CRD consistently boosts the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, outperforming LSP (and a global structure preserving variant of LSP) as well as baselines from 2D computer vision. An analysis of the representational similarity among teacher and student embedding spaces reveals that G-CRD balances preserving local and global relationships, while structure preserving approaches are best at preserving one or the other. Our code is available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns
